steps.overview: This step teaches you to pick a business process worth automating and break it into steps before you write any agent code. You learn when a fixed workflow beats an agent, which steps need an LLM (classify, extract, draft, decide) and which stay plain code, and where a human must approve. Every later step in this path depends on this map: the LangGraph graph, the human-in-the-loop interrupts, the cron schedule and the LangSmith evaluations.
objectives: Distinguish a workflow (fixed steps in code) from an agent (the model chooses the steps and tools) and justify which one a process needs.
Decompose a real process such as invoice handling or support email triage into ordered steps, tagging each as plain code or LLM.
Classify each LLM step as classify, extract, draft or decide, and define its input, output and success check.
Estimate automation value using time saved, error rate and volume before building.
Mark the steps where a human must stay in the loop and state the approve/edit/reject decision required.

concepts.explanation: A process where you, the developer, fix the steps and their order in code; an LLM may be called inside some steps. In LangGraph this is a StateGraph with fixed edges and conditional edges you write yourself. Workflows are predictable, cheap to test and the right default for most business processes.

A loop where the model decides which tool to call next and when to stop. In LangChain v1 you build it with create_agent(model, tools, system_prompt=...), which returns a compiled LangGraph graph. Use an agent only when the steps genuinely vary per case and cannot be listed in advance.

A step with deterministic logic: fetching email, parsing a PDF to text, validating a GSTIN format, matching an invoice number against a purchase order in a database, summing totals, sending a notification. If a rule or a lookup can do it, keep it in code. Code is faster, free per call, testable with unit tests and never hallucinates.

concepts.term: LLM step types: classify, extract, draft, decide
concepts.explanation: Classify sorts input into a fixed label set (for example billing, technical or refund). Extract pulls structured fields from messy text into a schema (vendor, amount, due date). Draft writes free text for a human or customer. Decide picks an action under judgment. Decide is the riskiest type and usually needs a human check.

Each LLM step should return a defined schema, for example a Pydantic model, not free prose. Then the next plain-code step can validate it, for example by checking that the amount is a positive number and the label is in the allowed list. Validation failures route to a human or a retry instead of passing silently.

A point where execution pauses until a person approves, edits or rejects. In LangGraph you use interrupt(payload) in a node and resume with Command(resume=value) on the same thread_id. For agents you use HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={...}). Place HITL before irreversible or external actions such as payments, customer emails and record deletion.

Time saved is minutes per item multiplied by volume. Error rate is the share of items handled wrongly, before and after automation. Volume is items per day or month. High volume, repetitive, rule-heavy processes with measurable outcomes give the best return, and these metrics later become your LangSmith evaluation targets.

Decide how the process starts. It can be event-driven (a new email or an uploaded invoice) or scheduled. Scheduled runs use Agent Server cron jobs via POST /runs/crons, which run in UTC unless you give an IANA timezone such as Asia/Kolkata. Recording the trigger in your map now keeps the deployment step simple.

keyFacts: Default to a workflow; move to an agent only when the order of steps cannot be known in advance.
create_agent from langchain.agents returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so agents and workflows run on the same runtime.
The four LLM step types to tag on your map are classify, extract, draft and decide.
Rule of thumb: if a regex, lookup, SQL query or arithmetic can do it, it stays plain code.
Put a human before any irreversible or outward-facing action: payments, sending email, changing records.
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware supports the allowed_decisions approve, edit and reject for each tool you list in interrupt_on.
interrupt() and resume need a checkpointer and the same thread_id; on resume the paused node re-runs from its start.
Value estimate = (manual minutes per item − remaining review minutes) × monthly volume, with error rate tracked before and after.
Cron schedules in Agent Server are UTC unless you set a timezone such as Asia/Kolkata.

example.caption: Worked process map: invoice handling (Code = plain code, LLM = model step, HITL = human)
example.code:
Trigger: new email with PDF in accounts@ inbox (event-driven)
1. Fetch email + attachment            Code  (mail API)
2. PDF -> text                         Code  (parser; OCR if scanned)
3. Is this an invoice?                 LLM classify -> {invoice, receipt, other}
4. Extract vendor, GSTIN, inv_no,
   amount, due_date, PO number         LLM extract -> Pydantic schema
5. Validate fields (GSTIN format,
   amount > 0, date parse)             Code  (fail -> human queue)
6. Match PO + vendor in ERP DB         Code  (SQL lookup, 3-way match)
7. Mismatch reason summary             LLM draft (only if step 6 fails)
8. Approve payment?                    HITL  approve / edit / reject
9. Post to ERP, notify vendor          Code  (after approval only)

Value estimate
Volume: 1,200 invoices/month
Manual: 8 min each = 160 h/month
After: 1.5 min review each = 30 h/month
Time saved: ~130 h/month
Error rate target: data-entry errors 4% -> <1% (measure on 100 sampled invoices)

Why code for 5, 6, 9: deterministic, auditable, zero hallucination risk.
Why HITL at 8: money leaves the company; irreversible.

pitfalls: Building an agent for a process with fixed steps. It adds cost, latency and unpredictability, and interviewers expect you to justify a workflow first.
Using an LLM for deterministic checks such as GSTIN format, totals or PO matching. These belong in code.
Letting an LLM 'decide' step take an external action with no human approval, for example sending a refund email automatically.
Skipping baseline metrics. Without manual time and error rate you cannot prove value or set evaluation thresholds later.
Having LLM steps return free text. Without a schema and a validation step, bad extractions flow silently into the ERP.
Placing HITL before side effects inside the same node. On resume the node re-runs from its start, so earlier side effects run twice. Put side effects after the interrupt or in a separate node.

workflow.title: How to map a process for automation

steps.label: Pick a high-volume process
steps.detail: Choose a repetitive process with clear inputs and outcomes, such as invoice handling or support email triage.

steps.label: Record the baseline
steps.detail: Measure monthly volume, manual minutes per item and the current error rate.

steps.label: List every step in order
steps.detail: Write each action from the trigger to the final outcome, including exceptions.

steps.label: Tag code or LLM
steps.detail: Mark each step as plain code, or as an LLM step of type classify, extract, draft or decide.

steps.label: Define schemas and checks
steps.detail: Give every LLM step a structured output and a following code step that validates it.

steps.label: Mark human checkpoints
steps.detail: Add approve, edit or reject points before irreversible or customer-facing actions.

steps.label: Choose workflow or agent
steps.detail: Use a fixed StateGraph workflow unless the step order truly varies per case.

project.title: invoice-triage-map
project.summary: This project maps an Indian GST invoice-handling process into fixed workflow steps. It marks each step as plain code or an LLM step (classify, extract, draft), keeps a human in the loop for risky invoices and measures the value. process_map.yaml is the design, plain_steps.py holds the deterministic rules, llm_steps.py holds the structured-output LLM steps, pipeline.py runs the workflow with a human review gate, and metrics.py turns the run log into time-saved and error-rate numbers.

files.code:
# invoice-triage-map (Step 1: Choose what to automate)

Goal: map one real process (vendor invoice handling) into steps.
Then mark which steps need an LLM and which stay plain code.

## Workflow, not agent
The steps are fixed and their order never changes, so this is a **workflow**.
An **agent** (create_agent in later steps) lets the model choose the steps.
Use an agent only when the steps are not known in advance.

## Step map (see process_map.yaml)
| # | Step | Type | Why |
|---|------|------|-----|
| 1 | Receive email + PDF text | plain code | Trigger: event (new email) |
| 2 | Is this an invoice? | LLM classify | Free-form documents |
| 3 | Pull fields | LLM extract | Layouts differ per vendor |
| 4 | GSTIN format, totals, duplicates | plain code | Exact rules, must be auditable |
| 5 | PO match + route | plain code (decide) | Business rule, no judgement needed |
| 6 | Approve high-value / exceptions | HUMAN | Money leaves the company |
| 7 | Query email to vendor | LLM draft | Natural language; a human sends it |

Rule of thumb: if you can write it as an `if`, keep it plain code.
Plain code is cheaper, faster, testable and gives the same answer every time.

## Structured output
Every LLM step returns a Pydantic model (`with_structured_output`).
Then plain code can validate the result instead of parsing prose.

## Value metrics
`python -m src.metrics` reports volume, auto-post rate, human-review rate,
extraction error rate (human corrections) and minutes saved.

## Files
- process_map.yaml: the design and the baseline numbers
- src/plain_steps.py: deterministic checks and routing
- src/llm_steps.py: classify / extract / draft
- src/pipeline.py: runs one invoice end to end and writes runs.jsonl
- src/metrics.py: computes value from runs.jsonl

# Design document for the invoice process. pipeline.py and metrics.py read it.
process: vendor_invoice_handling
pattern: workflow            # fixed steps; the model never picks the next step
trigger:
  type: event                # a new email in invoices@ inbox (later: webhook)
  alternative: schedule      # e.g. nightly batch via Agent Server cron, Asia/Kolkata
baseline:                    # measured by watching the AP team for one week
  manual_minutes_per_invoice: 9
  invoices_per_month: 1200
  manual_error_rate: 0.04    # wrong amount / duplicate paid
thresholds:
  auto_approve_limit_inr: 50000
  classify_min_confidence: 0.8
steps:
  - id: receive
    kind: plain_code
    why: Reading an email and PDF text is I/O, not judgement.
  - id: classify
    kind: llm
    llm_type: classify
    why: Invoices, quotes and credit notes look similar; wording varies.
  - id: extract
    kind: llm
    llm_type: extract
    why: Every vendor uses a different layout.
  - id: validate
    kind: plain_code
    why: GSTIN regex, subtotal + GST = total, duplicate check are exact rules.
  - id: route
    kind: plain_code
    llm_type: decide         # a decide step that we deliberately keep as rules
    why: The routing policy is written by finance; it must be auditable.
  - id: approve
    kind: human
    why: Payments above the limit or with exceptions need accountability.
  - id: draft_query
    kind: llm
    llm_type: draft
    why: Polite vendor emails are language work; a human reviews before sending.

"""Runs the fixed workflow on one sample invoice and logs the outcome."""
import json
import time
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

from src import llm_steps, plain_steps

CONFIG = yaml.safe_load(Path("process_map.yaml").read_text())
LIMIT = CONFIG["thresholds"]["auto_approve_limit_inr"]
MIN_CONF = CONFIG["thresholds"]["classify_min_confidence"]

SAMPLE = """TAX INVOICE  Sharma Traders, Pune  GSTIN: 27ABCDE1234F1Z5
Invoice No: ST/2026/0412   PO Ref: PO-1001
200 x Cartons @ 250.00   Subtotal: 50,000.00
CGST 9%: 4,500.00  SGST 9%: 4,500.00   Grand Total: 59,000.00"""


def human_review(fields, problems, po_status) -> dict:
    """HITL gate. In later steps this becomes interrupt() or HumanInTheLoopMiddleware."""
    print("\n--- HUMAN REVIEW ---")
    print(fields.model_dump_json(indent=2), "\nproblems:", problems, "po:", po_status)
    if problems:
        email = llm_steps.draft_query(fields, problems)
        print(f"\nDraft to vendor: {email.subject}\n{email.body}")
    decision = input("approve / reject: ").strip().lower() or "reject"
    fixed = input("Were any extracted fields wrong? (y/n): ").strip().lower() == "y"
    return {"decision": decision, "extraction_error": fixed}


def run(text: str) -> dict:
    start = time.perf_counter()
    doc = llm_steps.classify(text)                       # LLM: classify
    if doc.label != "invoice" or doc.confidence < MIN_CONF:
        return {"route": "not_invoice", "seconds": time.perf_counter() - start}
    fields = llm_steps.extract(text)                     # LLM: extract
    problems = plain_steps.validate(fields)              # plain code
    po_status = plain_steps.match_po(fields)             # plain code
    route = plain_steps.route(fields, problems, po_status, LIMIT)  # plain code decide
    record = {"route": route, "problems": problems, "po": po_status,
              "total": fields.total, "extraction_error": False}
    record["seconds"] = round(time.perf_counter() - start, 2)  # machine time only
    if route == "human_review":                          # human in the loop
        record.update(human_review(fields, problems, po_status))
    return record


if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = run(SAMPLE)
    print("\nResult:", result)
    with open("runs.jsonl", "a") as log:                 # feeds src/metrics.py
        log.write(json.dumps(result) + "\n")

"""Turns runs.jsonl into value metrics: volume, time saved, error rate."""
import json
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

baseline = yaml.safe_load(Path("process_map.yaml").read_text())["baseline"]
runs = [json.loads(line) for line in Path("runs.jsonl").read_text().splitlines() if line]

REVIEW_MINUTES = 3  # assumed time a person spends on a flagged invoice; measure yours

invoices = [r for r in runs if r["route"] != "not_invoice"]
volume = len(invoices)
auto = sum(r["route"] == "auto_post" for r in invoices)
review = sum(r["route"] == "human_review" for r in invoices)
rejected = sum(r["route"] == "reject" for r in invoices)
errors = sum(r.get("extraction_error", False) for r in invoices)

if volume == 0:
    raise SystemExit("No invoices in runs.jsonl yet. Run: python -m src.pipeline")

manual = baseline["manual_minutes_per_invoice"]
minutes_now = review * REVIEW_MINUTES          # auto-posted invoices cost ~0 human minutes
minutes_before = volume * manual
saved_per_invoice = (minutes_before - minutes_now) / volume
monthly_hours = saved_per_invoice * baseline["invoices_per_month"] / 60

print(f"Volume processed       : {volume}")
print(f"Auto-posted            : {auto / volume:.0%}")
print(f"Sent to human review   : {review / volume:.0%}")
print(f"Rejected (duplicates)  : {rejected}")
# Error rate = human said extraction was wrong. Compare with the manual baseline.
print(f"Extraction error rate  : {errors / volume:.0%} "
      f"(manual baseline {baseline['manual_error_rate']:.0%})")
print(f"Minutes saved/invoice  : {saved_per_invoice:.1f}")
print(f"Projected hours/month  : {monthly_hours:.0f}")

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the design foundations of the LangChain Academy courses: Introduction to LangGraph (workflows vs agents, interrupts, checkpointers), Ambient Agents with LangGraph (human review before outward actions such as sending email) and Introduction to LangSmith (baselines that later become evaluation thresholds). These are free self-paced courses with no formal proctored exam. The 'exam' is really the project review and the interviews that follow. There you will be asked to justify why a step is code, an LLM call, or a human approval, and to spot a design that is costly, unsafe or replays side effects.

compare.b: Agent (create_agent, the model picks tools in a loop)
compare.difference: In a workflow you write the order of steps. In an agent the model chooses the next step at runtime, which costs more tokens, adds latency and is harder to test.
compare.chooseA: Pick a workflow when you can draw the steps on a whiteboard before seeing the input, even if there are branches.
compare.chooseB: Pick an agent only when the number or order of tool calls depends on what the model finds, such as open-ended research or multi-system investigation.

compare.a: Conditional edge driven by an LLM classify step
compare.b: Agent deciding which tool to call
compare.difference: A classify step returns one label from a fixed set, and plain code routes on it. An agent can call any tool, any number of times.
compare.chooseA: Choose classify plus a conditional edge when the branches are known, such as billing, technical or refund.
compare.chooseB: Choose an agent when the branches cannot be listed in advance.

compare.b: interrupt() inside a custom StateGraph node
compare.difference: The middleware pauses before the listed tools inside a create_agent loop, with approve, edit and reject decisions. interrupt() is a low-level pause you place anywhere in your own graph.
compare.chooseA: Use the middleware when the risky action is a tool call made by an agent, such as send_email.
compare.chooseB: Use interrupt() when you built a fixed workflow and want an approval gate between specific nodes, for example before posting to the ERP.

compare.difference: Code gives the same answer every time and costs almost nothing. An LLM judge suits subjective quality, such as tone or helpfulness.
compare.chooseA: Use code for formats, totals, matches and lookups, such as GSTIN pattern, line sum equals invoice total, or PO number exists.
compare.chooseB: Use an LLM judge for qualities that no rule can express, such as whether a draft reply is polite and answers the question.

compare.a: Event-driven trigger (webhook, new email, file upload)
compare.difference: An event trigger runs per item as it arrives. A cron job fires on a time schedule, and each firing starts a new thread with the same input.
compare.chooseA: Choose an event trigger when each item needs a fast response, such as support triage.
compare.chooseB: Choose a cron job for batch or periodic work, such as a daily overdue-invoice digest at 9:00 Asia/Kolkata.

cues.cue: steps are always the same / fixed sequence
cues.pick: Workflow built with StateGraph
cues.why: A known order needs no model reasoning about what to do next.

cues.cue: validate format, match totals, look up vendor
cues.pick: Plain-code step
cues.why: Regex, SQL and arithmetic are deterministic, free and testable.

cues.cue: pull fields from an unstructured PDF or email
cues.pick: LLM extract step with a structured output schema, then code validation
cues.why: The model handles messy text, and the schema plus validation stop bad data reaching the ERP.

cues.cue: send, pay, refund, update record
cues.pick: Human approval before the action (HITL)
cues.why: Irreversible or outward-facing actions need review, and the approval must come before the side effect.

cues.cue: node ran twice / duplicate email after resume
cues.pick: Move the side effect after the interrupt or into a separate node
cues.why: On resume the paused node re-runs from its start.

cues.cue: prove ROI / justify the project
cues.pick: Baseline manual minutes, error rate and monthly volume
cues.why: Without a before number there is no saving to measure and no evaluation threshold.

cues.cue: resume did not work / state lost
cues.pick: Checkpointer plus the same thread_id in config
cues.why: Pause and resume read the saved checkpoint for that thread.

cues.cue: report runs at the wrong hour in India
cues.pick: Set the cron timezone to Asia/Kolkata
cues.why: Agent Server cron schedules default to UTC.

scenario.situation: A Pune distributor receives about 3,000 vendor invoices a month as PDFs by email. Today a clerk spends 6 minutes per invoice. The clerk reads the PDF, checks the GSTIN, matches the PO, confirms the totals and posts the invoice to the ERP, and about 4% of postings contain errors. The team lead proposes a create_agent with tools for every step and lets the model 'figure it out', including posting to the ERP. What is the best design?
reasoning: Check whether the step order is known: receive, extract, validate, match, approve, post. It is fixed, so an agent loop is not justified and a StateGraph workflow is the starting point.

Tag the steps. Extracting fields from the PDF is an LLM extract step with a schema. GSTIN format, PO match and total checks are plain code. Exceptions can go through an LLM classify step that routes on a fixed label.
Posting to the ERP changes records. Put a human approval (interrupt) before it, at least for exceptions or high-value invoices, in a node separate from the posting side effect.

Plan the measurement. With a baseline of 3,000 × 6 = 18,000 minutes a month, if review drops to 1 minute the saving is 3,000 × 5 = 15,000 minutes, or about 250 hours. Track the 4% error rate after go-live.
scenario.answer: Build a fixed LangGraph workflow. Use an LLM only for schema-bound extraction and exception classification, keep GSTIN, PO and totals checks in code, and gate the ERP posting behind a human approval in its own node. This is cheaper and more predictable than an agent, and the saving can be measured against the baseline.

memoryAids: CEDD = Classify, Extract, Draft, Decide: the only four reasons to call an LLM in a pipeline.
'If regex, SQL or maths can do it, the model must not.'
PAUSE before you PUSH: interrupt before Pay, Update or Send, never in the same node as the side effect.
cheatSheet: Default to a workflow. Choose an agent only when the step order is unknown before runtime.
Agents from create_agent and hand-built StateGraphs both run on LangGraph, so you can mix them later.
Route with classify plus a conditional edge, not an agent, when the branches are known.
Every LLM step returns structured output, and a code step validates it before anything downstream.
GSTIN format, totals, PO matching and duplicate checks stay in code.
A draft step produces text for a human. A decide step proposes, and a human approves any external action.
HITL goes before payments, sent emails and record changes, and its decisions are approve, edit or reject.
interrupt and resume need a checkpointer plus the same thread_id, and the paused node restarts from its start.
Keep side effects after the interrupt or in their own node to avoid running them twice.
Value = (manual minutes − review minutes) × monthly volume. Also record the error rate before and after.
Choose the trigger early: event (per item) or cron (batch). Cron defaults to UTC, so set Asia/Kolkata.
selfCheck: I can map invoice handling or email triage into steps and tag each one as code, classify, extract, draft, decide or human.
I can explain in one sentence why a fixed process should be a workflow and not an agent.
I can name three checks that must stay plain code and say why an LLM is the wrong tool for them.
I can place a human approval correctly and explain the replay risk of side effects in the same node.
I can calculate a monthly time-saved estimate from baseline numbers and say which error rate I will track.
I can choose between an event trigger and a scheduled cron trigger for a given process, including the timezone.

objective.question: A team wants to automate a process. Which situation best justifies building an agent instead of a fixed workflow?
options: The order of steps cannot be known in advance and depends on what is found along the way
The process uses an LLM in at least one step
The business wants the newest technology
The process has more than ten steps
objective.explanation: Default to a workflow. Move to an agent only when the order of steps cannot be known in advance. Many steps, or the presence of an LLM step, can still be handled by a fixed workflow.

objective.question: You are mapping an invoice-handling process. Which step should stay plain code?
options: Checking that the invoice total equals the sum of the line items
Writing a polite query to the vendor about a missing PO number
Labelling an incoming email as invoice, reminder or spam
Pulling vendor name and amount out of a free-text email body
objective.explanation: Summing line items is arithmetic, so it stays plain code: it is deterministic, cheap and testable. The other three need language understanding: extract, draft and classify.

objective.question: In support email triage, a step reads each customer email and routes it to Billing, Technical or General. Which LLM step type is this?
options: Classify
Decide
Draft
Extract
objective.explanation: Assigning one label from a fixed set is classify. Extract pulls out fields, draft writes text, and decide chooses an action against a policy or criteria.

objective.question: An LLM step extracts invoice_number, invoice_date and amount from emails. A plain-code step then matches them against the purchase order table. What is the best way to design the LLM step?
options: Return structured output against a defined schema so the next code step can validate and use the fields
Let the LLM run the SQL query against the PO table itself
Ask the LLM to return a confidence paragraph with the values
Return free-form text and parse it with string splitting
objective.explanation: Structured output against a schema gives typed fields that plain code can validate and pass on reliably. Free text is fragile to parse. Letting the LLM run SQL moves deterministic work into the model for no benefit.

objective.question: Which step in an invoice automation most clearly needs a human in the loop?
options: Releasing the payment to the vendor's bank account
Looking up the vendor in the vendor master
Extracting the GSTIN from the PDF
Classifying the email as an invoice
objective.explanation: Put a human before any irreversible or outward-facing action, such as payments, sending email or changing records. The other steps are internal and can be reversed, and their errors can be caught later.

objective.question: You configure HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with interrupt_on={"send_email": {...}}. Which allowed_decisions values can the reviewer be given for that tool?
options: yes, no, skip
approve, retry, cancel
approve, edit, reject
accept, modify, deny
objective.explanation: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware supports the allowed_decisions approve, edit and reject for each tool listed in interrupt_on. The other sets are not the documented values.

objective.question: A LangGraph node logs an audit row to the database, then calls interrupt() to ask for approval. After the reviewer resumes with Command(resume=...), the audit table has two rows for the same item. Why?
options: On resume the paused node re-runs from its start, so the code before interrupt() runs again
Command(resume=...) always starts a new thread
interrupt() does not work with a database
The checkpointer saves the state twice
objective.explanation: On resume the interrupted node re-runs from its beginning, so side effects placed before interrupt() repeat. Fix it by moving the side effect to a separate node or by making it idempotent. Resume uses the same thread; it does not create a new one.

objective.question: A developer resumes an interrupted graph but the run starts fresh instead of continuing. The graph was compiled with a checkpointer. What is the most likely cause?
options: stream_events was not used
The interrupt payload was a dictionary
The graph has conditional edges
The resume call used a different thread_id from the original run
objective.explanation: interrupt() and resume need a checkpointer and the same thread_id. With a new thread_id there is no saved checkpoint to continue from. Payload type and conditional edges do not stop a resume.

objective.question: Manual invoice handling takes 6 minutes per invoice. After automation, a human still reviews each invoice for 1 minute. Volume is 2,000 invoices per month. What is the estimated time saved per month?
options: 12,000 minutes
14,000 minutes
10,000 minutes (about 167 hours)
2,000 minutes
objective.explanation: Value estimate = (manual minutes − remaining review minutes) × monthly volume = (6 − 1) × 2,000 = 10,000 minutes. 12,000 ignores the review time that remains. Error rate should be tracked before and after alongside this figure.

objective.question: You create an Agent Server cron job with schedule "0 9 * * *" for a daily invoice summary and set no timezone. When does it fire for a team in India?
options: 2:30 PM IST, because the schedule is read as UTC
3:30 AM IST
It fails because a timezone is required
9:00 AM IST
objective.explanation: Cron schedules are interpreted in UTC unless a timezone is given. 09:00 UTC is 14:30 IST. Set timezone "Asia/Kolkata" to make it fire at 9:00 AM local time.

objective.question: Which trigger type fits a nightly job that reconciles all of the day's paid invoices against bank statements?
options: Scheduled trigger, such as an Agent Server cron job
Manual trigger from a chat UI only
A LangSmith alert
Event-driven trigger on each incoming email
objective.explanation: Work that runs at a fixed time over a batch suits a scheduled trigger, such as a cron job created via POST /runs/crons. Event-driven triggers fit per-item arrivals like new emails. Alerts are for monitoring, not for running business jobs.

objective.question: A colleague says agents need a separate runtime from workflows, so the team must choose one stack per project. What is the correct response?
options: True; workflows cannot use checkpointers
False; create_agent from langchain.agents returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so agents and workflows run on the same runtime
False; workflows run inside LangSmith only
True; agents run only on Deep Agents
objective.explanation: create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph. Agents and StateGraph workflows therefore share the same runtime, persistence and streaming. You can mix them, for example by using an agent as one node inside a fixed workflow.

objective.question: A support triage automation must send customer emails to an LLM, but compliance does not want customer email addresses reaching the model. What does this middleware configuration do?

code.code:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import PIIMiddleware

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4.1",
    tools=[lookup_ticket],
    middleware=[PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True)],
)

options: It blocks the whole request and raises an error if an email address is found
It hashes email addresses only in the model's output, after the model has seen them
It deletes traces that contain email addresses from LangSmith
It redacts email addresses in the input before the model processes it
objective.explanation: PIIMiddleware with strategy="redact" and apply_to_input=True replaces detected email addresses in the input, so the model never sees them. A blocking strategy would raise an error instead, output-only handling would still expose the data to the model, and trace retention is managed by LangSmith settings, not this middleware.

objective.question: A developer adds human approval before emails are sent. When the agent reaches send_email, nothing can be resumed later and the approval cannot be recorded. What is missing?
options: A checkpointer on create_agent and a thread_id in the invoke config
A webhook URL so the reviewer is notified
The tool must be renamed to start with 'hitl_'
A SummarizationMiddleware to shorten the conversation before the interrupt
objective.explanation: Human-in-the-loop pauses save state to a checkpointer, and resuming needs the same thread_id in config {"configurable": {"thread_id": ...}}. Summarization, webhooks and tool naming do not make a paused run resumable.

objective.question: Look at this LangGraph routing. How would you describe the design?

code.code:
def route(state):
    return state["category"]  # set by an LLM classify node

builder.add_edge(START, "classify")
builder.add_conditional_edges(
    "classify",
    route,
    {"billing": "billing_queue",
     "technical": "tech_queue",
     "unknown": "human_review"},
)

options: A workflow: the LLM only classifies, and plain code routes over a fixed set of paths
A cron job, because routing happens on a schedule
A multi-agent supervisor, because there are several queues
An agent, because an LLM is involved in choosing the next step
objective.explanation: The possible paths are fixed in code; the LLM produces a label and a plain Python function maps it to a node. That is a workflow with one LLM classify step, not an agent that picks its own steps or tools.

objective.question: An LLM classify step sometimes returns 'Billing Dept', 'billing ' or 'Payments' instead of 'billing', and the router fails. What is the best fix?
options: Use structured output with a fixed set of allowed values (for example a Literal of billing, technical, general, unknown) and send 'unknown' to human review
Add string-similarity matching in the router to guess the nearest label
Switch from a workflow to an agent so the model can choose its own queue
Increase the model temperature so it explores more labels
objective.explanation: Constraining the output to an enum via structured output makes the label machine-checkable, and an explicit 'unknown' gives a safe path for unclear emails. Higher temperature adds randomness, fuzzy matching hides errors, and an agent adds unpredictability to a simple routing task.

objective.question: A team schedules a daily invoice summary as an Agent Server cron job. A week later, auditors ask to see the previous runs' threads, but they are gone. Why?
options: on_run_completed defaults to "delete", so each new thread is removed after the run; set it to "keep"
Threads are only kept when end_time is set
The schedule is in UTC, so the threads were stored in a different region
Cron jobs reuse one thread and overwrite it each day
objective.explanation: Each firing of POST /runs/crons creates a new thread, and on_run_completed defaults to "delete". Setting "keep" retains those threads. Timezone and end_time control when the cron fires and stops, not retention.

objective.question: A team reports that its email triage automation is '96% accurate'. You find the figure came from 50 emails the developer wrote by hand. What is the main problem with this value claim?
options: The sample is not representative of real traffic, so the error rate on production emails is unknown
The figure should be reported as time saved, never as accuracy
Accuracy cannot be measured for classify steps
50 is too many examples for a reliable estimate
objective.explanation: Error rate must be measured on a representative sample of real historical items with known correct labels, and compared with the human baseline. Hand-written examples miss real-world messiness. Accuracy is a valid metric for classify steps, and it sits alongside time saved and volume.

objective.question: An invoice extraction step returns a confidence score. Reviewing every invoice is too slow, but finance will not accept unchecked errors on payments. Which design best balances value and safety?
options: Ask the LLM to approve its own extraction with a second prompt
Review a random 1% of invoices and auto-pay the rest regardless of checks
Auto-approve high-confidence invoices that also pass plain-code checks (PO match, totals), and send low-confidence or failed-check invoices to a human queue
Remove human review completely once the model's confidence is above 50%
objective.explanation: Combining deterministic validation with a confidence threshold sends only risky items to people, so review time drops while payment errors stay controlled. Model self-confidence alone is not reliable, self-approval is not independent, and random sampling ignores known risk signals.

objective.question: Which order of steps is correct for an invoice-handling workflow that posts to the ERP safely?
options: Match PO (code) → extract fields (LLM) → post to ERP (code) → human approval → validate schema (code)
Extract fields (LLM) → post to ERP (code) → human approval → validate schema (code) → match PO (code)
Human approval → extract fields (LLM) → decide approve/reject (LLM) → post to ERP (code) → validate schema (code)
Extract fields (LLM) → validate against schema (code) → match PO and totals (code) → human approval for exceptions → post to ERP (code)
objective.explanation: You must extract the data before you can validate or match it. Approval must come before the side effect, which is posting to the ERP. The other orders either post before checking or validate data that has already been used.

objective.question: A daily Agent Server cron job runs a payment-reminder agent. Each morning the agent has no memory of what it sent the day before. The team already set on_run_completed to "keep". What is the cause, and what is the fix?
options: Each firing of POST /runs/crons creates a new thread. Use POST /threads/{thread_id}/runs/crons to schedule runs on one existing thread.
Cron jobs never use checkpointers, so the agent must be redeployed with InMemorySaver
The input payload is cached, so the agent ignores state; add a random field to the input
on_run_completed must be "persist" to share memory across runs
objective.explanation: A standard cron creates a new thread on every firing, and "keep" only stops those threads from being deleted. To reuse one thread's history, schedule the cron on that thread. "persist" is not a valid value, and the Agent Server handles persistence automatically.

objective.question: Vendors sometimes email the same invoice twice. Which way of detecting duplicates is better here, and why?
options: In code, check a normalised key (vendor GSTIN + invoice number + financial year) against stored invoices
Send every invoice to a human, because duplicate detection cannot be automated
Use an agent with a search tool so it can decide how to look for duplicates
Ask the LLM whether the new invoice 'looks like' any invoice from the last 30 days
objective.explanation: Duplicate detection is a deterministic lookup, so code is exact, cheap and auditable. An LLM or agent adds cost and can miss or invent matches. Sending everything to a human throws away the value of automation.

objective.question: Before automating support email triage, which set of baseline figures should you record from the current manual process?
options: Number of LangGraph nodes and edges in the planned design
Number of support agents and their salaries only
Average handling time per email, misrouting or error rate, and monthly email volume
Model token price and context window size
objective.explanation: Time, error rate and volume prove the value of the automation and set evaluation thresholds for later. Model and graph details describe the solution, not the baseline. Headcount alone cannot show error reduction.

objective.question: Support must route urgent customer emails within 15 minutes of arrival. Which trigger is the better fit?
options: A manual trigger where an agent clicks 'run triage'
An hourly cron job that polls the inbox
An event-driven trigger: the mail provider's webhook starts a run for each new email
A nightly cron job that processes the whole inbox
objective.explanation: An event trigger starts work as soon as the email arrives, so it meets the 15-minute SLA. Nightly or hourly cron jobs batch the work and can miss the SLA. A manual trigger depends on a person.

objective.question: In LangSmith, rule A runs an online LLM-as-judge evaluator on triage runs and writes feedback key "triage_correct". Rule B triggers a webhook to alert the team about bad runs. Rule B often fires on runs that have no score yet. What is the fix?
options: Add a delay inside the webhook receiver
Make rule B's filter include eq(feedback_key, "triage_correct") so it only matches runs that have already been scored
Merge both rules into one rule with two actions
Set rule B's sampling rate to 100%
objective.explanation: Automation rules run on independent schedules, so rule B can see a run before rule A has scored it. Filtering on the evaluator's feedback key makes the webhook fire only after scoring. Sampling and delays do not guarantee the order.

objective.question: A team created an online evaluator rule last week without backfill. Now they want the past two weeks of extraction runs scored. What is true?
options: Online evaluators score old runs automatically at midnight UTC
Old runs cannot be evaluated in any way
Backfill is only offered when a rule is created, so they need a new rule with backfill, or an offline evaluate() over a dataset of those runs
Editing the existing rule and turning on backfill will score the old runs
objective.explanation: Online evaluators can be backfilled only when the rule is created. Another option is to add the runs to a dataset and run an offline experiment with evaluate(). The other options describe behaviour that does not exist.

objective.question: This cron job should send a GST filing reminder at 10:00 India time on the 18th of each month. What is wrong?
options: The timezone must be an IANA name such as "Asia/Kolkata", not an abbreviation like "IST"
assistant_id must be a thread ID
Day-of-month values above 12 are not allowed in cron
The schedule must use six fields, including seconds
objective.explanation: Timezones are given as IANA names, so use "Asia/Kolkata". Without a valid timezone the schedule is read in UTC. A standard five-field cron expression is correct here, and assistant_id identifies an assistant, not a thread.

objective.question: This multi-agent support design wraps a billing subagent as a tool. What is the mistake?

code.code:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.tools import tool
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

billing_agent = create_agent(model, tools=[lookup_invoice],
                             checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

@tool
def ask_billing(question: str) -> str:
    """Answer billing questions."""
    r = billing_agent.invoke({'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': question}]})
    return r['messages'][-1].content

main_agent = create_agent(model, tools=[ask_billing],
                          checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

options: Only the outermost graph should get a checkpointer; remove it from billing_agent
The main agent must not have a checkpointer; only subagents need one
Tools cannot call other agents
Subagents must be built with langgraph-supervisor instead
objective.explanation: In the subagents pattern only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer. langgraph-supervisor is no longer actively maintained, and wrapping worker subagents as tools is the recommended pattern.

objective.question: A support agent built with create_agent handles long email threads. After many back-and-forth messages, runs fail with context-length errors. Which built-in middleware addresses this most directly?
options: A model call limit middleware
SummarizationMiddleware(model=..., trigger=("tokens", 4000), keep=("messages", 20))
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={...})
PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True)
objective.explanation: SummarizationMiddleware condenses older history once a token trigger is reached and keeps recent messages. PII redaction and HITL do not shrink the context. A call limit only caps how many model calls are made.

objective.question: A web UI drives an approval graph with stream_events(..., version="v3"). How should the UI detect that the graph has paused for a reviewer?
options: Wait for a timeout and assume the graph is paused
Parse the last AI message for the word 'approve'
Call graph.compile() again and compare the state
Check stream.interrupted and read stream.interrupts for the payload
objective.explanation: Version v3 streaming surfaces stream.interrupted and stream.interrupts, which tell the UI that a pause happened and what the payload is. The other approaches are unreliable guesses.

objective.question: A developer wants to inspect the first checkpoint of an invoice thread. They take list(graph.get_state_history(config))[0], but it shows the final state. Why?
options: get_state_history lists checkpoints newest first, so index 0 is the latest; the first checkpoint is at the end
get_state_history only returns the current state
InMemorySaver keeps only one checkpoint
The thread_id is wrong, so a different thread is returned
objective.explanation: get_state_history returns checkpoints newest first, so the earliest one is the last item. A wrong thread_id would show unrelated data, not this thread's final state.

objective.question: A team must classify incoming expense emails into five fixed categories and extract three fields. A developer proposes create_deep_agent. Which choice is better here?
options: A supervisor built with langgraph-supervisor
A single prompt that returns free text for a human to read
A fixed workflow: a StateGraph with an LLM classify node, an LLM extract node and code validation
create_deep_agent, because it includes subagents and a filesystem
objective.explanation: The steps are fixed, so a workflow is cheaper, faster and more predictable. Deep agents are meant for long-running, open-ended tasks. langgraph-supervisor is no longer actively maintained, and free text skips validation.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between a workflow and an agent. Which should you start with, and why?
subjective.answer: A workflow has fixed steps that I write in code. The model may do work inside some steps, but the order is decided by me. In an agent, the model decides which step or tool to use next, in a loop, until it finishes. I default to a workflow. It is predictable, cheaper, easier to test and easier to explain to auditors. I only move to an agent when the order of steps cannot be known in advance, for example when an investigation depends on what each lookup returns. In LangChain v1 this is not a big technical jump. create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph, so an agent can sit as one node inside a workflow. I can also start with a workflow and later replace one branch with an agent, without changing the runtime.
keyPoints: Workflow: fixed order set in code
Agent: model chooses next step in a loop
Default to a workflow for predictability, cost and testing
Use an agent only when step order is unknown in advance
Both run on LangGraph; create_agent returns a compiled graph

subjective.question: Map an invoice-handling process into steps and mark which steps need an LLM.
subjective.answer: 1. Trigger: an email with an attachment arrives. This is event-driven and handled by plain code. 2. Classify the email as invoice, reminder, credit note or other. This is an LLM step. 3. Extract vendor name, GSTIN, invoice number, date, line items and total into a schema. This is an LLM step with structured output. 4. Validate the GSTIN format with a regex and check that the line items sum to the total. Plain code. 5. Look up the vendor in the vendor master and match the PO with SQL. Plain code. 6. Check for duplicates on invoice number plus vendor. Plain code. 7. If something does not match, draft a query to the vendor. This is an LLM step, and a human approves it before sending. 8. Post to the ERP and schedule the payment. A human approves first, because the action is irreversible. 9. Log the result. Plain code. Only three steps need an LLM; most of the pipeline is deterministic.
keyPoints: Classify and extract are LLM steps; extract uses a schema
Validation, lookups, duplicate checks and arithmetic are plain code
The vendor query is a draft step with human approval
Payment and ERP posting are gated by a human
Most steps stay plain code

subjective.question: Map a support email triage process and justify the plain-code steps.
subjective.answer: 1. Receive the email via a webhook or inbox poll. Plain code. 2. Look up the sender in the CRM to find the customer tier and any open tickets. This is plain code, because it is an exact lookup. 3. Classify the intent (billing, technical, account, spam) and the urgency. LLM step. 4. Extract the order ID, product and error message into structured fields. LLM step. 5. Apply routing rules: enterprise plus urgent goes to the L2 queue, and SLA timers start. Plain code, because these are business rules from a table. 6. Draft a reply using the knowledge base. LLM step. 7. A human agent approves, edits or rejects the draft before it is sent, because sending is outward-facing. The plain-code steps are the ones with exact answers. Using an LLM there would add cost, delay and random errors for no gain.
keyPoints: Lookups and routing rules stay plain code
Classify, extract and draft are the LLM steps
Sending a reply needs human approval
Plain code is deterministic, cheap and testable

subjective.question: What rule of thumb decides whether a step stays plain code? Give reasons.
subjective.answer: If a regex, a lookup, a SQL query or arithmetic can do it, it stays plain code. Examples are checking a PAN or GSTIN format, matching a PO number, summing line items or computing a due date. Plain code has four advantages. It is deterministic, so the same input always gives the same output. It is cheap and fast, with no token cost or model latency. It is easy to unit test and audit. It cannot hallucinate. LLM steps are for unstructured language, where rules break: reading messy emails, understanding intent, or writing replies. A good design wraps each LLM step with plain-code validation on both sides. When my checkpoint question comes up, I can point to each step and say why it is code: the answer is exact and the rule is known.
keyPoints: Regex, lookup, SQL or arithmetic means plain code
Determinism, cost, speed and testability
No hallucination risk
LLM steps only for unstructured language tasks
Validate LLM output with code

subjective.question: Describe the four LLM step types with a business example of each.
subjective.answer: Classify assigns one label from a fixed set. An example is tagging an email as invoice, complaint or spam. Extract pulls specific fields out of unstructured text into a schema. An example is reading the invoice number, amount and due date from a PDF. Draft writes new text for a person to read. An example is a reply to a customer or a query to a vendor about a missing PO. Decide chooses an action or outcome against criteria that are hard to encode as rules. An example is judging whether a refund request, written in free text, fits the policy's 'damaged on arrival' clause. Tagging each step on the process map with one of these types keeps LLM use narrow and testable. Each type can also be evaluated: accuracy for classify, field match for extract, rubric scoring for draft, and agreement with reviewers for decide.
keyPoints: Classify: label from a fixed set
Extract: fields into a schema
Draft: generated text for humans
Decide: judgement against fuzzy criteria
Each type is narrow and measurable

subjective.question: Why should LLM steps in an automation return structured output?
subjective.answer: The next step is usually plain code, and code needs predictable fields, not prose. With a schema, for example invoice_number as a string, amount as a number and currency from an enum, the output can be validated immediately. Missing or badly formatted fields are caught before they reach the ERP. Structured output also makes the step measurable. I can compare extracted fields with a labelled dataset field by field, and compute an error rate per field. For classify steps, an enum of allowed labels stops the model from inventing new categories. Structured output also makes routing simple, because a conditional edge can branch on a field value. In practice I define the schema first. I then add a code validation step, and send anything that fails validation to a human review path instead of guessing.
keyPoints: Downstream code needs typed, predictable fields
Enables validation before side effects
Makes per-field accuracy measurable
Enums limit classify labels
Validation failures route to human review

subjective.question: Where must a human stay in the loop, and how do you choose the review points?
subjective.answer: Put a human before any irreversible or outward-facing action, such as releasing payments, sending email to customers or vendors, or changing records in a system of record. I choose review points with three questions. Can the action be undone? Does it leave the company, reaching a customer, vendor or regulator? What does an error cost? I also add review when the model's output fails validation or the case falls outside known patterns, for example a new vendor or a very high amount. I keep review cheap. The human sees the extracted data and the draft side by side, and can approve, edit or reject. Over time, with an error rate measured on reviewed items, low-risk categories may move to sampled review. Payments and outbound messages usually keep a mandatory gate. Review time also goes into the value calculation.
keyPoints: Gate irreversible and outward-facing actions
Use reversibility, external reach and error cost to decide
Route validation failures and edge cases to humans
Offer approve, edit and reject
Count review minutes in the value estimate

subjective.question: Explain how human-in-the-loop pauses work in LangGraph and LangChain v1, and one pitfall to avoid.
subjective.answer: In a custom LangGraph graph, a node calls interrupt(payload) to pause. The payload, for example the draft email, is shown to the reviewer. The graph must be compiled with a checkpointer, and it must be invoked with config {"configurable": {"thread_id": ...}} so the state can be saved. To continue, I call Command(resume=value) on the same thread_id. For agents built with create_agent, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware does this for me. I list the tools in interrupt_on, for example send_email, with allowed_decisions approve, edit and reject. The pitfall is this: on resume, the paused node re-runs from its start. Any side effect placed before interrupt() in that node will run twice, such as writing a log row or calling an API. I put side effects in separate nodes after approval, or I make them idempotent. A wrong thread_id also breaks the resume.
keyPoints: interrupt(payload) pauses; resume with Command(resume=...)
Needs a checkpointer and the same thread_id
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with interrupt_on and approve, edit, reject
The node re-runs from its start on resume
Keep side effects out of the pre-interrupt code or make them idempotent

subjective.question: How do you estimate and report the value of an automation before building it?
subjective.answer: I use: value = (manual minutes per item − remaining review minutes) × monthly volume. For example, support triage takes 4 minutes manually and 1 minute with review, at 3,000 emails per month. (4 − 1) × 3,000 = 9,000 minutes, which is about 150 hours a month. Time alone is not enough, so I also measure the error rate before and after. Examples are wrong routing, wrong amounts, or duplicate payments. If the manual error rate is 3% and automation brings it to 1%, that has its own value. Volume matters too, because a process that runs 20 times a month rarely pays back the build and maintenance effort. I collect the baseline by timing a sample of real items and checking past errors, before writing any code. That makes the after-launch comparison honest.
keyPoints: Formula: (manual − review minutes) × monthly volume
Track error rate before and after
Low volume may not justify the build
Measure the baseline on real samples before building
Include remaining human review time

subjective.question: How do you choose the trigger type for an automation, and what scheduling detail often catches teams in India?
subjective.answer: I match the trigger to how the work arrives. If items arrive one by one, such as a new invoice email or a support ticket, I use an event-driven trigger: a webhook or inbox event starts a run per item. If the work is a batch at a fixed time, such as nightly reconciliation or a morning summary, I use a schedule. In Agent Server, I create a cron job with POST /runs/crons, giving a cron expression, an assistant_id and an input. Each firing creates a new thread with the same input. I can also schedule runs on one existing thread with POST /threads/{thread_id}/runs/crons. The detail that catches teams is time zones. Schedules are read as UTC unless a timezone is set. A '0 9 * * *' job without one fires at 2:30 PM IST, so I set timezone to Asia/Kolkata.
keyPoints: Event-driven for per-item arrivals
Scheduled cron for batch or time-based work
POST /runs/crons creates a new thread per firing
Cron schedules default to UTC
Set timezone Asia/Kolkata for IST

subjective.question: Interview: a manager asks you to 'build an agent that handles all our support email end to end'. How do you respond?
subjective.answer: I would first map the real process with the team: how emails arrive, how they are routed, what replies look like, and who approves what. Usually most of it has a known order: receive, look up the customer, classify, extract, route, draft, review, send. That is a workflow, not an agent. It is more predictable, cheaper and easier to test. I would tag the LLM steps, which are classify, extract and draft, and keep lookups and routing rules in plain code. Sending stays behind human approval at first. If one branch truly needs open-ended steps, such as investigating a technical issue across several tools, I would make that branch an agent with create_agent inside the workflow. I would agree value metrics up front: minutes saved per email, monthly volume, and the error rate before and after. Then we can prove it works before widening its autonomy.
keyPoints: Map the process before choosing an architecture
Default to a workflow; use an agent only for unknown-order branches
Tag the LLM steps and keep rules in code
Human approval before sending
Agree value metrics up front

subjective.question: When should a 'decide' step be done by an LLM, and when by rules? Use invoice approval as an example.
subjective.answer: If the decision can be written as clear rules on structured data, it is plain code. In invoice approval, these include: amount under ₹50,000 with a matched PO is auto-approved, above that needs a manager, and an unknown vendor is blocked. Code is exact, auditable and consistent. An LLM decide step fits when the criteria depend on reading language. Examples are judging whether an invoice description matches the services in the contract, or whether a vendor's dispute email raises a valid point. Even then, I keep the LLM as a recommender. It returns structured output with a decision, a reason and the evidence. Plain-code rules and a human gate stay around it, because approval leads to payment, which is irreversible. I measure agreement between the LLM's decision and reviewer decisions over time. That data tells me whether the step is trustworthy, and in which categories.
keyPoints: Clear rules on structured data mean plain code
Use an LLM only when criteria depend on reading language
LLM returns a structured decision with reasons
Keep a human gate before payment
Measure agreement with reviewers

subjective.question: Review this LLM step from an invoice pipeline. What is wrong with the design, and how would you split it?

code.code:
prompt = """Read this invoice. Extract the vendor, line items and amounts.
Add up the line items, compute 18% GST, check the total matches,
look up whether the PO number exists, and reply APPROVE or REJECT."""

result = llm.invoke(prompt + invoice_text)
if "APPROVE" in result.content:
    pay_invoice(invoice_text)

subjective.answer: This single prompt mixes one real LLM job with several jobs that should be plain code. Extraction from messy invoice text is a genuine LLM step. But adding line items, computing GST, comparing totals and checking that a PO exists are deterministic. Code does them exactly, cheaply and in an auditable way. An LLM can make arithmetic mistakes and cannot truly query the PO table. The approve decision is also parsed from free text, so a reply like 'I would not APPROVE' would trigger payment. I would split it into four parts. First, an LLM extract step with structured output: vendor, PO number, line items and total. Second, plain-code validation of schema, sums, GST and the PO lookup. Third, a rule-based decision: auto-approve only if every check passes and the amount is below a threshold. Fourth, human review for any exception before pay_invoice runs.
keyPoints: Only extraction needs the LLM
Arithmetic, lookups and matching stay plain code
Structured output instead of parsing free text
Payment is gated by rules plus human review for exceptions

subjective.question: A company wants to automate employee leave requests that arrive as free-text emails. Map the process into steps, mark the LLM steps, and say where a human stays in the loop.
subjective.answer: First, the trigger is event-driven: a new email arrives in the HR inbox. Step 1, plain code: fetch the email and look up the sender in the HR system. Step 2, LLM extract: pull out leave type, start date, end date and reason, using structured output with ISO dates. Step 3, plain code: validate the dates, compute working days with the holiday calendar, and check the leave balance. Step 4, decide, by rules: if the balance is sufficient and the leave is short, mark it for manager approval. Otherwise flag it. Step 5, human in the loop: the manager approves or rejects. This stays human because it is a people decision with accountability. Step 6, LLM draft: write a polite reply to the employee. Step 7, plain code: update the HR system and send the reply. Only extract and draft need an LLM. Everything about dates, balances and records stays in code because it must be exact.
keyPoints: Event-driven trigger on new email
LLM only for extract and draft
Dates, balances and record updates in plain code
Manager approval stays human for accountability

subjective.question: Before building, how would you check that an LLM classify or extract step is good enough for production?
subjective.answer: I would build a small test set from real historical items, not invented ones. For example, 100 to 200 past support emails or invoices, including messy and edge cases, each labelled with the correct output by people who do the work today. That also gives me the human baseline error rate. I would run the LLM step with structured output over this set and measure per-field accuracy for extraction, or per-class accuracy for classification. I would read the failures to see whether they are prompt problems, data problems or genuinely ambiguous cases that should go to a human. In LangSmith I can store this as a dataset and run evaluate() with code evaluators for exact field matches. That gives repeatable experiments when I change the prompt or model. The step is ready when its error rate on risky fields is acceptable, and when the low-confidence or 'unknown' outputs route safely to review.
keyPoints: Use real historical items with human labels
Measure per-field or per-class accuracy against a human baseline
Analyse failure types
Repeatable experiments via LangSmith datasets and evaluate()

subjective.question: An LLM extract step occasionally returns output that fails validation, for example a missing amount or an invalid date. How should the automation handle this?
subjective.answer: Treat validation failure as a normal, expected path, not a crash. First, the LLM step uses structured output, so plain code can check required fields, types, formats and business rules such as amount greater than zero and a date that is not in the future. If a check fails, I may allow one bounded retry. The retry can include the validation error in the prompt, or fall back to another model; LangChain v1 has built-in middleware for model fallback and tool retry. Retries must be capped so costs and latency stay predictable. If the item still fails, it goes to a human review queue with the original document, the partial extraction and the specific error, so the reviewer can fix it quickly. Nothing downstream, such as payments or replies, runs on unvalidated data. I would also track the failure rate as a metric, because a rising rate signals drift in input formats or a prompt problem.
keyPoints: Validate structured output in plain code
Bounded retry or model fallback
Escalate to a human with context
Never run downstream actions on invalid data; track the failure rate

subjective.question: Interview: your support triage workflow works well. The business now wants it to also resolve order-status and refund requests. When would you introduce an agent, and how would you keep it safe?
subjective.answer: I would keep the workflow as the outer structure and add an agent only where the steps genuinely vary. Order-status questions may need different lookups: order, shipment, payment. The model choosing which tools to call is useful there, so a create_agent with read-only tools for that branch is reasonable. Classification and routing stay as fixed workflow steps. Refunds move money, so the agent can propose a refund, but the refund tool goes behind HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with approve, edit and reject decisions, plus a checkpointer so the pause can be resumed on the same thread. Plain-code guardrails still apply, such as refund amount not exceeding the order value. I would also use model call limits so the agent cannot loop forever, and trace everything in LangSmith to measure resolution rate and errors. The agent is a node inside the workflow, not a replacement for it.
keyPoints: Agent only for the branch where steps vary
Read-only tools are low risk; money-moving tools need HITL
Checkpointer and thread_id for resumable approvals
Call limits, code guardrails and LangSmith tracing

subjective.question: Explain what this Agent Server cron job does and when it fires for an India-based finance team.

code.code:
{
  "assistant_id": "invoice_summary",
  "schedule": "30 3 * * 1-5",
  "input": {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise yesterday's unpaid invoices"}]},
  "on_run_completed": "keep",
  "end_time": "2026-12-31T00:00:00Z",
  "webhook": "https://erp.example.in/hooks/summary-done"
}

subjective.answer: This is posted to /runs/crons. It creates a scheduled run of the invoice_summary assistant. The schedule '30 3 * * 1-5' means 03:30, Monday to Friday. No timezone is given, so it is read as UTC, and 03:30 UTC is 09:00 IST. The team therefore gets the summary at 9 am India time on weekdays. Each firing creates a new thread and sends the same input message. Because on_run_completed is 'keep', those threads are kept rather than deleted (the default), so past summaries can be audited. end_time stops the cron at the end of 2026. The webhook URL is called when each run finishes, so the ERP or a notifier can pick up the result. An alternative is to write '0 9 * * 1-5' and set the IANA timezone 'Asia/Kolkata', which is clearer to read. The schedule fits a time-based trigger because the work is a batch summary, not a reaction to one event.
keyPoints: Cron in UTC by default: 03:30 UTC = 09:00 IST
Each firing creates a new thread with the same input
on_run_completed 'keep' retains threads; default is 'delete'
end_time stops the cron; webhook is called on completion

subjective.question: Your manager asks you to prioritise between automating invoice handling and support email triage. How do you decide using value metrics?
subjective.answer: I would estimate value for both with the same simple model. Value is roughly monthly volume multiplied by the minutes saved per item, after subtracting the human review time that remains. Then I adjust for error cost and risk. For each process I would collect the current volume, the handling time per item and the current human error rate from real data. Invoices may have lower volume, but errors cost real money and need more review, so the net time saved is smaller and the risk is higher. Triage may have high volume, quick wins from classification, and a low cost per error, because a misrouted email can be rerouted. I would also consider feasibility: data access, whether historical labels exist for testing, and how many steps stay plain code. Usually I start with the higher-volume, lower-risk process to prove value quickly. I report the expected hours saved, the target error rate and the review load, then measure the same metrics after launch.
keyPoints: Value = volume x net minutes saved after review
Factor in error cost and risk, not just time
Use real baseline data for volume, time and error rate
Prefer high-volume, low-risk first; measure after launch

subjective.question: Case study: a manufacturer wants to automate purchase-order approvals. POs arrive as PDFs by email. POs above ₹5 lakh need CFO approval, which can take two days. Every decision needs an audit trail. Design the automation.
subjective.answer: I would build a workflow, not an agent, because the steps are fixed. An email event trigger starts a run. Plain code extracts the PDF text, and an LLM extract step returns a schema with vendor, GSTIN, line items and total. Code then validates the schema, recomputes the total, checks the GSTIN format and matches the vendor master. Routing by amount is a code rule: at or below ₹5 lakh it goes to the department head, above it goes to the CFO. The approval node calls interrupt() with a summary payload. I compile with a checkpointer, or deploy on Agent Server, which persists automatically, and I use the PO number as the thread_id, so a resume two days later continues the same thread with Command(resume=...). Posting to the ERP happens in a separate node after approval, so it never runs twice. LangSmith traces give the audit trail, and the checkpoints show who decided what.
keyPoints: Workflow because the steps are fixed; event trigger
LLM only for extraction, with a schema; code for totals, GSTIN and threshold routing
interrupt() with a durable checkpointer and a stable thread_id for multi-day waits
Side effects in a separate node after approval
Audit trail from traces and checkpoints

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: a team replaced its triage workflow with a create_agent agent. Accuracy is the same, but cost per email doubled and latency tripled. Explain the likely cause and what you would do.
subjective.answer: The process has fixed steps: classify, extract, route. In a workflow each step is one model call with a clear schema. The agent now runs a loop. The model reasons about which tool to call, calls it, reads the result and decides again, so one email can take four or five model calls with growing context. That explains the higher cost and latency, and nothing in the task needs those decisions. I would open LangSmith traces to confirm the number of model calls and tokens per run. Then I would move back to a StateGraph workflow with one classify call and one extract call using structured output, plus code routing. If part of the work is truly open-ended, I would keep a small agent only for that branch, with a model call limit middleware. Then I would re-run the same evaluation dataset to show that accuracy holds at lower cost.
keyPoints: The agent loop adds extra model calls and context for fixed steps
Confirm with LangSmith traces: calls and tokens per run
Return to a workflow with structured LLM steps and code routing
Limit any remaining agent with a model call limit
Re-evaluate on the same dataset to prove parity

subjective.question: Compare polling the support inbox with a cron job every 5 minutes against an event-driven webhook from the mail provider. Which is better for triage, and when would you still use cron?
subjective.answer: For triage, the event-driven webhook is usually better. Each email starts its own run as soon as it arrives, so latency is low and there are no empty runs. Each email also gets its own thread and trace, which makes review and evaluation simple. Polling every 5 minutes adds up to 5 minutes of delay, wastes runs when the inbox is empty, and needs dedupe logic so that an email is not processed twice across polls. I would still use cron for work that is truly batch: a nightly reconciliation, a 9 a.m. summary of open tickets, or a safety sweep that picks up emails the webhook missed. For any cron, I set an IANA timezone such as Asia/Kolkata, because schedules default to UTC. I also decide whether on_run_completed should be "keep" for audit.
keyPoints: Webhook gives low latency and one run per email
Polling adds delay, empty runs and dedupe work
Cron suits batch summaries, reconciliation and safety sweeps
Set an IANA timezone; UTC is the default
Choose on_run_completed based on audit needs

subjective.question: Put these steps in the right order for taking an invoice automation from idea to production, and say why the order matters: deploy, build the workflow, record baseline metrics, set up online evaluators and alerts, map the process into code and LLM steps, build an evaluation dataset, run offline evaluation.
subjective.answer: The order is: map the process into code and LLM steps, record baseline metrics, build an evaluation dataset, build the workflow, run offline evaluation, deploy, then set up online evaluators and alerts. Mapping comes first because it decides what the LLM does and what stays code. The baseline of manual time, error rate and volume must be taken before anything changes, or you cannot prove value. The dataset should use real, anonymised invoices with correct answers. Building it before the workflow stops you tuning prompts to the examples you happen to see. Offline evaluation with evaluate() checks the result against the baseline error rate before any real payment is touched. After deployment, online evaluators score live runs and alerts send Slack or webhook notifications on error rate, latency or falling feedback scores, so drift is caught early.
keyPoints: Map first, then the baseline before any change
Build the dataset from real examples before building the workflow
Offline evaluate() against the baseline before deploying
Online evaluators and alerts after deployment to catch drift

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this support agent and say how you would fix them.

code.code:
from langchain.agents import create_agent

agent = create_agent(
    model,
    tools=[lookup_order, issue_refund, send_email],
    system_prompt=(
        'You are a support agent. If the customer sounds unhappy, '
        'issue a refund and email them a confirmation.'
    ),
)

agent.invoke({'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': email_text}]})

subjective.answer: There are three main problems. First, issue_refund and send_email are external side effects, and the model can call them with no human approval. Second, the refund decision rests on 'sounds unhappy'. That is a vague LLM judgement, when eligibility should follow business rules such as order status, refund window and amount. Third, there is no checkpointer and no thread_id, so even if I add approval, the run cannot pause and resume. To fix it, I would add HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with interrupt_on for issue_refund and send_email, with allowed_decisions approve, edit and reject. I would pass a checkpointer and invoke with a thread_id. I would move the eligibility check into plain code inside the refund tool, so the tool refuses ineligible orders whatever the model says. I would add a model call limit, and PIIMiddleware if compliance needs it.
keyPoints: Side-effect tools need HITL approval
Refund eligibility belongs in code rules, not 'sounds unhappy'
A checkpointer and thread_id are required to pause and resume
Add guardrails such as call limits and PII handling

subjective.question: This approval node sometimes auto-approves invoices without any reviewer seeing them. Find the bug.
subjective.answer: interrupt() pauses the graph by raising a special exception that LangGraph catches to save state and stop. The broad except Exception catches that exception first. So the pause never happens, decision is set to 'approve', and the graph carries on. That is exactly the auto-approval we see. This is a dangerous failure, because the code looks like it has a human gate. The fix is to never wrap interrupt() in a try/except that can catch it. Call interrupt() on its own. If other code needs error handling, put it in a separate block and catch only specific exceptions. A safe default should never be 'approve'. If something fails, route to reject or to a manual queue. I would also add a test that runs the graph, asserts that it stops at the interrupt, and checks that no decision is written until Command(resume=...) is sent on the same thread_id.
keyPoints: interrupt() works by raising an exception
A broad except swallows the pause and approves silently
Do not wrap interrupt() in try/except; catch only specific errors elsewhere
A fail-safe default is reject or manual review, never approve
Test that the graph actually pauses

subjective.question: Compare an LLM-as-judge evaluator with a code evaluator for an invoice extraction step. Which would you use for which checks?
subjective.answer: For extraction, most checks should be code evaluators, because the expected answer is exact. Is the invoice number an exact match? Is the amount equal within a tolerance? Is the date in the right format? Does the GSTIN pattern match? Code evaluators are cheap, fast, deterministic and easy to explain to finance. LLM-as-judge, for example openevals create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, fits fuzzy fields where several answers are valid. Examples are a vendor name with spelling variants, a free-text line-item description, or the quality of a drafted query email to the vendor. Judges cost money and can be inconsistent, so I check them against human labels on a sample first. In practice I run both in one evaluate() experiment, using code for numbers and IDs and the judge for text. The same evaluators can then run as online evaluators on live traffic.
keyPoints: Code evaluators for exact fields: IDs, amounts, dates, GSTIN
LLM-as-judge for fuzzy text and drafts
Judges cost more and need checking against human labels
Combine both in one evaluate() run and reuse them online

subjective.question: Case study: automate vendor onboarding. Vendors email PAN, GSTIN, a cancelled cheque and an address proof. Requirements: under one day turnaround, no fraud on bank details, and PII must be protected. Design the steps.
subjective.answer: The trigger is an email event. Plain code saves the attachments and runs OCR. An LLM classify step labels each document type, and an LLM extract step returns a schema with PAN, GSTIN, legal name, bank account, IFSC and address. Code then validates the formats: the PAN and GSTIN patterns, a check that the PAN appears inside the GSTIN, and the IFSC format. It also checks for duplicates in the vendor master. Any field that fails validation goes to a retry or to a human queue. A human must approve every new vendor, and every bank detail change in particular, because this is the main fraud risk. That review is an interrupt before the record is created in the ERP, and the create step sits in its own node.
