For PII I would apply redaction to data that does not need to reach the model, and keep the extracted data only in our systems. LangSmith traces need care because they may contain PII.
keyPoints: LLM for document classification and extraction, with a schema
Code for PAN/GSTIN/IFSC formats, cross-checks and duplicates
Mandatory human approval for new vendors and bank details
ERP write in a separate node after the interrupt
PII redaction and care with traces

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this cron job for a quarter-end collections campaign that should run weekdays at 10:00 India time until 31 March, with a record of every run for audit.
subjective.answer: There are three gaps. First, there is no timezone, so the schedule is read in UTC and the job fires at 10:00 UTC, which is 15:30 IST. Add the timezone "Asia/Kolkata". Second, there is no end_time, so the campaign keeps running after 31 March and keeps chasing customers. Set end_time to the end of the campaign. Third, on_run_completed defaults to "delete", so each firing's new thread is removed when the run ends and the audit trail is lost. Set it to "keep". I would also add a webhook URL, so a system is notified when each run is done and can record or check the result. Because sending reminders to customers is an external action, I would also make sure the agent has human approval on the send step, or at least strict template rules in code. The enabled flag lets finance pause the campaign quickly if a dispute comes up.
keyPoints: Missing IANA timezone, so it fires at 15:30 IST
Missing end_time
Default on_run_completed "delete" loses audit threads; use "keep"
Add a webhook; use enabled to pause
Guard the customer-facing send step

subjective.question: Which is better for prototyping a support triage flow with the operations team: Langflow or LangGraph code? When would you move from one to the other?
subjective.answer: Langflow is a separate open-source visual builder. You connect components into a flow and test it in the Playground. That is very good for a first prototype with the operations team, because they can see the steps, try real emails and tell you quickly where classification goes wrong. A flow can also be called through its API. I would move to LangGraph code when I need production control. That means durable human-in-the-loop with checkpointers and thread_ids, precise retries and validation, version control and tests, LangSmith evaluation in CI, and deployment on Agent Server with cron jobs and background runs. In short, Langflow helps you agree what to automate and how the steps look. LangGraph and LangChain v1 are where you build the reliable version. I would keep the step map the same in both, so that what the team agreed in Langflow carries over directly.
keyPoints: Langflow: visual components, Playground, fast feedback from the business
It can be exposed through an API
Move to code for durable HITL, tests, evaluation and deployment
Keep the same step map across both

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: a month after launch, finance says the invoice extraction makes more mistakes. How do you find the cause using LangSmith?
subjective.answer: I would start with the data, not the prompt. In LangSmith I filter traces by date and by low online-evaluator scores or failed validation, and compare them with the launch period. Then I look for a pattern. Is it a new vendor template, scanned rather than digital PDFs, Hindi text, or a model or prompt change in the release history? I add the failing traces to an annotation queue so finance can label the correct values, and then add them to the evaluation dataset. I re-run evaluate() on the old and new versions to find whether the drop comes from the inputs or the code. After fixing it, for example with a vendor-specific hint, better OCR or a schema change, I check that the full dataset still passes. I would also add an alert on the feedback score or the validation error rate, so the next drift is caught by the system rather than by finance.
keyPoints: Filter traces by time, scores and validation failures
Find the pattern: input change versus code or model change
Annotation queue, then add the examples to the dataset
Re-run evaluate() to compare versions and confirm the fix
Add alerts on feedback score or error rate

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this process map for invoice handling and correct it.

code.code:
Step 1  Read email attachment            -> LLM
Step 2  Extract fields as a paragraph     -> LLM
Step 3  Add line items, check total       -> LLM
Step 4  Check GSTIN format                -> LLM
Step 5  Decide approve or reject          -> LLM
Step 6  Send payment confirmation to vendor -> automatic

subjective.answer: Step 1 is plain code: downloading the file and running OCR or PDF parsing needs no LLM. Step 2 is correctly an LLM extract step, but it returns free text. It should return structured output against a schema, followed by a code validation step. Steps 3 and 4 are deterministic, so summing line items, comparing the total and checking the GSTIN pattern belong in code, where they are exact and free. Step 5 should mostly be code rules: PO match, tolerance and amount thresholds. An LLM can add a short explanation of exceptions, and a human approves the exceptions and high-value invoices. Step 6 is an external side effect with no human gate. It must come after approval, sit in its own node, and run only once. The map is also missing PO matching, duplicate checks and a baseline of current time and error rate.
keyPoints: Attachment reading is code
Extraction must be structured and validated
Totals and GSTIN checks belong in code
Decide with rules plus a human for exceptions
No automatic side effect without approval; add missing checks

subjective.question: Case study: a bank's support team wants triage with sentiment flags, auto-replies for simple FAQs, and escalation of complaints to a human within 30 minutes. Customer emails contain account details. Design it, stating the trigger, step types, HITL points and metrics.
subjective.answer: The trigger is an email event webhook, so each email starts its own run, which helps meet the 30-minute escalation target. PII redaction runs first, for example PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True) plus similar rules for account numbers, so the model sees only what it needs. One LLM classify step returns structured output with a category, a complaint flag and a sentiment label from fixed values. Code routes on that output. Complaints go straight to a human queue, with an alert if one stays unassigned. FAQs get an LLM draft step grounded on approved answers. At the start every draft goes through human approval with approve, edit or reject. Once evaluation shows a low error rate, only low-risk categories are auto-sent. For metrics I would track the baseline handling time, the misrouting rate, the time to escalate complaints, the edit rate on drafts and volume per category, with alerts on error rate and latency.
keyPoints: Event trigger to meet the escalation SLA
Redact PII before the model
Structured classify step; routing in code; complaints go to humans
Drafts approved by humans at first; auto-send only for proven low-risk cases
Metrics: handling time, misrouting, escalation time, edit rate

steps.overview: This step teaches the LangChain building blocks that every automation later in the path relies on. You will use chat models, messages and prompt templates, Pydantic structured output, document loaders and splitters, and rate-safe batch processing. The LangChain Academy courses on LangGraph, Ambient Agents and LangSmith assume you can already turn messy documents into validated, typed data at scale.
objectives: Build a prompt | model chain with ChatPromptTemplate and init_chat_model and explain each message role.
Define a Pydantic schema with field constraints and bind it with with_structured_output for extraction and classification.
Load PDFs, emails and web pages into Document objects and decide when and how to split them.
Run a chain over many inputs with batch, max_concurrency and return_exceptions without losing the source of any failure.
Validate 50 invoices end to end and log every failure with its file name.

concepts.explanation: A chat model takes a list of messages and returns an AIMessage. init_chat_model("provider:model", temperature=0) from langchain.chat_models gives one interface across providers, so you can switch models without rewriting code. Use temperature 0 for extraction, so the same input gives stable output.

SystemMessage sets rules and role. HumanMessage carries the user input or document text. AIMessage is the model reply and may hold tool_calls. ToolMessage returns a tool result. Agents and LangGraph state are built from these same message objects.

ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([("system", ...), ("human", "{text}")]) turns variables into a message list. It is a Runnable, so prompt | model builds a chain with LCEL. Keep instructions in the system message and the document text in the human message.

model.with_structured_output(Invoice) returns a Runnable that gives an Invoice instance, not raw text. The Pydantic class, its field descriptions and its constraints become the schema sent to the model. Pass include_raw=True to get a dict with raw, parsed and parsing_error, which helps you debug failures instead of raising them.

Extraction pulls values such as vendor, amount and due date into typed fields. Classification forces a choice from a fixed set, best expressed with Literal["invoice", "credit_note", "receipt"] or an Enum. Both use the same with_structured_output pattern.

Loaders return Document objects with page_content and metadata. PyPDFLoader (needs pypdf) returns one Document per page, with source and page in metadata. Email loaders such as UnstructuredEmailLoader and web loaders such as WebBaseLoader live in langchain_community. Keep metadata["source"], because that is how you trace a failure back to its file.

RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter from langchain_text_splitters cuts text by paragraphs, then lines, then words, using chunk_size and chunk_overlap. Split long documents for retrieval or to fit the context window. Do not split a short invoice for extraction, because fields would end up in different chunks.

Every Runnable has batch(inputs, config={"max_concurrency": N}, return_exceptions=True). It runs inputs in parallel up to N at a time and returns results in input order. return_exceptions=True puts the exception in that slot instead of failing the whole batch.

keyFacts: batch returns results in the same order as the inputs, so zip(files, results) keeps the file-to-result mapping.
The concurrency limit goes in the config: chain.batch(inputs, config={"max_concurrency": 5}).
By default return_exceptions is False, so one bad invoice raises and you lose the whole batch. Set it to True for pipelines.
with_structured_output(Schema, include_raw=True) returns {"raw", "parsed", "parsing_error"} and does not raise.
PyPDFLoader returns one Document per page; the metadata includes source and page.
RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter measures chunk_size in characters by default. Its default separators are paragraph, newline, space, then character.
A GSTIN has 15 characters: 2-digit state code, 10-character PAN, entity number, the letter Z, and a check character.
Store money as Decimal and dates as datetime.date in Pydantic, not float or str.
Use LangChain v1 imports: langchain.chat_models, langchain_core.prompts, langchain_text_splitters. Avoid the legacy LLMChain.

example.caption: Extract 50 invoices into validated Pydantic objects and log failures with their source file
example.code:
import logging
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader

logging.basicConfig(filename="failures.log", level=logging.ERROR)
GSTIN = r"^[0-9]{2}[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z][1-9A-Z]Z[0-9A-Z]$"

class Invoice(BaseModel):
    vendor: str = Field(description="Supplier legal name")
    amount: Decimal = Field(gt=0, description="Total payable in INR incl. GST")
    due_date: date = Field(description="Payment due date, ISO format")
    gstin: str = Field(pattern=GSTIN, description="Supplier GSTIN")

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([("system", "Extract the supplier invoice fields exactly."), ("human", "{text}")])
chain = prompt | init_chat_model("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5", temperature=0).with_structured_output(Invoice)

files = sorted(Path("invoices").glob("*.pdf"))
texts = ["\n".join(d.page_content for d in PyPDFLoader(str(f)).load()) for f in files]
results = chain.batch([{"text": t} for t in texts], config={"max_concurrency": 5}, return_exceptions=True)

valid = []
for f, r in zip(files, results):
    if isinstance(r, Exception) or r is None:
        logging.error("%s: %r", f.name, r)
    else:
        valid.append(r)
print(f"{len(valid)}/{len(files)} valid; failures in failures.log")

pitfalls: Leaving return_exceptions=False. One invoice with a bad GSTIN raises and the other 49 results are lost.
Running batch with no max_concurrency limit on 50+ files. This can hit provider rate limits (HTTP 429). Set a limit that fits your quota.
Scanned PDFs have no text layer, so PyPDFLoader returns empty page_content. Check for empty text and route those files to OCR before you call the model.
Splitting a short invoice into chunks before extraction. This separates the vendor from the total. Splitters are for long documents and retrieval.
Using float for amount or str for due_date. Validation then passes values like '30/02/2026' or rounding errors. Use Decimal, date and regex patterns.
Logging only the error message without the file name. The checkpoint requires every failure to be traceable to its source file.

steps.label: Define the Pydantic schema
steps.detail: Write typed fields with descriptions and constraints for vendor, amount, due_date and GSTIN.

steps.label: Load documents with metadata
steps.detail: Use PyPDFLoader per file, join the page texts, and keep the source path.

steps.label: Build prompt and model chain
steps.detail: Pipe a ChatPromptTemplate into init_chat_model(...).with_structured_output(Invoice) at temperature 0.

steps.label: Batch with a concurrency limit
steps.detail: Call chain.batch with max_concurrency and return_exceptions=True so every input returns a result or an exception.

steps.label: Separate valid and failed records
steps.detail: Zip files with results and log every exception or None result with its file name.

steps.label: Review and re-run failures
steps.detail: Fix prompts, OCR or schema rules and re-batch only the failed files until all records validate.

project.title: invoice-extractor
project.summary: A LangChain v1 batch pipeline that loads 50 invoice files (PDF or text), trims them with a text splitter, and extracts vendor, amount, due date and GSTIN into validated Pydantic objects using init_chat_model, ChatPromptTemplate and with_structured_output. schema.py shows structured output and validation, loading.py shows document loaders and splitters, extract.py shows prompts, batch with max_concurrency and per-file failure logging, and make_samples.py creates test invoices, including deliberately bad ones.
project.run:
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env   # then add your OPENAI_API_KEY
python scripts/make_samples.py
python -m src.extract invoices

files.code:
# invoice-extractor (Step 2: LangChain for automation tasks)

Goal: extract vendor, amount, due date and GSTIN from 50 invoices into
validated Pydantic objects. Every failure is logged with its source file.

## Files
- `src/schema.py`: the `Invoice` Pydantic model. It does classification
  (`document_type`) and extraction (the other fields), plus GSTIN validation.
- `src/loading.py`: `PyPDFLoader` / `TextLoader` and `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`.
- `src/extract.py`: `init_chat_model`, `ChatPromptTemplate`,
  `with_structured_output`, and `batch` with `max_concurrency`.
- `scripts/make_samples.py`: writes 50 sample `.txt` invoices. 3 are bad on purpose.

## Run
```
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env
python scripts/make_samples.py
python -m src.extract invoices
```
Output:
- `out/invoices.jsonl`: one validated record per line.
- `out/failures.jsonl`: `{source, stage, error}` for each failure.

## Checkpoint
The run should report 47 valid records and 3 failures:
- a bad GSTIN (validation error),
- a missing due date (validation error),

The script exits with code 1 if any file fails, so a CI job or scheduler can alert on it.

- Scanned PDFs have no text layer and need OCR first. They are logged at the `load` stage.
- Set `LANGSMITH_TRACING=true` to see each batch call as a trace (used in Step 4).

"""Document loaders and text splitter: file -> text for the prompt."""
from pathlib import Path

from langchain_community.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader, TextLoader
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

# Split on paragraphs, then lines, then words. Overlap keeps the context
# that sits across a chunk boundary.
SPLITTER = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=4000, chunk_overlap=200)

SUPPORTED = {".pdf", ".txt"}


def load_invoice_text(path: Path) -> str:
    """Load one file and return prompt-sized text."""
    suffix = path.suffix.lower()
    if suffix == ".pdf":
        loader = PyPDFLoader(str(path))  # one Document per page
    elif suffix == ".txt":
        loader = TextLoader(str(path), encoding="utf-8")
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unsupported file type: {suffix}")

    docs = loader.load()  # list[Document] with page_content and metadata
    text = "\n".join(d.page_content for d in docs).strip()

    chunks = SPLITTER.split_text(text)
    if not chunks:
        raise ValueError("no text found (scanned PDF? run OCR first)")

    # Invoices keep the header (vendor, GSTIN) at the top and the totals at
    # the bottom. For long files, send only the first and last chunks.
    if len(chunks) > 2:
        chunks = [chunks[0], chunks[-1]]
    return "\n...\n".join(chunks)

"""Batch-extract invoices into validated Invoice objects."""
import json
import logging
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.chat_models import init_chat_model
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate

from .loading import SUPPORTED, load_invoice_text
from .schema import Invoice

load_dotenv()
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("invoices")

# System + human messages; {source} and {text} are template variables
PROMPT = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You extract fields from Indian GST invoices. Use only the document text. "
     "Do not guess. If a field is missing, return an empty string for it. "
     "amount is the grand total payable, including GST."),
    ("human", "Source file: {source}\n\n<document>\n{text}\n</document>"),
])


def build_chain():
    # init_chat_model picks the provider from the 'provider:model' string
    model = init_chat_model(os.getenv("MODEL", "openai:gpt-4.1-mini"), temperature=0)
    # with_structured_output parses the reply into Invoice and raises if validation fails
    return PROMPT | model.with_structured_output(Invoice)


def main(folder: str) -> int:
    files = sorted(p for p in Path(folder).iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in SUPPORTED)
    inputs, sources, failures, records = [], [], [], []
    for f in files:  # load stage: a bad file must not stop the whole run
        try:
            inputs.append({"source": f.name, "text": load_invoice_text(f)})
            sources.append(f.name)
        except Exception as e:
            failures.append({"source": f.name, "stage": "load", "error": str(e)})

    # batch runs calls in parallel; max_concurrency caps them for rate limits.
    # return_exceptions=True returns the error in place of a result, so one bad invoice cannot crash the run.
    results = build_chain().batch(
        inputs,
        config={"max_concurrency": int(os.getenv("MAX_CONCURRENCY", "5")), "tags": ["invoice-batch"]},
        return_exceptions=True,
    )
    for source, result in zip(sources, results):  # results keep input order
        if isinstance(result, Exception):
            failures.append({"source": source, "stage": "extract", "error": str(result)[:500]})
        elif result.document_type != "invoice":
            failures.append({"source": source, "stage": "classify", "error": f"type={result.document_type}"})
        else:
            records.append({"source": source, **result.model_dump(mode="json")})

    out = Path("out")
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    (out / "invoices.jsonl").write_text("".join(json.dumps(r) + "\n" for r in records))
    (out / "failures.jsonl").write_text("".join(json.dumps(f) + "\n" for f in failures))
    for f in failures:
        log.error("FAILED %s [%s]: %s", f["source"], f["stage"], f["error"])
    log.info("valid=%d failed=%d total=%d", len(records), len(failures), len(files))
    return 1 if failures else 0  # non-zero exit lets schedulers raise an alert


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "invoices"))

"""Write 50 sample invoices to ./invoices (47 good, 3 bad on purpose)."""
import random
import string
from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

random.seed(42)  # same files on every run
VENDORS = ["Sharma Traders Pvt Ltd", "Kaveri Steel Works", "Blue Lotus IT Services LLP",
           "Ganga Logistics", "Deccan Paper Mills Ltd"]
STATES = ["27", "29", "07", "33", "24"]  # Maharashtra, Karnataka, Delhi, TN, Gujarat


def gstin() -> str:
    pan = "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_uppercase, k=5)) + f"{random.randint(1000, 9999)}" + random.choice(string.ascii_uppercase)
    return random.choice(STATES) + pan + "1Z" + random.choice(string.ascii_uppercase + string.digits)


def invoice(i: int, title="TAX INVOICE", gst=None, due=True) -> str:
    base = random.randint(5_000, 2_00_000)
    issued = date(2026, 1, 1) + timedelta(days=i)
    due_line = f"Due Date: {(issued + timedelta(days=30)).strftime('%d/%m/%Y')}" if due else ""
    return (f"{title}\n{random.choice(VENDORS)}\nGSTIN: {gst or gstin()}\n"
            f"Invoice No: INV-{1000 + i}\nInvoice Date: {issued.strftime('%d/%m/%Y')}\n{due_line}\n"
            f"Bill To: MasterClass Learning Pvt Ltd\n\nTaxable Value: Rs {base:,}.00\n"
            f"IGST @18%: Rs {base * 0.18:,.2f}\nGrand Total: Rs {base * 1.18:,.2f}\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    folder = Path("invoices")
    folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for i in range(1, 51):
        if i == 13:
            text = invoice(i, gst="27ABC1234")  # bad GSTIN -> validation error
        elif i == 27:
            text = invoice(i, due=False)  # no due date -> validation error
        elif i == 42:
            text = invoice(i, title="CREDIT NOTE")  # classification rejects it
        else:
            text = invoice(i)
        (folder / f"invoice_{i:03d}.txt").write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
    print("wrote 50 files to", folder)

revision.examFocus: This step has no proctored exam of its own. It builds the base skills that the LangChain Academy LangGraph and LangSmith courses assume: model calls, prompt templates, structured output and batch runs. It is also what interviewers probe with 'how would you extract fields from 1,000 documents reliably?' questions. Expect questions that test whether you choose the robust option: typed schemas, safe batch settings, a text-layer check before the model call, and failures you can trace to a file.

compare.difference: The plain form returns a validated Pydantic object and raises if parsing fails. The include_raw form returns a dict with raw, parsed and parsing_error, so you can inspect or log a failure without an exception.
compare.chooseA: Pick it for interactive or single calls where an exception is the signal you want.
compare.chooseB: Pick it for pipelines that must log the raw model reply next to the parsing error for each file.

compare.difference: batch returns one list in input order once every call has finished. batch_as_completed yields (index, result) pairs as each call finishes, so you must use the index to map results back to files.
compare.chooseA: Pick batch when you need simple zip(files, results) mapping and can wait for the whole set.
compare.chooseB: Pick batch_as_completed when you want to stream progress or write results as each one finishes on a large job.

compare.a: Extraction schema (many typed fields such as vendor, amount, due_date, gstin)
compare.b: Classification schema (one field limited to Literal or Enum labels, e.g. invoice | credit_note | other)
compare.difference: Extraction copies values out of the text. Classification makes the model pick one label from a closed set, and Pydantic rejects any label outside that set.
compare.chooseA: Pick extraction when the task says 'pull out', 'capture' or 'populate a record'.
compare.chooseB: Pick classification when the task says 'route', 'tag', 'triage' or 'categorise', and constrain the labels with Literal.

compare.a: Send the whole invoice text to the model
compare.difference: Splitting breaks a document into chunks. That suits retrieval over long documents, but it separates related fields that a one- or two-page invoice needs kept together.
compare.chooseA: Pick the whole document for short invoices, receipts and emails where all fields must be read together.
compare.chooseB: Pick splitting for long contracts or manuals that exceed the context window, or that you will index for retrieval.

compare.difference: Typed fields reject impossible values such as 30/02/2026 or a malformed GSTIN, and Decimal keeps paise exact. float and str accept almost anything.
compare.chooseA: Pick typed fields whenever the data feeds accounting, approvals or payments.
compare.chooseB: Pick plain str only for free-text fields such as notes or line descriptions.

cues.cue: one bad document must not stop the run
cues.pick: return_exceptions=True in batch
cues.why: Failed items come back as exception objects in their slot, and the other results are kept.

cues.cue: HTTP 429 / rate limit errors during a bulk job
cues.pick: config={"max_concurrency": N} sized to the provider quota
cues.why: This caps the number of parallel model calls, while batch still runs the items in parallel.

cues.cue: PDF returns blank text / scanned invoice
cues.pick: Check page_content.strip() and route the file to OCR
cues.why: Scanned PDFs have no text layer, so calling the model on empty text only wastes tokens and produces made-up fields.

cues.cue: switch providers without code changes
cues.pick: init_chat_model("provider:model") from langchain.chat_models
cues.why: A single factory reads the provider from the string, so changing the model is a config change.

cues.cue: value must be one of a fixed set
cues.pick: Literal[...] or Enum field in the Pydantic schema
cues.why: Validation rejects any label the model invents.

cues.cue: trace every failure to its file
cues.pick: Log the source path (zip(files, results) or doc.metadata["source"]) with the error
cues.why: The error message alone cannot tell you which of 50 invoices failed.

cues.cue: legacy LLMChain / predict in an answer option
cues.pick: Eliminate it; prefer prompt | model.with_structured_output(...) runnables
cues.why: LangChain v1 composes runnables with the pipe operator, and the legacy chain classes are not the current approach.

cues.cue: exact money, no rounding drift
cues.pick: Decimal type for amount
cues.why: float cannot represent many decimal values exactly, so sums drift by paise.

scenario.situation: A finance team runs a LangChain pipeline over 50 vendor invoices each night. It uses prompt | model.with_structured_output(Invoice) and calls chain.batch(texts) with no config. Last night one scanned invoice and one with a 14-character GSTIN appeared, the job crashed, and no records were saved. The team also sees occasional 429 errors. What is the best fix?
reasoning: The crash and lost records point to return_exceptions defaulting to False, so set return_exceptions=True and the good results are kept.
The 429 errors point to unlimited parallel calls, so add config={"max_concurrency": N} sized to the provider quota. Retrying everything in a loop would not address the cause.
The scanned invoice needs a pre-check: if the loaded text is empty, send the file to OCR before any model call. A bigger model or a text splitter does not create a missing text layer.
The bad GSTIN should fail Pydantic validation (Field pattern, 15 characters). Log it with the file name from zip(files, results) so the failure is traced, not silently accepted as a str.
Eliminate any option that switches to LLMChain or splits the invoices into chunks, because neither addresses the failures.
scenario.answer: Check each file for empty text and route empties to OCR. Then call chain.batch(texts, config={"max_concurrency": N}, return_exceptions=True), zip the results with the file paths, and log each exception or validation error with its source file. This keeps the 48 good records, respects rate limits and makes every failure traceable.

memoryAids: Batch safety is 'ORC': Order is kept, Return exceptions, Cap concurrency.
Pre-flight check is 'Text before tokens': no text layer means OCR, never the model.
GSTIN shape is '2-10-1-Z-1': state code, PAN, entity number, letter Z, check character, 15 in total.
cheatSheet: init_chat_model('provider:model') gives one interface across providers. Import it from langchain.chat_models.
ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([('system', ...), ('human', '{text}')]) and compose with prompt | model.
model.with_structured_output(PydanticModel) returns a validated object. Add include_raw=True to get raw, parsed and parsing_error without raising.
Classification means a Literal or Enum field. Extraction means many typed fields with a Field(description=...) on each, as hints for the model.
Use Decimal for money, datetime.date for dates, and a regex pattern plus length 15 for GSTIN.
PyPDFLoader gives one Document per page, with source and page in the metadata. Join the pages of a short invoice before extraction.
If page_content.strip() is empty, the PDF is scanned. Route it to OCR.
Do not split short invoices. RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter is for long documents and retrieval, and its chunk_size counts characters.
batch keeps input order, so use zip(files, results). batch_as_completed yields (index, result) as calls finish.
Put max_concurrency inside config. return_exceptions is a separate batch argument; set it to True for pipelines.
Log the file path, the error type and the raw output for every failure.
Avoid LLMChain and other legacy chain classes. Use runnables with v1 imports from langchain_core and langchain_text_splitters.

objective.question: You call model.with_structured_output(Invoice, include_raw=True).invoke(text). The model returns JSON with an invalid date. What do you get?

An empty string
A dict with keys raw, parsed and parsing_error, where parsed is None and parsing_error holds the error
A pydantic ValidationError is raised immediately
objective.explanation: With include_raw=True the call does not raise on parsing failures. It returns raw, parsed and parsing_error, so you can log the raw output and the error.

objective.question: You load a 3-page invoice PDF with PyPDFLoader. What does load() return?
options: A list of strings with no metadata
Three Documents, but metadata is empty unless you add it
Three Documents, one per page, each with source and page in metadata
One Document containing all three pages
objective.explanation: PyPDFLoader returns one Document per page and records source and page in the metadata. You often join pages before extracting fields from a short invoice.

objective.question: You set RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=100) with defaults. What does chunk_size=1000 mean?
options: 1000 words per chunk
1000 lines per chunk
1000 characters per chunk, measured by length function len
1000 tokens per chunk
objective.explanation: By default the splitter measures length in characters. To split by tokens you must use a token-based length function or a token-aware constructor.

objective.question: In what order does RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter try its default separators?
options: Newline, paragraph break, character, space
Sentence end, paragraph, character
Space, newline, paragraph, character
objective.explanation: It tries the largest natural boundary first, the paragraph break, then newline, space and finally single characters. This keeps related text together as much as possible.

objective.question: Which Pydantic field types are best for an invoice amount and due date?
options: amount: str, due_date: str
amount: Decimal, due_date: datetime.date
amount: int, due_date: datetime.datetime
amount: float, due_date: str
objective.explanation: Decimal avoids binary floating-point rounding errors with money, and date validates a real calendar date. float and str cause rounding issues and allow invalid values.

objective.question: Which regular expression matches the GSTIN structure: 2-digit state code, 10-character PAN, entity number, the letter Z, then a check character?

objective.question: A nightly job must load 5,000 PDF invoices from a folder without holding every page in memory at once. Which loader method fits?

loader.load() followed by del on each Document

objective.question: What does this loop print, and in what order?

A single list of results after all calls finish
Only successful results; exceptions are skipped
Results in input order, and idx is always 0..n-1 in sequence

objective.question: During a 50-invoice batch, some calls fail with HTTP 429 rate-limit errors, but those invoices succeed when rerun. What is the best fix?

objective.explanation: 429 errors are transient. Retrying with backoff (with_retry uses exponential jitter by default) and limiting parallel calls addresses the cause. Higher concurrency makes rate limiting worse, and temperature or streaming do not affect quotas.

objective.question: Put these steps of the invoice pipeline in the correct order: (a) validate into the Invoice model and log failures with the file path, (b) load each PDF with PyPDFLoader, (c) check for empty text and route scanned files to OCR, (d) join the pages of each invoice into one text, (e) run the structured-output chain with batch.

b, c, d, e, a
