- Backfill of an online evaluator is only offered when the rule is created.
- The sampling rate controls cost. Score a sample of production traffic, not every run, at scale.

# LangSmith tracing: these two variables are all the agent needs to emit traces
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=lsv2_xxx
# Traces land in this project; the evaluator, rule and alert are created on it
LANGSMITH_PROJECT=invoice-agent-prod
# Only needed for EU or self-hosted instances; the default is the US cloud
# LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT=https://eu.api.smith.langchain.com

# Model provider used by create_agent
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-xxx

# Name of the annotation queue used by the rule (must match monitoring_spec.yaml)
REVIEW_QUEUE_NAME=invoice-review

"""Send mixed production-like traffic so the monitoring has something to catch."""
import time

from langsmith import Client

from agent import answer

REQUESTS = [
    ("What is the status of INV-101?", "u1"),        # good
    ("How much is INV-102 and is it paid?", "u2"),  # good
    ("Is my invoice paid?", "u3"),                  # bad: no id, low score expected
    ("Tell me a joke about accountants", "u4"),     # bad: off-format answer
    ("Status of INV-555?", "u5"),                    # not found
    ("Status of INV-999?", "u6"),                    # tool raises: error run
    ("Check INV-999 again please", "u7"),            # error run
    ("INV-999 amount?", "u8"),                       # error run
    ("INV-101 amount?", "u9"),                       # good
    ("Summarise everything you know", "u10"),        # bad
]

for question, user in REQUESTS:
    try:
        print(user, "->", answer(question, user))
    except Exception as exc:  # errors are still traced, with status=error
        print(user, "-> ERROR:", exc)
    time.sleep(1)

# Traces are sent in a background thread; flush before the script exits
Client().flush()
print("Done. Open project invoice-agent-prod in LangSmith.")

"""Create the annotation queue that the automation rule sends low scores to."""
import os

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langsmith import Client

load_dotenv()
client = Client()  # reads LANGSMITH_API_KEY (and LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT if set)
name = os.environ.get("REVIEW_QUEUE_NAME", "invoice-review")

# Reuse the queue if it already exists, so the script is safe to re-run
existing = [q for q in client.list_annotation_queues(name=name)]
if existing:
    queue = existing[0]
    print("Queue already exists:", queue.id)
else:
    queue = client.create_annotation_queue(
        name=name,
        description="Runs with invoice_quality = 0. Reviewers correct and label them.",
    )
    print("Created queue:", queue.id)

print("Next: create the evaluator, rule and alert from monitoring/monitoring_spec.yaml")

# Settings to create in the LangSmith UI for project invoice-agent-prod.
# Kept in git so the monitoring setup is reviewable and repeatable.

online_evaluator:
  name: invoice-format-check
  type: code                       # or llm_as_judge with a rubric prompt
  item_type: runs
  filter: and(eq(is_root, true), eq(name, "invoice-agent"))
  sampling_rate: 1.0               # 100% while testing; lower it in real prod
  code: evaluators/online_code_evaluator.py
  feedback_key: invoice_quality    # 1 = good, 0 = bad
  backfill: last 1 day             # only offered when the rule is created

automation_rule:
  name: low-score-to-review
  item_type: runs
  # Filter on the evaluator's feedback so the rule fires only AFTER scoring
  filter: and(eq(feedback_key, "invoice_quality"), eq(feedback_score, 0))
  sampling_rate: 1.0
  action:
    type: add_to_annotation_queue
    queue: invoice-review          # created by monitoring/setup_queue.py
  # Optional second action for regression tests: add_to_dataset invoice-failures

alert:
  name: invoice-agent-error-rate
  metric: error_rate               # other options: latency, feedback score
  filter: eq(name, "invoice-agent")
  aggregation_window: 5m
  threshold: "> 20%"               # traffic.py makes 3 of 10 runs fail
  notify:
    - type: slack                  # native Slack integration
      channel: "#invoice-agent-alerts"
    # - type: webhook
    #   url: https://ops.example.in/hooks/langsmith

# Optional second alert:
# metric: feedback score (invoice_quality), avg < 0.7 over 15m -> Slack

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the LangChain Academy Introduction to LangSmith course, covering tracing, online evaluation and production monitoring. It also maps to the monitoring parts of the Ambient Agents course, where background agents run with nobody watching. There is no proctored exam, so expect scenario questions in interviews and course quizzes. Typical questions ask which piece to use (rule, evaluator, queue, alert), why production shows no traces, and why a low-score rule never fires.

compare.difference: A rule acts on each matching run or thread, one at a time (queue it, copy it to a dataset, call a webhook). An alert watches an aggregate metric over a time window and notifies people when it crosses a threshold.
compare.chooseA: Pick a rule when each bad run must be routed somewhere for review or reuse.
compare.chooseB: Pick an alert when someone must be told the error rate, latency or average score has moved, without watching a dashboard.

compare.difference: Online evaluators score sampled live runs, which have no reference answer. Offline evaluate() runs a target over a fixed dataset, usually with reference outputs, before release.
compare.chooseA: Pick online when the question says live traffic, production quality or drift.
compare.chooseB: Pick offline when the question says regression test, compare prompts or models before deploy, or a golden dataset.

compare.difference: An LLM judge scores fuzzy qualities such as helpfulness or tone and costs a model call per run. A code evaluator checks deterministic things such as valid JSON, a required field or a regex, and is cheap and exact.
compare.chooseA: Pick an LLM judge for subjective, reference-free quality criteria.
compare.chooseB: Pick code when the check can be written as a rule, or when volume and cost matter.

compare.difference: A queue sends runs to humans to review and label. A dataset action stores runs as examples for later offline evaluation or few-shot prompts, with no human step.
compare.chooseA: Pick a queue when a person must judge or correct the run.
compare.chooseB: Pick a dataset when you want to grow a test set from real traffic automatically.

compare.difference: A rule webhook fires once for each matching run and carries that run's data, so code can act on it (open a ticket, retry). An alert webhook fires when an aggregate threshold is crossed.
compare.chooseA: Pick a rule webhook for per-run automation in another system.
compare.chooseB: Pick an alert webhook when a pager or incident tool must hear about a metric breach.

cues.cue: Traces appear locally but not from the deployed agent
cues.pick: Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY in the deployment environment
cues.why: Environment variables do not travel from your laptop, so production never sends traces.

cues.cue: Runs are in the wrong project or mixed together
cues.pick: Set LANGSMITH_PROJECT per environment
cues.why: Without it, runs go to the default project, and your rules and alerts are scoped to a different project.

cues.cue: The low-score queue rule never fires, or fires inconsistently
cues.pick: Add eq(feedback_key, "<key>") to the follow-up rule's filter
cues.why: Rules run on independent schedules, so the rule must wait for the evaluator's feedback to exist.

cues.cue: Score quality on live traffic with no expected answer
cues.pick: Reference-free LLM-as-judge, not CORRECTNESS_PROMPT
cues.why: Live runs have no reference output to compare against.

cues.cue: High volume, and the judge cost is rising
cues.pick: Lower the sampling rate, or switch to a code evaluator
cues.why: Each sampled run triggers one paid judge call.

cues.cue: Tell the on-call team when failures spike
cues.pick: Error-rate alert to Slack or a webhook
cues.why: Alerts watch aggregate metrics and notify people; rules do not.

cues.cue: Score the last week of runs with a new evaluator
cues.pick: Choose backfill while creating the rule
cues.why: Backfill is offered only at creation time and cannot be added afterwards.

cues.cue: Monitor a scheduled cron agent
cues.pick: The same project rules and alerts
cues.why: Cron and background runs on the Agent Server are traced like any other run.

scenario.situation: A finance team runs a nightly invoice-triage agent as a cron job on LangSmith Deployment. They added an online LLM-as-judge evaluator that writes a 'helpfulness' score. They also added a rule with the filter 'score < 0.5' that sends runs to an annotation queue. The queue stays empty even though reviewers find obviously bad runs in the project. What is the most likely fix?
reasoning: Traces exist in the project, so tracing is working and the environment variables are not the issue.
The evaluator is scoring runs, so the scoring side is not the problem.
Rules run on independent schedules, so the queue rule can check a run before the helpfulness feedback exists and skip it.
Only the filter targets the feedback directly. An alert would only notify people, and raising the sampling rate would not fix the timing.
The fix is to filter the queue rule on the feedback key and its score, so it matches only after scoring.
scenario.answer: Change the queue rule's filter to include eq(feedback_key, "helpfulness") together with the low-score condition. The rule then picks up runs only after the evaluator has scored them.

memoryAids: Rule = I-F-S-A: Item type, Filter, Sampling rate, Action. Actions are 'DQ-WR': Dataset, Queue, Webhook, Retention.
Rules route runs; alerts ring people.
Online has no answer key: no reference, so judge with criteria, not correctness.
cheatSheet: Tracing needs both variables in every environment where the code runs, including the deployment.
Use LANGSMITH_PROJECT to separate dev and prod. Rules and alerts are scoped per project.
A trace is a tree of runs. The root run holds the overall input, output, latency and error; child runs show LLM and tool calls.
Feedback is a key plus a score on a run. It comes from evaluators, humans or the SDK.
Online evaluators come in two kinds: LLM-as-judge for subjective quality and code for deterministic checks.
Choose backfill while creating the evaluator rule. You cannot add it later.
Every follow-up rule (queue or webhook) must filter on the evaluator's feedback key.
Sampling below 1.0 keeps judge cost under control on high-volume projects.
An annotation queue is for human review. Add-to-dataset grows your offline test set.
Alerts cover error rate, latency and feedback scores, and notify Slack natively or a webhook.
Offline evaluate() gates releases; online evaluators watch production. You need both.
Cron and background runs are covered by the same rules and alerts.
selfCheck: I can explain why a deployed agent produces no traces and fix it with environment variables.
I can build an online evaluator, choose LLM-as-judge or code, and set a sensible sampling rate.
I can write a queue rule that filters on the evaluator's feedback key so it fires only after scoring.
I can choose between a rule and an alert for a given requirement and justify the choice.
I can set up an error-rate alert to Slack or a webhook and say what threshold and window I would use.
I can show one bad run that was scored, queued and alerted on with nobody watching a dashboard.

objective.question: You deploy a LangChain v1 agent built with create_agent and want every run sent to LangSmith. Which pair of environment variables is required?
options: LANGSMITH_PROJECT and LANGSMITH_ENDPOINT
LANGCHAIN_DEBUG=true and OPENAI_API_KEY
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_PROJECT
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY
objective.explanation: Tracing needs LANGSMITH_TRACING=true to turn it on and LANGSMITH_API_KEY to authenticate. LANGSMITH_PROJECT only chooses the project name, and LANGCHAIN_DEBUG is local console debugging, not LangSmith tracing.

objective.question: A team turns on tracing correctly, but their invoice-processing runs appear mixed with other experiments in a project called 'default'. What is the most likely cause?
options: LANGSMITH_PROJECT was not set, so runs went to the default project
Online evaluators move runs into the default project
The sampling rate on the automation rule was set too low
The API key belongs to the wrong workspace
objective.explanation: If LANGSMITH_PROJECT is not set, runs land in the default project. Evaluators and sampling rates do not move runs between projects, and a wrong-workspace key would put runs in a different workspace, not fix the project name.

objective.question: Which set of parts defines a LangSmith automation rule?
options: A dataset, an evaluator list and an experiment name
A cron expression, an assistant_id and an input
An item type (runs or threads), a filter, a sampling rate and an action
A model, a prompt and an output parser
objective.explanation: An automation rule is item type plus filter plus sampling rate plus action. The cron expression, assistant_id and input describe an Agent Server cron job, and dataset plus evaluators describe an offline evaluate() call.

objective.question: Which of these is NOT an action an automation rule can take?
options: Add matching traces to an annotation queue
Extend data retention for matching traces
Automatically re-run the failed trace with a different model
Add matching traces to a dataset
objective.explanation: Rule actions are add to dataset, add to annotation queue, trigger a webhook and extend data retention. Re-running a trace with another model is not a rule action; you could trigger that yourself from a webhook receiver.

objective.question: On Monday you create an online LLM-as-judge evaluator without backfill. On Wednesday your manager asks you to score last week's runs with it by editing the rule. What happens?
options: Backfill is only offered when the rule is created, so editing will not score past runs; run an offline evaluation or create a new rule with backfill instead
Online evaluators always score all historical runs automatically
Past runs are scored only if their data retention was extended
You can enable backfill on the existing rule at any time
objective.explanation: Online evaluators can backfill past runs only at the moment the rule is created, not later. To cover older runs you need a new rule created with backfill, or an offline evaluation over a dataset of those runs.

objective.question: You have an online evaluator writing feedback key 'helpfulness' and a second rule that sends low-helpfulness runs to an annotation queue. The queue rule fires on runs that have no score yet. What is the correct fix?
options: Make the queue rule filter on the evaluator's feedback key, e.g. eq(feedback_key, "helpfulness"), plus a low-score condition
Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=false for unscored runs
Merge both rules into one rule with two actions
Increase the queue rule's sampling rate to 100%
objective.explanation: Automation rules run on independent schedules, so the follow-up rule must filter on the evaluator's feedback key so it only matches runs that have been scored. Sampling rate does not control order, and disabling tracing would hide the runs entirely.

objective.question: Your document-extraction agent must always return valid JSON with an 'invoice_number' field. You want to score every live run for this. Which online evaluator type fits best?
options: An LLM-as-judge evaluator using CORRECTNESS_PROMPT
A human annotation queue with 100% sampling
A latency alert
A code evaluator that parses the output and checks the field
objective.explanation: A structural, deterministic check like valid JSON with a required field is best done with a code evaluator: cheap, fast and exact. LLM-as-judge suits subjective qualities, and human review or alerts do not score each run automatically.

objective.question: Your support agent handles very high traffic, and the LLM-as-judge online evaluator is becoming expensive. What is the most appropriate change?
options: Lower the rule's sampling rate so only a fraction of matching runs are scored
Switch the agent to a cron job
Delete the evaluator and rely only on error-rate alerts
Turn off tracing for half the users
objective.explanation: The sampling rate controls what fraction of matching runs the rule acts on, so lowering it cuts judge cost while keeping a quality signal. Disabling tracing loses visibility, and error alerts alone miss wrong-but-successful answers.

objective.question: Which notification channels can LangSmith alerts send to?
options: Slack (native integration) or a webhook
Only the LangSmith UI notification bell
Microsoft Teams only, via a plugin
Email only
objective.explanation: LangSmith alerts notify Slack through a native integration or any system through a webhook. Other tools can be reached by pointing the webhook at them.

objective.question: A nightly report agent runs as an Agent Server cron job in the Asia/Kolkata timezone. How do you monitor it for errors and low quality?
options: Cron and background runs are traced like any other run, so the same online evaluators, rules and alerts on that project cover them
You must create a separate LangSmith account for scheduled runs
Set on_run_completed to "keep" to enable tracing
Cron runs are not traced, so add manual logging
objective.explanation: Cron and background runs on the Agent Server are traced like normal runs, so existing rules and alerts apply. on_run_completed only controls whether the thread is kept or deleted, not tracing.

objective.question: Before releasing a new prompt for your approval-flow agent, you want to compare it against the current version on 50 known test cases. What should you use?
options: An error-rate alert
An offline experiment with evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...])
An annotation queue rule
An online evaluator with backfill
objective.explanation: Comparing versions on fixed, known examples before release is offline evaluation with evaluate() on a dataset. Online evaluators and alerts work on live traffic after release; you need both, but this question is about pre-release testing.

objective.question: A trace for one agent request shows a slow total time. How do you find which step caused the delay?
options: Look only at the root run's output
Read the annotation queue
Check the project's sampling rate
Open the trace and check the latency of each child run (LLM calls, tool calls) under the root run
objective.explanation: A trace is a tree of runs: a root run with child runs for each model call, tool call or graph node, each with its own latency. The root output and sampling rate do not show where time was spent.

objective.question: An automation rule in your invoice project is configured as shown. What does it do?

code.code:
Item type: runs
Filter: and(eq(feedback_key, "correctness"), lt(feedback_score, 0.5))
Sampling rate: 1.0
Action: Add to annotation queue "invoice-review"

options: Runs a new correctness evaluator on 50% of runs and queues the failures
Queues runs that have no correctness feedback yet, so they can be scored by hand
Sends all runs to the queue and hides those with a score below 0.5
Sends every run that has a correctness score below 0.5 to the invoice-review queue
objective.explanation: The filter matches runs that carry correctness feedback with a score under 0.5, and a sampling rate of 1.0 applies the action to all matches. The rule only adds runs to a queue. It does not create an evaluator, and the feedback_key condition excludes unscored runs.

objective.question: You attach an LLM-as-judge online evaluator to a rule with sampling rate 0.1. About 20,000 runs match the filter each day. What should you expect?
options: All 20,000 runs are scored, but only 10% of the feedback is saved
Each run is scored with 10% of the judge model's context window
About 2,000 randomly sampled matching runs are scored each day
The first 10% of the day's runs are scored, then scoring stops
objective.explanation: The sampling rate is the fraction of matching runs the action is applied to. A rate of 0.1 scores about 10% of the matches, chosen by sampling rather than the first ones of the day. It does not save only part of the feedback or change how the judge is called.

objective.question: Your web app shows a thumbs-up/thumbs-down button under each agent reply. You want these votes stored on the right trace, so you can filter and alert on them. Which approach is correct?

code.code:
from langsmith import Client
client = Client()

# run_id captured when the agent reply was produced
client.create_feedback(
    run_id,
    key="user_score",
    score=1 if thumbs_up else 0,
)

options: This attaches feedback with key user_score to the run, so rules and alerts can use it
This starts an online evaluator called user_score
This creates a new dataset example from the run
This is wrong; user feedback can only be added in the LangSmith UI
objective.explanation: create_feedback attaches a feedback key and score to an existing run. Rules can then filter on eq(feedback_key, "user_score"), and alerts can watch the score. It does not create dataset examples or evaluators, and feedback is not limited to the UI.

objective.question: An online evaluator meant to judge the agent's final answer is also scoring every child LLM call and tool call. This doubles cost and fills the results with meaningless scores. What is the best fix?
options: Add eq(is_root, true) to the rule's filter so only top-level runs are evaluated
Turn off tracing for tool calls
Switch the evaluator from LLM-as-judge to code
Lower the sampling rate to 0.5
objective.explanation: Filtering on is_root limits the rule to the top-level run, which holds the final input and output of the trace. Lowering the sampling rate only cuts volume and still scores child runs. Switching evaluator type or disabling tool tracing does not fix the targeting problem and loses useful data.

objective.question: Your email assistant handles multi-turn conversations. Quality managers want to judge whether the whole conversation resolved the customer's issue, not each reply on its own. How should the automation rule be set up?
options: Item type threads, so the evaluator scores the conversation as a whole
A cron job that copies conversations into a dataset every night
Item type runs, with sampling rate 1.0 and an average of the scores
Item type runs, with a filter on the last message only
objective.explanation: Automation rules can target runs or threads. A thread groups the turns of one conversation, so a thread-level rule can judge overall resolution. Scoring single runs, or averaging per-run scores, misses context that spans several turns.

objective.question: Auditors require that every invoice-approval trace with a rejected decision is kept longer than your project's default retention. Which solution needs the least custom code?
options: Create an automation rule that filters for rejected decisions and uses the extend data retention action
Raise the alert threshold so rejected runs are not deleted
Add the runs to an annotation queue, since queued runs are never deleted
Export all traces daily with a script and store them in S3
objective.explanation: Extending data retention is a built-in automation rule action, and a filter can target only the relevant traces. A custom export script works but adds code to maintain. Alerts do not affect retention, and an annotation queue is a review tool, not a retention mechanism.

objective.question: Several pipelines log to one LangSmith project. You want an online evaluator to score only the invoice pipeline. What does this setup achieve?
options: The metadata creates a separate project named acme
The rule only fires if the customer metadata is also in the filter
The tag is recorded on the trace, and the rule's filter limits the evaluator to invoice-pipeline runs
The tag is ignored, because create_agent graphs do not accept config
objective.explanation: create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph, which accepts tags and metadata in the run config. These are recorded on the trace, and has(tags, ...) matches them in a rule filter. Metadata does not create projects, and the filter matches on the tag alone.

objective.question: You are setting up this step's hands-on task from scratch. Which order of steps is correct?
options: Enable tracing in the deployment and confirm traces arrive; add the online evaluator rule; add a queue rule filtered on the evaluator's feedback key and a low score; create the error-rate alert; send a known-bad test run
Add the online evaluator; send a test run; enable tracing; create the queue rule without a feedback key filter; create the alert
Create the annotation queue rule; enable tracing locally only; add the online evaluator with backfill to score future runs; create the alert
Create the error-rate alert; create the queue rule; enable tracing in the deployment; add the online evaluator; send a test run
objective.explanation: Rules and alerts only see runs that are traced, so tracing in the deployed environment comes first. The queue rule depends on the evaluator's feedback key, so the evaluator comes before it. A known-bad test run at the end proves the chain works. The other orders either skip production tracing or build rules before the things they depend on exist.

objective.question: A teammate attaches this judge as an online evaluator on the production project. Scores are missing or meaningless. What is the mistake?

code.code:
from openevals.llm import create_llm_as_judge
from openevals.prompts import CORRECTNESS_PROMPT

judge = create_llm_as_judge(
    prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT,
    feedback_key="correctness",
    model="openai:o3-mini",
)

options: CORRECTNESS_PROMPT compares the output with a reference output, and live production runs have no reference output
create_llm_as_judge only works for code evaluators
o3-mini cannot be used as a judge model
feedback_key must always be 'score' for online evaluators
objective.explanation: CORRECTNESS_PROMPT is reference-based and is meant for offline experiments on datasets that have expected outputs. Live runs have no reference, so online judges should use reference-free criteria such as helpfulness, tone or faithfulness to the retrieved context. Feedback keys are free-form, and the judge model choice is not the problem.

objective.question: Two requirements arrive. (A) Page the on-call engineer when more than 5% of runs fail in a 15-minute window. (B) Put every individual failed run in front of a reviewer. Which setup is correct?
options: Both: one online LLM-as-judge evaluator
Both: a single alert, because alerts can also add runs to annotation queues
A: alert on error rate to Slack or a webhook; B: automation rule that filters on errored runs and adds them to an annotation queue
A: automation rule with a webhook action; B: an alert on error rate
objective.explanation: Alerts watch aggregate metrics such as error rate and notify people. Automation rules act on individual runs, for example by adding them to a queue, a dataset or a webhook. Swapping the two, or using an evaluator for paging, mixes up these roles.

objective.question: An online evaluator has scored runs for a week, and the scores are visible on traces. A feedback-score alert for the same project has never fired, even on days with obvious bad answers. What is the most likely cause?

code.code:
Online evaluator:  feedback_key = "answer_quality"
Alert:             metric = feedback score
                   feedback key = "correctness"
                   condition = average < 0.6 over 1 hour

options: The alert watches the feedback key 'correctness', but the evaluator writes 'answer_quality', so the alert has no data
The alert window must be exactly 24 hours
Online evaluator scores are only kept for offline experiments
Alerts cannot use feedback scores
objective.explanation: Feedback is stored per key. An alert on a key that nothing writes will never see a score, so it never crosses the threshold. Alerts do support feedback scores, and the window length is not the cause.

objective.question: A claims-processing project receives about 100,000 runs a day. You must check every run for valid JSON output. You also want a tone check using an LLM judge, within a small model budget. Which design is best?
options: A code evaluator rule for JSON validity at sampling 1.0, plus a separate LLM-as-judge tone rule at a low sampling rate such as 0.02
A code evaluator at sampling 0.02 and an LLM judge at 1.0
No online evaluation; review a random sample by hand each week
One LLM-as-judge rule at sampling 1.0 that checks both JSON validity and tone
objective.explanation: Code checks are cheap and deterministic, so you can run them on every run. LLM judges cost a model call each time, so sampling keeps tone monitoring affordable. Running the judge on every run at this volume quietly multiplies model cost.

objective.question: Low-scoring runs from your approval agent should eventually become regression test cases. Which action is better for the rule that catches them, and why?
options: Add them to an annotation queue, so a human confirms the problem and writes the correct output before the run becomes a dataset example
Extend data retention only, because datasets cannot hold production traces
Trigger an error-rate alert for each run
Add them straight to a dataset, because the agent's output can be used as the reference output
objective.explanation: A low-scoring run's output is by definition suspect, so using it unreviewed as a reference would bake the bad answer into your tests. A reviewer in an annotation queue can correct the output first. Adding straight to a dataset suits cases where the output is already trusted.

objective.question: Your LLM judge returns integer helpfulness scores from 1 to 10. The queue rule below never adds any run to the annotation queue, even though many runs score 2 or 3. Why?

code.code: and(eq(feedback_key, "helpfulness"), lt(feedback_score, 0.5))

options: Scores are on a 1–10 scale, so no score is ever below 0.5; the threshold must match the evaluator's scale, for example lt(feedback_score, 4)
Annotation queues only accept runs with errors
feedback_key filters are not allowed in queue rules
The filter must use or() instead of and()
objective.explanation: The filter compares raw feedback scores. A 0–1 threshold can never match scores on a 1–10 scale. Filtering on the feedback key is correct, and it should stay; the threshold is what needs fixing.

objective.question: A short-lived serverless function invokes your agent and exits right away. LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY are set, but many traces never appear in LangSmith. What is the most likely cause?
options: The API key only works for local machines
Tracing requires a checkpointer with a thread_id
Traces are uploaded in the background, and the process exits before pending traces are sent; flush them before returning
LangSmith refuses traces from serverless platforms
objective.explanation: The LangSmith SDK batches and sends traces asynchronously. If the runtime freezes or exits immediately, the batched traces are lost, so you must flush (or wait for) pending traces before the function returns. Tracing does not depend on a checkpointer.

objective.question: Your document pipeline has a thumbs-up/down button, but fewer than 1% of users click it. You want an alert that reliably signals a drop in quality. Which feedback is the better basis for the alert?
options: Latency only, because quality cannot be measured live
Error rate only, because wrong answers always raise errors
Scores from an online evaluator running on a steady sample of runs, with user feedback used as a secondary signal
User thumbs feedback only, because it comes from real users
objective.explanation: Sparse, self-selected user votes make an aggregate alert noisy and slow to react. An online evaluator on a steady sample gives consistent volume for a threshold. Wrong answers usually do not raise errors, so error rate alone misses them.

objective.question: This code online evaluator works on most runs but fails with a KeyError on some of them. Those runs get no score and are never queued. What is the cause?
options: Runs that errored or returned no output have empty or missing outputs, so the lookup and json.loads fail; handle missing or invalid output and return a 0 score
int() cannot be returned as a score
The feedback key must equal the function name
Code evaluators cannot import json
objective.explanation: Errored runs often have no 'output' field. The evaluator crashes on exactly the bad runs you most want to catch. It should defend against missing or invalid JSON and score those runs as 0 instead of throwing.

objective.question: In a create_agent trace, you want to see the exact messages sent to the model on the second model call, including the system prompt. Where do you look?
options: The project's latency chart
The annotation queue
The inputs of the second LLM (chat model) child run inside the trace
The root run's inputs only
objective.explanation: The root run shows what the caller passed in. Each model call is a child run whose inputs hold the full message list sent to the model at that point, including the system prompt and earlier tool results.

objective.question: The on-call team uses an incident tool that accepts HTTP calls but has no Slack. Which alert destination fits?
options: An annotation queue
An online evaluator
A webhook destination pointing at the incident tool's HTTP endpoint
Slack only, because alerts support nothing else
objective.explanation: LangSmith alerts can notify Slack through the native integration or call a webhook. A webhook lets any HTTP-capable system receive the alert. Queues and evaluators are not alert destinations.

objective.question: Reviewers have corrected runs in an annotation queue. You now want to check whether a new prompt fixes them. Order the remaining steps.
options: Add the corrected runs as examples to a dataset; run evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]) for the current and new prompt; compare the experiments; deploy the better version and watch the online evaluator scores
Deploy the new prompt; delete the queue; enable backfill on the old evaluator to rescore everything
Create an alert; set sampling to 1.0; wait a week; deploy
Run evaluate() on production; add runs to the queue; change the prompt; deploy
objective.explanation: Corrected runs become dataset examples with trusted reference outputs. Offline experiments then compare the prompts on those cases. After deployment, online evaluators confirm that live behaviour improved. Backfill is only offered when a rule is created, so you cannot turn it on later for an existing evaluator.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between a trace and a run in LangSmith.
subjective.answer: A run is one unit of work that LangSmith records, such as a single model call, a tool call, a retriever call or a LangGraph node. Each run has inputs, outputs, timing, token use, errors and any feedback attached. A trace is the full tree of runs for one top-level request. The root run is the whole agent invocation, and the child runs are the steps inside it. When I debug, I open the trace to see the whole story. Then I drill into child runs to find the exact model call that hallucinated or the tool call that failed or was slow. Evaluators and rules usually work on runs, often the root run, and feedback scores attach to runs too.
keyPoints: A run is one step: LLM, tool, retriever or node
A trace is the tree of runs for one request
The root run is the whole invocation and child runs are its steps
Each run has its own inputs, outputs, latency, errors and feedback

subjective.question: How would you turn on LangSmith tracing for a LangChain v1 agent built with create_agent, and what would you check first?
subjective.answer: I set three environment variables before the process starts. LANGSMITH_TRACING=true turns tracing on. LANGSMITH_API_KEY authenticates with my workspace. LANGSMITH_PROJECT gives the runs a clear project name, for example invoice-agent-prod. Without it, runs go to the default project. No code change is needed, because create_agent returns a compiled LangGraph graph, and LangChain and LangGraph trace automatically when these variables are set. I then invoke the agent once. In the LangSmith UI I check that the run appears in the right project. I also check that the trace shows the model calls and tool calls as child runs, and that inputs and outputs look correct. If I use PIIMiddleware to redact emails, I confirm the redacted values are what reach the model.
keyPoints: LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY are required
LANGSMITH_PROJECT avoids runs landing in the default project
No code changes needed for LangChain/LangGraph
Verify with one test run: project, child runs, inputs and outputs

subjective.question: Walk through how you would set up this step's hands-on task: an online evaluator, a rule that sends low-scoring runs to an annotation queue, and an error-rate alert.
subjective.answer: First, I make sure the agent traces into its own project. Second, I add an online evaluator on that project, for example an LLM-as-judge that writes a feedback key called helpfulness. I set a sampling rate and decide at creation time whether to backfill recent runs, because backfill is not possible later. Third, I create an annotation queue and a second automation rule. Its action is to add runs to that queue, and its filter uses the evaluator's feedback key, for example eq(feedback_key, "helpfulness") with a low-score condition. Rules run on independent schedules, so this filter makes the queue rule fire only after scoring. Fourth, I create an alert on error rate for the project and send it to Slack or a webhook. To test it, I force a bad run and confirm it is scored, queued and alerted on.
keyPoints: Dedicated project via LANGSMITH_PROJECT
Online evaluator writes a named feedback key; decide backfill at creation
Queue rule filters on that feedback key and a low score
Error-rate alert to Slack or a webhook
End-to-end test with a deliberately bad run

subjective.question: Why must a follow-up automation rule filter on the evaluator's feedback key? What goes wrong if it does not?
subjective.answer: In LangSmith, each automation rule runs on its own independent schedule. There is no guarantee that the online evaluator scores a run before the queue or webhook rule looks at it. If the follow-up rule filters only on something like the run name, it can match runs that have not been scored yet. Then two things go wrong. Good runs get pushed to reviewers or webhooks for no reason. Bad runs may be missed because the score arrives after the rule has already checked them. Filtering on the feedback key, for example eq(feedback_key, "helpfulness"), means the rule only matches runs that already carry that score. I add a condition on the score value so only low scores trigger the action. This makes the pipeline score first, then act.
keyPoints: Rules run on independent schedules
Without the filter, unscored runs can match
Causes noisy queues/webhooks and missed bad runs
eq(feedback_key, ...) plus a score condition gives score-then-act ordering

subjective.question: Compare LLM-as-judge and code online evaluators. When would you use each in a business automation?
subjective.answer: A code evaluator is a function that checks the run deterministically. It is cheap, fast and exact. I use it for rules I can write down. Examples are: is the output valid JSON, does it contain an invoice number, is the amount a number, did the agent call the approval tool before send_email. An LLM-as-judge evaluator uses a model with a grading prompt to score qualities that are hard to code, like helpfulness, tone, faithfulness to the source document or whether a summary is correct. It costs model tokens and can be inconsistent, so I keep the prompt specific. I also sample rather than score everything, and I check the judge against human labels from the annotation queue. In practice I combine them: code checks run on all traffic, and LLM judges run on a sample.
keyPoints: Code evaluators: deterministic, cheap, for format and rule checks
LLM-as-judge: subjective quality such as helpfulness or faithfulness
Judge has cost and variance; sample and calibrate with humans
Combine both in production

subjective.question: How do you choose a sampling rate for an automation rule?
subjective.answer: The sampling rate is the fraction of matching runs that a rule acts on, so it is a trade-off between coverage and cost or effort. For a code evaluator, cost is tiny, so I can sample most or all runs. For an LLM-as-judge on high traffic, every scored run costs tokens, so I pick a fraction that still gives enough scored runs per day to spot a trend. For annotation queue rules, the limit is human time. I sample so reviewers get a manageable number of items, and I use a tight filter such as low scores or errors so the sample is high value. For low-volume but high-risk flows, like payment approvals, I keep a high sampling rate. I revisit the rate as traffic grows.
keyPoints: Sampling rate = fraction of matching runs acted on
Code evaluators can sample high; LLM judges cost tokens
Queue sampling is limited by reviewer capacity
Tight filters plus sampling; higher rates for high-risk flows

subjective.question: Online evaluators can backfill only when the rule is created. What are the practical implications?
subjective.answer: Backfill is a one-time choice made when I create the online evaluator rule. If I want the evaluator to score runs that already exist, I must choose backfill then. I cannot edit the rule next week and ask it to score older runs. So before I create the rule, I decide whether I need history, for example to get a baseline score for the last few days, or to compare the period before and after a prompt change. If I forget, I have two options. I can create a new rule with backfill, or I can collect the older runs into a dataset and run an offline evaluation with evaluate(). It also means I should finalise the evaluator prompt and feedback key carefully. Changing them later creates a gap between older and newer scores.
keyPoints: Backfill is chosen only at rule creation
Cannot add backfill later by editing
Plan for baselines before creating the rule
Workarounds: new rule with backfill, or offline evaluate() on a dataset

subjective.question: What is an annotation queue and how does it close the loop between production and offline evaluation?
subjective.answer: An annotation queue is a list of runs waiting for a human to review them. A reviewer opens each run, sees its inputs and outputs, and adds feedback, corrections or a reference answer. In production, I feed the queue with an automation rule that filters on low evaluator scores or errors. Reviewers then see the runs that most need attention, not random traffic. The loop closes when reviewed runs, with corrected outputs, are added to a dataset. That dataset becomes the test set for offline experiments with evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]). The next prompt or model change is tested against real failures before release. Human labels also help me check whether my LLM-as-judge agrees with people.
keyPoints: Queue = runs awaiting human review and feedback
Fed by a rule filtering on low scores or errors
Reviewed runs go to a dataset with corrected outputs
Dataset drives offline evaluate() regression tests
Human labels calibrate the LLM judge

subjective.question: Which alerts would you configure for a production document-processing agent, and where would you send them?
subjective.answer: I would configure three kinds of alert on the agent's project. First, error rate, to catch tool failures, API outages or exceptions. Second, latency, because slow runs can break downstream SLAs, such as invoices that must post before a cut-off. Third, feedback score, for example the average of my online evaluator's correctness or helpfulness key. This catches runs that do not throw errors but give wrong answers. I set thresholds from normal behaviour seen in traces, not guesses, so alerts are not noisy. For channels, I use the native Slack integration for the team's on-call channel. I use a webhook when the alert must reach an incident tool or trigger automation, such as pausing a cron job. Each alert gets a clear owner.
keyPoints: Error rate, latency and feedback score alerts
Feedback alerts catch silent quality failures
Thresholds based on observed baselines
Slack native for people; webhook for incident tools or automation

subjective.question: Your agent runs every morning as an Agent Server cron job. How do LangSmith monitoring features apply to it?
subjective.answer: An Agent Server cron job is created with POST /runs/crons, or client.crons in the Python SDK. It needs a schedule, an assistant_id and an input, and a timezone like Asia/Kolkata if I do not want UTC. Each firing creates a new thread and a run, and that run is traced like any other run. So nothing special is needed for monitoring. The same online evaluators score these runs, the same automation rules queue low scores, and the same error-rate, latency and feedback alerts fire on them. This matters because no user is watching a scheduled agent, so alerts are the only quick signal of failure. The cron's webhook tells me a run finished. LangSmith tells me whether it finished well. I can filter by run metadata or name if I want rules just for the cron.
keyPoints: Cron runs are traced like normal runs
Same evaluators, rules and alerts apply
No user is watching, so alerts are essential
Cron webhook signals completion; LangSmith signals quality

subjective.question: Why do you need both offline and online evaluation? Give an example of what each catches.
subjective.answer: Offline evaluation runs my agent on a fixed dataset with evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]), for example with an openevals create_llm_as_judge using CORRECTNESS_PROMPT. It is a controlled, repeatable test before release. It catches regressions: a new prompt that breaks known invoice formats, or a model swap that lowers accuracy. Its limit is that it only knows the cases in the dataset. Online evaluation scores live production runs as they happen. It catches what the dataset never covered: new document layouts, odd user requests, drift after a vendor model update, or a tool that starts returning bad data. The two feed each other. Online low scores go through annotation queues into the dataset, and the improved dataset makes the next offline test stronger.
keyPoints: Offline: evaluate() on a dataset, before release, repeatable
Offline catches regressions on known cases
Online: scores live traffic and catches new inputs and drift
Online failures feed back into offline datasets

subjective.question: Users say the email assistant gives wrong replies, but there are no errors and the error-rate alert is quiet. How would you investigate and prevent this in future using LangSmith?
subjective.answer: No errors means the runs succeed technically but fail on quality, so error alerts cannot see the problem. I would start in the project and filter traces by the time of the complaints or by user metadata. Then I open a few traces and read the child runs: the retrieved context, the model prompt and output, and any tool results. This shows whether the fault is bad retrieval, a weak prompt or bad tool data. To prevent it, I add an online LLM-as-judge evaluator for reply correctness with a sensible sampling rate. I add a rule that filters on that feedback key and low scores and sends those runs to an annotation queue. I also add an alert on the feedback score. Reviewed failures go into a dataset for offline regression tests on the fix.
keyPoints: Quality failures do not show up as errors
Inspect child runs to find the root cause
Add online evaluator plus feedback-key-filtered queue rule
Add a feedback-score alert
Turn failures into a dataset for offline tests

subjective.question: A create_agent support agent sometimes calls the wrong tool, for example refund_order instead of check_status. Explain how you would use a LangSmith trace to find out why.
subjective.answer: I open the trace and look at the run tree, not just the final output. The root run shows the user input and the final answer. Under it, I find the LLM run that chose refund_order. I check its inputs: the system prompt, the message history, and the tool descriptions the model actually received. Often the cause is visible there. Two tool descriptions may overlap, the history may be truncated, or a summarisation step may have dropped key context. Then I check the tool run's inputs and outputs, to see what arguments were passed. I compare this trace with a good trace for a similar request. Once I know the cause, I fix the tool descriptions or the prompt. I then add the failing input to a dataset, so the fix is tested in offline evaluation before release.
keyPoints: Navigate the run tree from the root run to child LLM and tool runs
Inspect the exact prompt, history and tool schemas the model saw
Compare the failing trace with a successful one
Turn the failure into a dataset example for regression testing

subjective.question: Design a code online evaluator for an invoice-extraction agent. What would it check, what feedback would it write, and why use code here instead of an LLM judge?
subjective.answer: The agent must return JSON with fields such as invoice_number, total and due_date. My code evaluator parses the root run's output. It writes a feedback key such as valid_extraction: 1 if the JSON parses, the required fields exist, the total is a number and the date is a valid format; otherwise 0. It could also write separate keys, such as has_invoice_number, to make failures easier to diagnose. Code fits because these checks are deterministic. They are cheap, fast and never vary between runs, so I can usually run them at sampling rate 1.0. An LLM judge would cost money per run, could give inconsistent results, and adds no value for format rules. I keep the LLM judge for subjective questions, such as whether a summary is faithful. A follow-up rule then filters on eq(feedback_key, "valid_extraction") with a score of 0, and sends those runs to an annotation queue.
keyPoints: Deterministic checks: parse JSON, required fields, types and formats
Write clear feedback keys, optionally one per check
Code is cheap and consistent, so a high sampling rate is affordable
Follow-up rule filters on the feedback key to route failures

subjective.question: Your operations team wants a ticket created in their internal system for every run judged 'unsafe'. Describe how you would build this with LangSmith automation rules, and the pitfalls to avoid.
subjective.answer: First, I create an online evaluator, for example an LLM-as-judge that writes the feedback key safety. Second, I create a separate rule with the webhook action. Its filter is and(eq(feedback_key, "safety"), eq(feedback_score, 0)). Automation rules run on independent schedules, so filtering on the feedback key ensures the webhook fires only after scoring is done, never on unscored runs. The webhook receiver creates the ticket. It should be idempotent: store the run ID and ignore duplicates, so retries do not create two tickets. It should also return a response quickly and do the heavy work asynchronously. I protect the endpoint with a secret and avoid copying sensitive trace content into tickets; a link to the trace is enough. Finally, I test the setup with a known unsafe input and confirm that one ticket is created.
keyPoints: Two rules: an evaluator, then a webhook rule filtered on its feedback key
The receiver is idempotent, keyed on run ID
Secure the endpoint and limit the sensitive data sent
Test end to end with a known bad input

subjective.question: Your agent receives two kinds of feedback: user thumbs-up/down from the app, and online evaluator scores. How do they differ, and how would you use both for alerts and review?
subjective.answer: Both are stored as feedback on runs, with a key and a score, but they come from different sources. User feedback is sparse and noisy, because most users do not vote, but it reflects real satisfaction. It is attached with client.create_feedback using a key such as user_score. Evaluator feedback is systematic: it scores a sampled share of runs on defined criteria, such as correctness or format. I give them distinct keys so they are never mixed. I set an alert on a drop in the average evaluator score, because it is the more stable signal. For user feedback, I route thumbs-down runs to an annotation queue with a rule filtered on eq(feedback_key, "user_score") and a score of 0. When users complain about runs the evaluator scored high, that gap shows the judge prompt needs improving.
keyPoints: Both are key/score feedback on runs, but with different sources
User feedback is sparse but real; evaluator feedback is consistent and sampled
Use distinct feedback keys and filter on each separately
Disagreement between the two shows where to improve the judge

subjective.question: After launching error-rate, latency and feedback-score alerts, the team is getting so many Slack messages that they ignore them. How would you fix the alert setup?
subjective.answer: First, I review the recent alerts and sort them into real incidents and noise. Then I tune the thresholds and windows. I use rates over a time window, not single failures; for example, error rate above a level the business cares about over several minutes. This stops one timeout from paging people. I set latency thresholds from measured normal behaviour, not guesses. For feedback scores, I alert on a sustained drop in the average, not on single low scores. Single bad runs belong in an annotation queue, not in Slack. I scope alerts to the right project or pipeline, so experiments do not trigger production alerts. Critical alerts go to an on-call channel or a webhook into the incident tool. Lower-priority signals go to a quieter channel. I revisit the thresholds after a few weeks.
keyPoints: Classify past alerts as real incidents or noise
Use rates over windows with thresholds based on measured baselines
Send single bad runs to queues, not alerts
Scope alerts per production project and route them by severity

subjective.question: Your HR document pipeline processes employee records containing personal data. What does this setting do, and what other precautions would you take when tracing this pipeline in LangSmith?

code.code:
export LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
export LANGSMITH_API_KEY=...
export LANGSMITH_PROJECT=hr-docs-prod
export LANGSMITH_HIDE_INPUTS=true

subjective.answer: This turns on tracing to the hr-docs-prod project. LANGSMITH_HIDE_INPUTS=true stops run inputs from being sent to LangSmith, so raw employee records do not appear in traces. You still get the run structure, timings and errors. LANGSMITH_HIDE_OUTPUTS does the same for outputs if those also contain personal data. The trade-off is that hidden data cannot be read by LLM-as-judge evaluators, or by reviewers in annotation queues. So I would consider masking only sensitive fields instead of hiding everything. PIIMiddleware with redaction helps on the model side, but it does not change what tracing records, so I still check a real trace to confirm what is stored. I would also restrict access to the project, set suitable retention, and avoid sending trace content through webhooks.
keyPoints: LANGSMITH_HIDE_INPUTS keeps inputs out of traces; a matching HIDE_OUTPUTS variable exists
Hidden data cannot be scored by LLM judges or reviewed by humans
Consider masking specific fields instead of hiding everything
Verify by inspecting a real trace; control access, retention and webhook payloads

subjective.question: How would you prove this step's checkpoint: that a bad run is scored, queued for review and alerted on, without anyone watching a dashboard?
subjective.answer: I run a controlled end-to-end test in the production-like project. First, I prepare inputs that I know will fail. For example, a document that produces invalid JSON or a poor answer for the evaluator to score low, and an input that makes a tool raise an error. I send these through the real agent with tracing on, adding a test tag to make them easy to find. Then I wait for the rules to run on their schedules, without opening the dashboard. Success means three things. The evaluator feedback key appears with a low score. The run lands in the annotation queue through the rule filtered on that key. The error-rate alert reaches Slack or the webhook once the threshold is crossed. I record the time each step took, then remove or label the test runs, so they do not distort production metrics.
keyPoints: Inject known bad and error-producing inputs, tagged as tests
Check that the feedback key and low score appear
Check that the run arrives in the queue through the feedback-key filter
Confirm the alert is delivered without manual watching, and record timings

subjective.question: Case study: a legal contract-review agent handles about 50,000 runs a day. Requirements: every output must be valid JSON; summaries must stay faithful to the contract text; only two reviewers are available, about 30 reviews a day; and ops wants Slack alerts for outages and quality drops. Design the LangSmith setup.
subjective.answer: First, I would confirm LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and the API key are set in the deployed environment. I would also make sure the pipeline logs to its own project. For JSON validity, I would add a code online evaluator at sampling 1.0, because it is cheap and deterministic. For faithfulness, I would add a reference-free LLM-as-judge that compares the summary with the retrieved contract text. At 50k runs a day, I would sample it at about 1–2% to control cost. Next, a queue rule filters on the faithfulness feedback key and a low score, with its own sampling tuned so the queue stays near 30 items a day. Invalid-JSON runs go to the same queue, at higher priority. Finally, I would set alerts: error rate and latency for outages, and the average faithfulness and JSON-validity scores for quality. All of them go to the ops Slack channel.
keyPoints: Production tracing and a dedicated project
Code evaluator on all runs; reference-free LLM judge sampled
Queue rule filtered on the feedback key and sized to reviewer capacity
Separate alerts for outages (error rate, latency) and quality (feedback scores)

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: the online evaluator shows low scores on many traces, but the annotation queue stays empty. List the likely causes in the order you would check them.
subjective.answer: First, I check that the queue rule is on the same project as the evaluator, and that it is enabled. Second, I read the rule's filter. It should filter on the evaluator's exact feedback key, not just 'low score'. The key name must match character for character. Third, I check the threshold against the score scale. A filter of lt(feedback_score, 0.5) never matches scores on a 1–10 scale or boolean scores stored as 0 and 1 if the logic is inverted. Fourth, I check the sampling rate. A very low rate on the queue rule may simply not have picked any matching runs yet. Fifth, I remember that rules only act on runs arriving after creation. Old low-scoring runs are not picked up later. Finally, I send a known-bad run and watch it get scored, then queued.
keyPoints: Same project and rule enabled
Filter on the exact feedback key
Threshold matches the score scale
Sampling rate and the rule only seeing new runs
Verify with a known-bad test run

subjective.question: After moving an agent from langgraph dev to an Agent Server deployment, the LangSmith project shows no new traces, the evaluators score nothing and the alerts are silent. Walk through your diagnosis.
subjective.answer: Silent alerts here are not good news. They mean there is no data. I would first check the deployment's environment variables. LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and a valid LANGSMITH_API_KEY must be set there, not only in my local .env file. Next, I check the project name. If the deployment uses a different project, or the default one, the traces exist but my rules and alerts are watching the wrong project. Then I confirm the API key belongs to the right workspace and has not been revoked. I would send one test request and search for it by time or metadata. Once traces appear, I confirm the evaluator starts scoring new runs. Runs from the gap will not be scored later, because backfill is only offered when a rule is created. To prevent this, I would add a deployment checklist item, and a low-traffic or no-data check where the platform supports it.
keyPoints: Tracing env vars must be set in the deployed environment
Project name mismatch sends traces elsewhere
Check API key validity and workspace
Send a test run and confirm
Gap runs will not be rescored

subjective.question: Which is better for judging an email assistant's replies: a reference-free LLM-as-judge online, or CORRECTNESS_PROMPT in offline evaluate() runs? Explain when each fits.
subjective.answer: They answer different questions, so neither replaces the other. CORRECTNESS_PROMPT compares the output with a reference answer. That only works offline, on a dataset where each example has an expected output. I would use it before releases, in evaluate() experiments that compare prompt or model versions on known cases. Online, live emails have no reference. So I would use reference-free criteria, for example: is the reply polite, does it answer the customer's actual question, does it avoid inventing policy, and does it stay faithful to the thread content. These judges catch drift on real traffic that the dataset never covered. In practice, I would run both. The offline correctness check gates releases, and the online reference-free judge monitors production. Low online scores feed an annotation queue, and they become new reference examples.
keyPoints: CORRECTNESS_PROMPT needs a reference, so it is offline only
Reference-free criteria for live runs
Offline gates releases; online catches drift
Queue turns live failures into new references

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this monitoring design for an invoice agent and correct them.

code.code:
Rule 1: filter = all runs (including child runs)
        sampling = 1.0
        action = online LLM judge (CORRECTNESS_PROMPT)
Rule 2: filter = lt(feedback_score, 0.5)
        sampling = 1.0
        action = add to dataset 'invoice-golden'
Alert:  error rate > 5% -> Slack

subjective.answer: Rule 1 has three problems. First, it scores child runs, so every model and tool call gets a meaningless score and the cost multiplies; it should filter to root runs. Second, it uses CORRECTNESS_PROMPT, which needs a reference output that live runs do not have; it should use reference-free criteria or a code check of the extracted fields. Third, sampling 1.0 with an LLM judge is expensive at volume, so I would sample the judge and keep a cheap code evaluator at 1.0. Rule 2 does not filter on the feedback key, so it can match other feedback or check runs before scoring. It should be and(eq(feedback_key, "..."), lt(feedback_score, 0.5)). It also adds bad outputs straight into a golden dataset; it should send them to an annotation queue first. The alert is fine, but I would add a feedback-score alert for silent quality drops.
keyPoints: Filter evaluator to root runs
Replace reference-based judge online
Sample the LLM judge; code check at 1.0
Filter rule 2 on the feedback key
Queue before dataset; add a feedback alert

subjective.question: Put in order the steps to roll out a new LLM-as-judge online evaluator safely, and explain why each step comes where it does.
subjective.answer: Step 1: write a reference-free judge prompt with clear criteria and a fixed score scale. Test it offline on a handful of known good and bad runs. Step 2: create the rule on root runs only, with a modest sampling rate. If the recent history matters, choose backfill now, because it is only offered at creation. Step 3: calibrate. Send a sample of the judged runs to an annotation queue and compare the human labels with the judge's scores. Adjust the prompt or threshold until they agree. Step 4: add the follow-up queue rule, filtered on the judge's feedback key and a calibrated low threshold. Step 5: add a feedback-score alert once you know the normal score range, so the threshold is not a guess. Step 6: review cost and adjust the sampling rate. The order matters: alerting on an uncalibrated judge creates noise and loses trust.
keyPoints: Offline test of the judge prompt first
Root runs, modest sampling, backfill decided at creation
Calibrate against human labels
Queue rule on the feedback key, then alert using the known baseline

subjective.question: For low-scoring runs, which is better: a rule that posts each run to a Slack channel through a webhook, or a rule that adds them to an annotation queue? Justify your choice.
subjective.answer: For review work, the annotation queue is usually better. A queue holds each run with its full trace. Reviewers can work through it at their own pace, add feedback and corrections, and move good examples into a dataset. Nothing gets lost when a chat channel scrolls. Posting every low-scoring run to Slack turns individual runs into notifications. At any real volume, people start ignoring them. A webhook per run makes sense when another system must act on each run, for example by opening a ticket for an unsafe output. Even then, the rule must filter on the feedback key so it fires after scoring. For people, I would combine an annotation queue for individual runs with an alert on the aggregate feedback score. That way Slack only hears about trends, not each bad answer.
keyPoints: Queue supports structured review and feeds datasets
Per-run Slack messages cause alert fatigue
Webhooks suit system actions on individual runs
Use alerts for aggregate trends

subjective.question: Your approval agent uses HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on send_email with approve, edit and reject. Managers want to know how often humans reject or edit the agent's draft, and to be alerted if rejections spike. How would you do this with LangSmith?
subjective.answer: The human decision is the most valuable quality signal here, so I would record it as feedback on the run. When the reviewer's decision comes back and the graph resumes with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id, my app also calls the LangSmith client to create feedback on that run. I would use a key such as 'human_decision', with a score of 1 for approve, 0.5 for edit and 0 for reject, plus a comment. Because the feedback sits on the right trace, I can filter runs by rejection and send them to an annotation queue to see why the drafts failed. I would also set a feedback-score alert on 'human_decision' to Slack when the average drops below a baseline. Optionally, an online judge can score drafts before review, and I compare its scores with human decisions to calibrate it.
keyPoints: Log the human decision as feedback with a stable key
Attach it to the correct run when resuming
Queue rejected runs for root-cause review
Alert on the average decision score

subjective.question: An LLM-as-judge online evaluator gives almost every run a top score, including runs users complained about. What could be wrong, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: I would check four things. First, what the judge actually sees. If the prompt is mapped to the wrong field, for example the raw inputs instead of the final answer, or a truncated message list, it is judging the wrong thing. I open a judged trace and read the evaluator's own run. Second, the criteria. Vague prompts like 'is this good?' drift towards high scores. I would write specific, checkable criteria and examples of bad answers. Third, the scale. A 1–10 scale invites generosity, while a binary or short rubric is easier to keep consistent. Fourth, a weak judge model. Then I calibrate: I pull the complained-about runs and a random sample into an annotation queue, label them, and compare the labels with the judge's scores. I change the prompt until they agree, and only then trust thresholds and alerts.
keyPoints: Verify the judge's input mapping by reading its run
Specific criteria and a tight scale
Consider judge model strength
Calibrate against human labels from a queue

subjective.question: Spot the mistake: a team catches errors with one automation rule, shown below, and no alerts. Why is this weak, and what should they use?

code.code:
Rule: filter = errored runs
      sampling = 0.1
      action = add to annotation queue 'errors'
(no alerts configured)

subjective.answer: This design has two gaps. First, sampling 0.1 means about 90% of errored runs never reach the queue. For errors, which are usually low volume and high value, sampling should be high, often 1.0, unless volume truly overwhelms reviewers. Second, and more serious, a rule acts on individual runs. It does not notify anyone. If an outage makes half of all runs fail, the queue quietly fills and nobody knows until someone opens it. That breaks the goal of not watching a dashboard. They need an error-rate alert, plus usually a latency alert, sent to Slack or a webhook, so people hear about aggregate problems at once. The queue rule stays for root-cause review of individual failures. Rules are for acting on runs; alerts are for telling people about trends.
keyPoints: Low sampling loses most error runs
Rules do not notify people
Add error-rate and latency alerts
Keep the queue for per-run root-cause review

subjective.question: A Deep Agent created with create_deep_agent runs a long research task with subagents and file operations. The final report is wrong. How do you read its large trace to find where it went wrong?
subjective.answer: I would not read the trace top to bottom. First, I open the root run and compare its input with the final output, to state clearly what is wrong. Then I walk the tree backwards from the output. Which subagent or step produced the bad content? Was it a wrong tool result, or a model misreading a correct one? I expand the subagent calls and check what task the main agent delegated. A vague delegation is a common cause. I look at file write and read steps to see whether the agent saved or loaded the wrong content. I also check where summarization ran, because important details can be dropped there. At each suspicious model call, I read that child run's inputs to see exactly what context the model had. Latency and token counts help spot loops. Once I find the cause, I add the run to a dataset as a regression case.
keyPoints: Start at the root: input versus output
Trace backwards to the producing step
Inspect subagent delegation, file steps and summarization
Read the model child run inputs at the suspect point
Turn the case into a regression example

subjective.question: Spot the problem: you set a feedback-score alert at average helpfulness below 0.6 over 15 minutes. The project gets about 200 runs an hour, and the judge samples 5%. The alert flaps constantly. Why, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: At 200 runs an hour with 5% sampling, the judge scores about 10 runs an hour, so only two or three in a 15-minute window. One or two harsh scores swing the average below 0.6, and the alert fires and clears again and again. The metric is noise, not signal. To fix it, I would increase the number of data points behind each alert decision. I can lengthen the window, for example to a few hours, or raise the sampling rate. At this low volume, a higher rate costs little. I would also set the threshold from the observed normal range, not a guess. Where possible, I would keep a steadier signal, such as a code evaluator at 1.0, for fast alerts, and leave sampled LLM judge averages for slower trend alerts.
keyPoints: Too few scored runs per window
Lengthen the window or raise sampling at low volume
Threshold set from the baseline
Use high-volume signals for fast alerts

subjective.question: The model bill for your agents doubled the week you set up monitoring, although user traffic is flat. How would you find and fix the cause with LangSmith?
subjective.answer: Flat traffic with doubled cost points at the monitoring itself, so I would check the evaluator runs first. Each LLM judge call is a model call, and LangSmith traces it. I look at token usage and cost for the judge's runs compared with the agent's runs. Then I check each online evaluator rule for three likely causes. First, sampling 1.0 on a high-volume project. Second, a missing root-run filter, so child LLM and tool runs are also judged, multiplying calls per request. Third, several rules judging the same runs with overlapping criteria. I also check whether the judge uses an unnecessarily large model. To fix it: filter to root runs, lower the sampling rate, move deterministic checks to code evaluators, merge overlapping judges and pick a cheaper judge model. After that, I compare the cost per day again.
keyPoints: Suspect the evaluators when traffic is flat
Compare judge run tokens and cost with agent runs
Check sampling, root-run filter and duplicate rules
Use code evaluators, a cheaper judge and lower sampling

steps.overview: This step teaches you to build AI automations visually in Langflow, the open-source drag-and-drop builder for LangChain-style flows. You will rebuild the Week's invoice extractor on the canvas, test it in the Playground and trigger it over HTTP. Langflow has no official certification, so your proof of skill is a published, API-callable flow whose output matches your coded pipeline on the same 10 invoices.
objectives: Install Langflow locally and build a flow by connecting components on the canvas
Add an Agent, tools and a vector store to a flow and test it in the Playground
Trigger a flow through its run API or a Webhook component using an API key and tweaks
Compare visual-flow output with a coded LangChain/LangGraph pipeline on a fixed invoice set
Decide when a flow should stay visual and when to move it into LangGraph code

concepts.explanation: A flow is a graph of components wired together on the canvas. Each component has typed inputs and outputs, and you can only connect compatible ports. Common components are Chat Input, Prompt Template, a Language Model, Agent, Parser, Structured Output and Chat Output. A flow is saved and exported as a JSON file, so you can version it in Git.

The Playground is the built-in chat and test panel for a flow. You send an input, see the final output and inspect what each component produced. Use it to debug prompts and parsing before you expose the flow over the API. It needs a Chat Input or Chat Output component to give a chat-style view.

The Agent component wraps an LLM that decides which tools to call. Many components can be switched into Tool Mode, which exposes them as tools on the Agent's Tools input. The agent uses the component's name and description to choose it, so write clear descriptions. Conceptually this mirrors create_agent(model, tools, ...) in LangChain v1 code.

Vector store components such as Chroma or Astra DB take documents plus an embedding model for ingestion, and a search query for retrieval. A typical RAG flow has two parts: an ingest path (File, Split Text, embeddings, vector store) and a query path (Chat Input, vector store search, Parser, Prompt, model). You can also expose the vector store search as a tool for an Agent.

For invoices you need fixed fields, not chat text. Use a Structured Output component (or a strict prompt plus a JSON parser) with a schema such as invoice_number, vendor, invoice_date, currency and total. Keep the field names and types identical to the Pydantic model in your coded pipeline so outputs can be compared field by field.

Every flow can be called with POST /api/v1/run/{flow_id_or_endpoint_name}. The JSON body carries input_value, input_type and output_type, plus optional tweaks. Authenticate with an x-api-key header created in Langflow settings. The response nests the result under outputs, then outputs again, then results.

Tweaks override component settings for one API call without editing the saved flow. They are keyed by component ID, for example a model component's temperature or a file path. Use them to pass per-request values, such as a different invoice file or model name, from your calling script.

Add a Webhook component to a flow to accept event payloads at POST /api/v1/webhook/{flow_id}. The received JSON becomes data inside the flow, which you then parse and route to the extractor. It suits event-driven triggers such as a mail tool or a document system posting "new invoice arrived".

keyFacts: Install with uv pip install langflow and start with uv run langflow run; the default UI and API address is http://localhost:7860.
Langflow Desktop is an alternative installer; Docker is an option for servers.
Run endpoint: POST /api/v1/run/{flow_id}; webhook endpoint: POST /api/v1/webhook/{flow_id}.
Send the API key in the x-api-key header; never hard-code it in an exported flow or a public repo.
Tweaks are keyed by component ID, which you copy from the component or the API access pane of the flow.
Flows are exported and imported as JSON; commit that JSON so the visual flow is reviewable and reproducible.
Langflow has no official certification; on this path the proof is a published flow plus a matching evaluation result.

Decision rule: stay visual for linear prototypes and demos; move to LangGraph when you need checkpointed human approval (interrupt plus Command(resume=...)), complex branching or loops, unit tests, or Agent Server cron jobs.

example.caption: Run all 10 invoices through the Langflow flow over HTTP and compare with the coded pipeline's saved results

pitfalls: Reading the wrong part of the response: the text sits deep in outputs, then outputs, then results, then message; inspect one raw response before writing the parser.
Different prompts or models in the flow and the code: use the same model, temperature 0 and the same schema, or the checkpoint comparison is meaningless.
Comparing raw strings for dates and amounts: normalise formats (ISO dates, numbers without commas or currency symbols) on both sides first.
Leaving the API key inside an exported flow JSON or committing it to GitHub; use environment variables.
Forcing human approval or long-running state into a visual flow; that is a signal to move the flow into LangGraph with a checkpointer and interrupt().
Using tweaks with stale component IDs after you rebuild a component; IDs change, so re-copy them from the API access pane.

files.code:
# invoice-extractor-langflow (Week 8: Langflow visual automations)

Goal: the Langflow flow and the coded pipeline return the same fields for 10 invoices.

## 1. Build the flow on the canvas (http://localhost:7860)
Create a new Blank Flow named `invoice-extractor`. Wire these components:

    Chat Input -> Structured Output -> Parser -> Chat Output
                        ^
                  Language Model

- Language Model: provider OpenAI, model gpt-4.1-mini, temperature 0.
- Structured Output: connect the model to it.
  - Paste SYSTEM_PROMPT from schema.py into its system prompt or instructions field.
