Align the prompt, schema types and descriptions; turn off memory
Resolve ambiguity with explicit rules

subjective.question: The invoice flow works in the Playground, but the same input through the API fails with a missing-credential error on the model component. How do you troubleshoot it?
subjective.answer: The Playground runs as me, with my global variables. An API call runs as the user who owns the API key, and that may be a service account. If the model's API key is a global variable that exists only for my user, the API run cannot find it. Steps: 1. Read the error and the flow log to confirm which component and which variable failed. 2. Check which user created the API key being used. 3. Check that the global variable exists for that user, or load it from the server environment, so every user gets it. 4. Confirm that the server process actually has the environment variable, for example in the Docker or systemd configuration. 5. Check that no tweak in the request overrides the credential field with an empty value. 6. Re-run the same request with curl and compare. I document the service account and its variables so this does not happen again.
keyPoints: The Playground and the API can run as different users
Global variables are scoped to users
Load secrets from the server environment
Check tweaks for overrides of credential fields
Reproduce the failure with curl and document the service account

subjective.question: Three business units need the invoice extractor. Each has a different vendor master collection, and one must use a different model provider. Compare one shared flow driven by tweaks with three separate flows. Which is better?
subjective.answer: If the logic is the same and only parameters differ, such as the collection name or temperature, one shared flow with tweaks per unit keeps a single source of truth: a fix lands everywhere at once. The risks are that each client must hold the correct component IDs, a rebuilt component breaks every client's tweaks, and swapping a whole model provider is a structural change, not a parameter. So I would use a hybrid. Two units share one flow, with tweaks for the collection name. The unit that needs a different provider gets its own flow. The shared logic, vendor validation and normalisation, stays in a reusable subflow that all flows call, so it is still written once. Each flow is versioned in Git without keys, and the same 10-invoice regression set runs against every variant. If variants keep multiplying, moving to code with configuration is cleaner.
keyPoints: Tweaks suit parameter differences, not structural changes
Shared flows need stable component IDs
Use a separate flow for a different provider
Reuse common logic through a subflow
Run the same regression set on every variant

steps.overview: This final step takes one automation from your laptop to production. You package the graph with langgraph.json, test it locally with `langgraph dev` and LangSmith Studio, and deploy it to LangSmith Deployment (Agent Server) with cron schedules, tracing, online evaluators and alerts. You then finish the three LangChain Academy courses and write a case study with real numbers: hours saved, accuracy, approval rate, cost and latency. That case study is what you will show in interviews.
objectives: Configure langgraph.json and run an agent locally with `langgraph dev`, then debug it in LangSmith Studio.
Deploy the graph to LangSmith Deployment and schedule it with cron jobs that use an IANA timezone, webhooks and end times.
Define cost, latency and error budgets, and enforce them with LangSmith automation rules, online evaluators and alerts.
Measure hours saved, accuracy and approval rate from traces and human-review decisions.
Complete the LangChain Academy courses on LangGraph, Ambient Agents and LangSmith, and present a recorded demo plus case study.

concepts.explanation: This is the config file that the LangGraph CLI and Agent Server read. 'dependencies' lists packages or local paths, for example ["."]. 'graphs' maps a graph ID to 'path/to/file.py:variable', where the variable is a compiled graph such as the output of create_agent. 'env' points to a .env file or inline variables.

This CLI command starts a local in-memory Agent Server with hot reload. It needs the inmem extra of langgraph-cli. It serves your graphs from langgraph.json and lets LangSmith Studio connect to them, so you can step through runs, inspect state and resume interrupts. It is for development only, because state is not kept durably.

This is the managed runtime for LangGraph apps. It is built on four objects: assistants, threads, runs and cron jobs. It provides built-in persistence, so you do not attach your own checkpointer, and a task queue for background runs. Human-in-the-loop interrupts survive restarts because checkpoints are stored server-side.

POST /runs/crons takes a schedule (cron expression), an assistant_id and an input. Each firing creates a new thread and sends the same input. Times are in UTC unless you pass an IANA timezone such as 'Asia/Kolkata'. Other options are on_run_completed ('delete' is the default, or 'keep'), end_time, enabled and a webhook that is called when the run finishes. POST /threads/{thread_id}/runs/crons instead reuses one existing thread.

Use HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(interrupt_on={...}) in create_agent, or interrupt() in a custom node. Either one pauses the run and stores the payload. The reviewer resumes with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id, and the paused node re-runs from its start. Record every approve, edit and reject decision, because these become your approval-rate metric.

A budget is an agreed limit for one automation. Examples: maximum cost per run in rupees, p95 latency, and a tolerated error rate over a time window. If you exceed the budget, you change something: cheaper model fallback, model call limits, tool retry, or pausing the cron. Write the budgets down before launch so your alerts have thresholds.

A rule has four parts: an item type (runs or threads), a filter, a sampling rate and an action. Actions include adding to a dataset, adding to an annotation queue, calling a webhook and extending retention. Online evaluators (LLM-as-judge or code) score live runs. Backfill of past runs happens only when the rule is created. Rules run on independent schedules, so a webhook rule should filter on eq(feedback_key, "...") so it fires only after scoring.

Alerts fire when a threshold is crossed on metrics such as error rate, latency or feedback score. They notify through the native Slack integration or a webhook. Map each alert to one of your budgets so that every page tells you which budget is burning.

Hours saved = items processed × (manual minutes − review minutes) ÷ 60. Accuracy comes from a LangSmith experiment, evaluate() on a labelled dataset, or from online evaluator scores. Approval rate = approved without edits ÷ total proposals. Report edit and reject rates separately. Add cost per item and p95 latency taken from traces.

keyFacts: `langgraph dev` runs an in-memory local server for development and Studio. Use LangSmith Deployment for durable production runs.
In langgraph.json, 'graphs' values use the 'file.py:variable' format, and the variable must be a compiled graph.
The Agent Server handles persistence automatically. Do not pass your own checkpointer to graphs you deploy there.
Cron schedules are in UTC unless a timezone is set. For India use 'Asia/Kolkata'; for example, 09:00 IST equals 03:30 UTC.
Each cron firing creates a new thread. on_run_completed defaults to 'delete'. Set 'keep' if you need to inspect those threads later.
Use end_time to stop a cron and enabled to pause it without deleting it. The cron webhook is called when the run is done.
Tracing needs LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY set in the deployment environment.
Online evaluators can be backfilled only when the rule is created. They are not retroactive later.
A webhook automation that should act on scores must filter on eq(feedback_key, "<key>"), because rules run independently.
Alerts go to Slack (native) or a webhook, on error rate, latency or feedback thresholds.

curl -X POST "$DEPLOYMENT_URL/runs/crons" \

pitfalls: Forgetting the timezone. '0 9 * * *' without 'Asia/Kolkata' fires at 14:30 IST, not 09:00.
Treating `langgraph dev` as production. It is in-memory, so threads and interrupts are lost on restart.
Resuming an approval on a new thread_id, or putting side effects such as sending an email before interrupt(). The node re-runs from its start on resume, so those side effects run twice.
Building a webhook rule that does not filter on the evaluator's feedback_key. It fires before scoring finishes and acts on unscored runs.
Reporting vague results like 'saved lots of time'. Interviewers expect baseline manual time, volume, approval or edit rates, accuracy on a dataset, cost per item and p95 latency.
Leaving on_run_completed as 'delete' and then finding there are no threads to audit when a scheduled run misbehaves.

"""Create the weekday 09:00 IST cron job, or trigger one run now with --once."""
import asyncio
import os
import sys

import httpx
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langgraph_sdk import get_client

load_dotenv()
URL = os.environ.get("AGENT_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:2024")  # langgraph dev default port
API_KEY = os.environ.get("LANGSMITH_API_KEY", "")
ASSISTANT_ID = "invoice_agent"  # the graph name in langgraph.json
INPUT = {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Process today's pending invoices."}]}


def create_cron() -> None:
    body = {
        "assistant_id": ASSISTANT_ID,
        "schedule": "0 9 * * 1-5",     # 09:00 Mon-Fri
        "timezone": "Asia/Kolkata",    # without this, the schedule is read as UTC
        "input": INPUT,                # the same input is sent on every firing
        "on_run_completed": "keep",    # keep threads so reviewers can resume interrupts
    }
    if os.environ.get("CRON_WEBHOOK_URL"):
        body["webhook"] = os.environ["CRON_WEBHOOK_URL"]  # called when each run is done
    r = httpx.post(f"{URL}/runs/crons", json=body, headers={"x-api-key": API_KEY})
    r.raise_for_status()
    print("Cron created:", r.json())


async def run_once() -> None:
    # Local test: one run on a new thread, the same as one cron firing.
    client = get_client(url=URL, api_key=API_KEY or None)
    thread = await client.threads.create()
    await client.runs.wait(thread["thread_id"], ASSISTANT_ID, input=INPUT)
    state = await client.threads.get_state(thread["thread_id"])
    print("Thread", thread["thread_id"], "paused before:", state["next"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(run_once()) if "--once" in sys.argv else create_cron()

"""Approval inbox: find interrupted threads, ask a human, resume, log the decision."""
import asyncio
import csv
import datetime as dt
import os

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langgraph_sdk import get_client

load_dotenv()
URL = os.environ.get("AGENT_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:2024")
ASSISTANT_ID = "invoice_agent"
LOG = "decisions.csv"  # metrics.py reads this to compute the approval rate


async def main() -> None:
    client = get_client(url=URL, api_key=os.environ.get("LANGSMITH_API_KEY"))
    threads = await client.threads.search(status="interrupted", limit=50)
    for t in threads:
        state = await client.threads.get_state(t["thread_id"])
        for task in state["tasks"]:
            for intr in task["interrupts"]:
                # HumanInTheLoopMiddleware sends action_requests (tool name + args)
                decisions = []
                for req in intr["value"]["action_requests"]:
                    print(f"\n{req['name']} {req['args']}")
                    choice = input("approve / reject? ").strip().lower()
                    if choice == "approve":
                        decisions.append({"type": "approve"})
                    else:
                        reason = input("Reason: ")
                        decisions.append({"type": "reject", "message": reason})
                    with open(LOG, "a", newline="") as f:
                        csv.writer(f).writerow(
                            [dt.datetime.now().isoformat(), t["thread_id"],
                             req["args"].get("invoice_id"), choice]
                        )
                # Resume on the same thread. The paused node re-runs and applies the decisions.
                await client.runs.wait(
                    t["thread_id"], ASSISTANT_ID,
                    command={"resume": {"decisions": decisions}},
                )
                print("Resumed", t["thread_id"])


if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

"""Check cost, latency and error budgets, and print the case-study numbers."""
import csv
import datetime as dt
import os
import statistics

from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langsmith import Client

load_dotenv()
PROJECT = os.environ["LANGSMITH_PROJECT"]
BUDGET = {"error_rate": 0.02, "p95_latency_s": 60, "cost_per_run_usd": 0.05}
MANUAL_MIN_PER_INVOICE = 12  # baseline you measured before automating
REVIEW_MIN_PER_INVOICE = 1   # time a human now spends per approval

since = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc) - dt.timedelta(days=7)
runs = list(Client().list_runs(project_name=PROJECT, is_root=True, start_time=since))
if not runs:
    raise SystemExit("No runs in the last 7 days")

errors = sum(1 for r in runs if r.error)
latencies = sorted((r.end_time - r.start_time).total_seconds() for r in runs if r.end_time)
costs = [float(r.total_cost) for r in runs if r.total_cost is not None]
p95 = statistics.quantiles(latencies, n=20)[-1] if len(latencies) >= 2 else latencies[0]

actual = {
    "error_rate": errors / len(runs),
    "p95_latency_s": p95,
    "cost_per_run_usd": sum(costs) / len(costs) if costs else 0.0,
}
print(f"Runs (7 days): {len(runs)}")
for k, limit in BUDGET.items():
    status = "OK" if actual[k] <= limit else "OVER BUDGET"
    print(f"{k:18} {actual[k]:.3f}  (budget {limit})  {status}")

# Approval rate and hours saved, from the human decisions logged by review.py
rows = list(csv.reader(open("decisions.csv"))) if os.path.exists("decisions.csv") else []
approved = sum(1 for r in rows if r[3] == "approve")
if rows:
    saved_min = len(rows) * (MANUAL_MIN_PER_INVOICE - REVIEW_MIN_PER_INVOICE)
    print(f"Invoices reviewed: {len(rows)}")
    print(f"Approval rate:     {approved / len(rows):.0%}")
    print(f"Hours saved:       {saved_min / 60:.1f}")

# invoice-approval-agent
Every weekday at 09:00 IST this agent checks pending invoices against purchase orders.
It pauses for human approval before every payment. All runs are traced and monitored in LangSmith.

## Setup
Create `.env` with these keys:
```
OPENAI_API_KEY=...
LANGSMITH_API_KEY=...
LANGSMITH_TRACING=true
LANGSMITH_PROJECT=invoice-approval-agent
AGENT_URL=http://127.0.0.1:2024   # change to your deployment URL after you deploy
CRON_WEBHOOK_URL=                  # optional
```

## Local
1. `langgraph dev` starts the Agent Server and opens LangSmith Studio.
2. `python scripts/schedule_cron.py --once` runs once. The run pauses at `post_payment`.
3. `python scripts/review.py` lets you approve or reject each payment and resume the thread.

## Production (LangSmith Deployment)
1. Deploy the repo with `langgraph.json`. Set `AGENT_URL` to the deployment URL.
2. `python scripts/schedule_cron.py` creates the weekday 09:00 Asia/Kolkata cron.
   Each firing creates a new thread. Threads are kept so reviewers can resume them.

## Monitoring (LangSmith UI)
- **Online evaluator:** an LLM-as-judge on root runs, feedback key `invoice_correctness`.
  It checks that mismatched invoices are flagged. Backfill is only possible when you create the rule.
- **Automation rules:**
  - Filter `eq(feedback_key, "invoice_correctness")` with low scores. Action: add to annotation queue.
    Filtering on the feedback key makes the rule fire only after scoring.
  - Filter on errored runs. Action: add to the regression dataset.
- **Alerts:** send to Slack when error rate > 2%, p95 latency > 60 s, or average `invoice_correctness` drops.

## Budgets
The agent code protects the budgets: `ModelCallLimitMiddleware` caps cost and `ToolRetryMiddleware` cuts errors.
`python scripts/metrics.py` checks the last 7 days against these limits:
- error rate 2%
- p95 latency 60 s
- cost $0.05 per run

## Case study template (use your real numbers)
- Baseline: X invoices/week x 12 min done by hand.
- After: runs, approval rate, hours saved (all from metrics.py).
- Accuracy: online evaluator score, plus a sample of runs you labelled by hand.
- Reliability: error rate, p95 latency and cost per run against the budgets.
- Demo: cron fires, run pauses, human approves, trace appears in LangSmith, alert reaches Slack.

revision.examFocus: This step maps to the deployment and production modules of LangChain Academy's Introduction to LangGraph, Ambient Agents with LangGraph and Introduction to LangSmith. These are self-paced courses with no proctored exam, so the real test is the interview that follows. Interviewers probe whether you can tell local dev from production, schedule correctly in IST, keep human approval safe on resume, wire evaluators, rules and alerts in the right order, and defend a case study with real numbers.

compare.difference: langgraph dev is in-memory and meant for development and debugging in Studio. Agent Server gives durable persistence, a task queue for background runs and cron jobs.
compare.chooseA: Pick it when the question is about iterating on a graph, stepping through interrupts in Studio, or testing langgraph.json locally.
compare.chooseB: Pick it when threads, pending approvals or schedules must survive restarts, or when the word 'production' appears.

compare.difference: The stateless cron creates a fresh thread every firing with the same input. The thread cron keeps adding runs to one existing thread, so state and history build up.
compare.chooseA: Use it for independent daily jobs, such as a morning invoice digest where each day stands alone.
compare.chooseB: Use it when each run must see earlier results, such as a running weekly summary that builds on the previous one.

compare.difference: With delete, the thread each firing creates is removed after the run. With keep, it stays so you can inspect state and audit it.
compare.chooseA: Choose delete for high-volume, low-risk jobs where traces in LangSmith are enough and thread clutter is a concern.
compare.chooseB: Choose keep for approval flows, finance or compliance jobs, or any schedule you may need to debug or audit later.

compare.b: Offline experiment with evaluate() on a dataset
compare.difference: Online evaluators score live production runs as they arrive, with sampling. evaluate() runs your target against a fixed dataset so you can compare versions before release.
compare.chooseA: Pick online when the question says 'monitor quality in production', 'live traffic' or 'sample 10% of runs'.
compare.chooseB: Pick offline when it says 'before deploying', 'regression test', 'compare prompts', or 'accuracy figure for the case study'.

compare.b: Automation rule with a webhook action
compare.difference: An alert fires when an aggregate metric crosses a threshold, such as error rate, latency or feedback score. An automation rule acts on individual matching runs or threads, such as sending them to a dataset, an annotation queue or a webhook.
compare.chooseA: Use an alert when on-call people must know that the system as a whole is degrading.
compare.chooseB: Use a rule when each bad or flagged run needs its own action, such as a human review queue or a downstream ticket.

cues.cue: 'state lost after restart' / 'pending approvals disappeared'
cues.pick: They were running on langgraph dev. Move to LangSmith Deployment.
cues.why: The dev server is in-memory. Agent Server persists threads and interrupts.

cues.cue: 'job fires at 2:30 pm instead of 9 am in India'
cues.pick: Add timezone "Asia/Kolkata", or rewrite the cron in UTC as '30 3 * * *'.
cues.why: Cron schedules are read as UTC unless you set an IANA timezone, and IST is UTC+5:30.

cues.cue: 'email sent twice after approval'
cues.pick: Move the side effect after interrupt() or into a separate node, and resume on the same thread_id with Command(resume=...).
cues.why: On resume the interrupted node re-runs from its start, so any code before interrupt() runs again.

cues.cue: 'webhook acted on runs that had no score'
cues.pick: Add eq(feedback_key, "<key>") to the webhook rule's filter.
cues.why: Rules run on independent schedules, so the webhook can run before the evaluator has scored the run.

cues.cue: 'need scores on last month's traces'
cues.pick: Backfill when you create the online evaluator rule. Otherwise, run an offline evaluate() over a dataset built from those traces.
cues.why: Backfill is offered only at rule creation. Evaluators do not apply retroactively later.

cues.cue: 'graph failed to load' / 'checkpointer conflict on deploy'
cues.pick: Check that the langgraph.json graphs entry points to 'file.py:variable', that the variable is a compiled graph, and remove your own checkpointer.
cues.why: Agent Server supplies persistence itself and expects a compiled graph object.

cues.cue: 'pause the schedule over Diwali without losing it'
cues.pick: Set enabled to false, or use end_time if it should stop permanently at a set date.
cues.why: enabled toggles the cron without deleting it, while end_time ends it.

cues.cue: 'quantify impact for leadership'
cues.pick: Report baseline manual minutes × volume, review time, approve/edit/reject rates, dataset accuracy, cost per item and p95 latency.
cues.why: Concrete before-and-after numbers are what interviewers and managers trust.

scenario.situation: A Pune-based NBFC built a LangGraph agent that reads overnight loan documents, drafts a summary email to credit officers and waits for approval before sending. In testing with langgraph dev it worked. In production, approvals sometimes vanish after a redeploy, the job runs at 14:30 IST instead of 09:00 IST, and officers occasionally get the same email twice. The team must fix this with the least custom infrastructure. What should they do?
reasoning: Vanishing approvals point to in-memory state. Move the graph to LangSmith Deployment and remove the hand-passed checkpointer, because Agent Server handles persistence.
The 5½-hour shift is a UTC problem. Create the cron with schedule '0 9 * * *' and timezone 'Asia/Kolkata', and set on_run_completed to 'keep' so each day's thread can be audited.

Duplicate emails mean the send happens before or inside the node that calls interrupt(). Put the send after approval, for example with HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on the send_email tool or a separate send node, and resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id.
Reject options such as writing a custom scheduler, adding an external database checkpointer or retrying sends. Each adds infrastructure without fixing the root cause.
Add tracing env vars to the deployment, plus a Slack alert on error rate and p95 latency, so regressions show up early.
scenario.answer: Deploy on LangSmith Deployment without a custom checkpointer, schedule the cron with timezone Asia/Kolkata and on_run_completed 'keep', and gate the email side effect behind the approval, resuming on the same thread_id. Each fix targets one root cause with built-in features.

memoryAids: DEV = Disappears Every reVive: langgraph dev forgets everything on restart. Production goes to the Agent Server.
'Nine IST = Three-thirty UTC': add 5:30 to UTC to get IST, or subtract 5:30 from IST to get UTC. Better still, always pass Asia/Kolkata.
Case study 'VTACCL': Volume, Time saved, Approval/edit rate, Accuracy, Cost per item, Latency (p95).
cheatSheet: langgraph.json maps graph names to 'path/file.py:variable'. The variable must be compiled, for example create_agent(...) output or builder.compile().
Deploying to Agent Server: no custom checkpointer. Persistence, threads and the task queue are built in.
langgraph dev is for Studio and debugging only. Never treat it as production.
Cron: '0 9 * * *' with timezone 'Asia/Kolkata' gives 09:00 IST. The same expression without a timezone gives 14:30 IST.
Stateless cron gives a new thread per firing. Thread cron reuses one thread, so state accumulates.
Set on_run_completed to 'keep' for anything you may need to audit. The default 'delete' removes the evidence.
Pause a cron with enabled=false. Stop it at a date with end_time. Use the cron webhook to react when a run finishes.
Approval resume must use the same thread_id with Command(resume=...). Never place side effects before interrupt().
Set LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY in the deployment env, not just on your laptop.
Backfill online evaluators at rule creation only. A score-dependent webhook rule must filter eq(feedback_key, ...).
Alerts (Slack or webhook) cover aggregate thresholds: error rate, latency, feedback score. Rules cover per-run actions: dataset, annotation queue, webhook, retention.
Budgets to state: cost per item, p95 latency and an error-rate ceiling. Hours saved = volume × (manual minutes − review minutes) ÷ 60.
selfCheck: I can write a valid langgraph.json, run it with langgraph dev, open it in Studio and explain why that setup is not production.
I can create a cron job that fires at a given IST time, choose between stateless and thread crons, and justify my on_run_completed, enabled and end_time settings.
I can find and fix a double side effect in an approval flow and show a correct resume on the same thread_id.
I can set up an online evaluator, a score-filtered webhook rule and a Slack alert, and explain why their order and filters matter.
I can present a case study with baseline time, volume, approval/edit rates, dataset accuracy, cost per item and p95 latency, backed by LangSmith traces.
I have completed the three LangChain Academy courses and can demo my deployed automation end to end in under five minutes.

objective.question: Your project has a file agent.py that defines `graph = builder.compile()`. Which `graphs` entry in langgraph.json correctly registers it?
options: "invoice_agent": "./agent.py:builder"
"invoice_agent": "./agent.py"
"invoice_agent": "agent.graph()"
"invoice_agent": "./agent.py:graph"
objective.explanation: Values in `graphs` use the 'file.py:variable' format, and the variable must be a compiled graph. `builder` is an uncompiled StateGraph, a call expression is not the format, and a bare file path names no variable.

objective.question: A teammate runs `langgraph dev`, connects LangSmith Studio, and then proposes using the same process as the production server for a nightly automation. What is the main problem?
options: `langgraph dev` only supports graphs built with create_deep_agent
`langgraph dev` disables interrupts
`langgraph dev` runs an in-memory local server meant for development, so it is not durable for production runs
`langgraph dev` cannot connect to LangSmith Studio
objective.explanation: `langgraph dev` is an in-memory development server for local testing and Studio. For durable production runs, use LangSmith Deployment (Agent Server). Studio connection and interrupts work fine locally.

objective.question: You deploy an approval agent to LangSmith Deployment. Your code calls `create_agent(..., checkpointer=InMemorySaver())`. What should you change?
options: Remove the checkpointer, because the Agent Server handles persistence automatically
Move the checkpointer to every subagent instead
Keep it, because the Agent Server needs an explicit checkpointer
Replace InMemorySaver with a SQLite saver file in the container
objective.explanation: The Agent Server provides persistence automatically, so you should not pass your own checkpointer to a deployed graph. Subagents never get their own checkpointer either, because only the outermost graph is checkpointed.

objective.question: A Bengaluru finance team wants a cron job to fire every day at 09:00 IST. Which configuration is correct?
options: schedule "30 3 * * *" with timezone "Asia/Kolkata"
schedule "0 9 * * *" with timezone "Asia/Kolkata"
schedule "30 14 * * *" with no timezone
schedule "0 9 * * *" with no timezone
objective.explanation: Cron schedules are read in UTC unless you set an IANA timezone. So "0 9 * * *" with Asia/Kolkata fires at 09:00 IST, and "30 3 * * *" without a timezone would also work. Option A fires at 14:30 IST, and option B fires at 03:30 IST.

objective.question: Your daily cron runs fine, but the next morning you cannot find any of its threads to debug a bad output. What is the most likely cause?
options: Cron jobs always reuse a single thread that gets overwritten
LANGSMITH_TRACING was set to true
The webhook URL deleted the thread
on_run_completed was left at its default of "delete"
objective.explanation: Each cron firing creates a new thread, and on_run_completed defaults to "delete". Set it to "keep" if you need to inspect those threads later. A webhook only receives a call when the run is done; it does not delete threads.

objective.question: During a month-end freeze you must stop a scheduled reconciliation agent for one week, then restart it with the same settings. What is the best approach?
options: Set end_time to one week from now
Set enabled to false, then set it back to true after the freeze
Change on_run_completed to "keep"
Delete the cron and recreate it later
objective.explanation: The `enabled` flag pauses a cron without deleting it. `end_time` stops the cron permanently at that time, deleting loses the configuration, and on_run_completed only controls whether threads are kept.

objective.question: Operations wants a Slack message when the error rate of the production invoice agent crosses a threshold. Which LangSmith feature fits best?
options: A LangSmith alert on error rate, sent through the native Slack integration
An annotation queue rule
A cron webhook on every run
An online evaluator with backfill enabled
objective.explanation: LangSmith alerts fire on thresholds such as error rate, latency and feedback scores, and send to Slack natively or to a webhook. A cron webhook fires on every completed run, not on a threshold.

objective.question: A deployed agent runs correctly, but no traces appear in LangSmith. It worked locally. What should you check first?
options: Whether on_run_completed is "keep"
Whether the cron timezone is Asia/Kolkata
Whether LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY are set in the deployment environment
Whether langgraph.json lists the graph as a compiled variable
objective.explanation: Tracing needs both LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY in the environment where the code runs. Local env vars do not carry over automatically. The other settings do not control trace export.

objective.question: You create an online LLM-as-judge evaluator for correctness without backfill. Two weeks later you want last month's runs scored. What is true?
options: Backfill is only possible when the rule is created, so it cannot be applied later to the existing rule
Backfill requires a cron job on the deployment
Online evaluators are always retroactive
You can edit the rule and enable backfill at any time
objective.explanation: Online evaluators can be backfilled only when the rule is created; they are not retroactive later. To score older runs, you would need another approach, such as adding them to a dataset and running an offline evaluate() experiment.

objective.question: An online evaluator writes the feedback key "correctness". You add a webhook automation rule to notify finance about low-scoring runs, but it often fires before any score exists. What fixes this?
options: Add the filter eq(feedback_key, "correctness") to the webhook rule
Put both rules in the same cron schedule
Change the item type from runs to threads
Lower the sampling rate of the webhook rule
objective.explanation: Automation rules run on independent schedules. Filtering the webhook rule on eq(feedback_key, "correctness") makes it act only on runs that already have that score. Changing the sampling rate or item type does not fix the ordering problem.

objective.question: A node creates a draft payment record in the ERP and then calls interrupt() for manager approval. After resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id, you see duplicate draft records. Why?
options: On resume, the interrupted node re-runs from its start, so code before interrupt() executes again
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware runs every tool twice
The Agent Server persists state only on the last node
Command(resume=...) always starts a new thread
objective.explanation: When a graph resumes, the node that called interrupt() re-runs from the beginning, so side effects placed before the interrupt repeat. To avoid duplicates, move side effects after the interrupt, into a separate node, or make them idempotent.

objective.question: You set a target of 99% successful runs per month for an automation that runs about 3,000 times a month. What is the monthly error budget?
options: 30 failed runs
300 failed runs
99 failed runs
3 failed runs
objective.explanation: The error budget is the allowed failure share: 1% of 3,000 runs is 30 failed runs. Once the budget is spent, you should prioritise reliability fixes over new features.

objective.question: What does this langgraph.json do when you run `langgraph dev` or deploy to LangSmith Deployment?
options: It means the project has no dependencies, because "." is a placeholder for an empty list
It registers only the first graph; a second entry needs a second langgraph.json file
It merges both graphs into one graph called invoice_agent and ignores daily_digest
It installs the project in the current directory as a dependency, registers two separate graphs by ID, and loads environment variables from the .env file
objective.explanation: "dependencies": ["."] tells the CLI to install the local project, each key under "graphs" registers its own graph ID from a file path and variable, and "env" points to an env file. Graphs are never merged, and one config file can register many graphs.

objective.question: A document pipeline handles about 8,000 runs a day. You add an online LLM-as-judge evaluator to the runs with a sampling rate of 0.25. What is the best estimate of extra judge calls per day for your cost budget?
options: About 2,000, because only about a quarter of matching runs are scored
About 250, because the sampling rate is a percentage of 1,000 runs
Zero until you backfill, because online evaluators score only past runs
8,000, because sampling only affects which runs show in the UI
objective.explanation: The sampling rate is the fraction of runs that match the filter and get sent to the evaluator, so 0.25 × 8,000 ≈ 2,000 judge calls a day. Online evaluators score live runs. Backfill is a one-time option when you create the rule.

objective.question: In production, reviewers say they cannot fix a wrong recipient address. Their only choices are to approve or reject the whole email. What is the correct change?
options: Replace HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with a call to interrupt() inside send_email
Add "edit" to allowed_decisions for send_email so reviewers can change the tool arguments before it runs
Add a checkpointer=InMemorySaver() argument so edits are saved
Add lookup_customer to interrupt_on so reviewers see the address earlier
objective.explanation: allowed_decisions controls what a reviewer can do with an interrupted tool call. Adding "edit" lets them correct arguments such as the recipient. Interrupting lookup_customer does not fix send_email. On the Agent Server, persistence is automatic, so an in-memory checkpointer is wrong.

objective.question: A manager approves a pending invoice in your custom approval UI. The deployed agent runs again, but it drafts a brand-new reply, and the original thread stays interrupted. The UI sends Command(resume=...) with config {"configurable": {"thread_id": str(uuid4())}}. What is wrong?
options: The Agent Server does not support interrupts, so approvals must happen outside LangGraph
The manager must call graph.get_state_history() before resuming
The resume must use the thread_id of the interrupted run; a new thread_id starts a fresh thread with no saved checkpoint
Command(resume=...) only works with stream_events version="v1"
objective.explanation: The checkpointer uses thread_id to find and resume the saved state. Each new UUID points to an empty thread, so the interrupted thread never resumes. The Agent Server fully supports interrupts and persistence.

objective.question: A company wants subject-matter experts to review and correct live extractions that an online evaluator scored low. Only after correction should they become regression examples. Which LangSmith automation rule action fits first?
options: Trigger a webhook to the ERP to reverse the extraction
Add matching traces to an annotation queue, filtered on the low evaluator feedback score
Extend data retention on all runs
Add matching traces to a dataset directly
objective.explanation: Annotation queues are built for human review and correction. Corrected items can then go into a dataset. Adding straight to a dataset would save uncorrected outputs as references, and extending retention does not trigger any review.

objective.question: Your latency budget for an approval-drafting automation is p95 under 30 seconds. LangSmith shows an average latency of 12 s and a p95 of 45 s. What is the right conclusion?
options: The budget is breached: at least 5% of runs take longer than 30 s, so investigate the slow tail (for example retries, long documents or tool timeouts)
The budget is met if the p99 is under 60 s
The budget cannot be judged without p50
The budget is met, because the average is well under 30 s
objective.explanation: A p95 target means 95% of runs must finish within 30 s. A p95 of 45 s breaks it, whatever the average is. Averages hide slow tail runs, which are usually caused by retries or very large inputs.

objective.question: For your case study, the automation produced 400 drafts in a month. Reviewers approved 300 unchanged, edited and then approved 60, and rejected 40. Which statement is the most honest to present in an interview?
options: Approval rate 90%, with no other breakdown
Approved unchanged 75%, approved after edit 15%, rejected 10%, with the definition of each stated
Accuracy 90%, because approved drafts are correct by definition
Approval rate 100%, because every draft was reviewed
objective.explanation: Splitting unchanged, edited and rejected drafts shows how much human effort is still needed, and an interviewer can check every number. Folding edits into one 90% figure overstates automation. Approval rate is also not the same as measured accuracy against a reference.

objective.question: You are taking an invoice automation from your laptop to production. Which order of steps is correct?
options: Create the cron job → write langgraph.json → deploy → test with langgraph dev → set alerts
Write langgraph.json → deploy → set alerts → test with langgraph dev on the production server → create the cron job
Write langgraph.json → test locally with langgraph dev and Studio → deploy to LangSmith Deployment with environment variables → create the cron job with a timezone → set alerts and online evaluators
Deploy to LangSmith Deployment → write langgraph.json → create the cron job → test in Studio with langgraph dev → set alerts
objective.explanation: The config must exist before langgraph dev or a deployment can load the graph. You test locally first and deploy next. Crons need a deployed assistant to target, and alerts need live runs to watch. The other orders schedule or monitor something that does not exist yet, or treat langgraph dev as production.

objective.question: This deployment builds, but every run fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'invoice_agent'`. graph.py contains `from invoice_agent.tools import parse_pdf`. Locally the code ran inside an activated virtual environment. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add "." (the project folder with its pyproject.toml) to "dependencies" so the local package and its requirements are installed
Remove the "env" key, because .env files block imports
Rename the graph variable from graph to app
Change the graph path to use a dotted module name instead of a file path
objective.explanation: "dependencies" tells the build what to install. An empty list means your own package is never installed in the image, so its imports fail. The file:variable path format is valid, and the env key and the variable name have nothing to do with imports.

objective.question: A festive-season reminder cron must run daily until 31 March and then stop on its own, with no one having to remember to turn it off. Which cron setting does this?
options: Set enabled to false in the create request
Use POST /threads/{thread_id}/runs/crons instead
Set end_time to the end of 31 March
Set on_run_completed to "delete"
objective.explanation: end_time stops the cron automatically after a given time. on_run_completed only decides whether threads are kept. enabled=false at creation means the cron never fires. Thread crons change where runs happen, not when the schedule ends.

objective.question: After you deploy this approval node, no invoice ever pauses for a manager, and every invoice is marked rejected straight away. What is the cause?
options: interrupt() pauses the graph by raising a special exception, and the broad except catches it, so the pause never reaches the runtime
The node must return a Command, not a dict
The payload must be a string, not a dict
interrupt() can only be used inside HumanInTheLoopMiddleware
objective.explanation: LangGraph pauses a run by raising an internal interrupt exception out of the node. Catching Exception swallows it, so the code falls through to "reject". Never wrap interrupt() in a broad try/except. A dict payload and a dict return are both valid, and interrupt() works in any node.

objective.question: In this subagents design, what is the mistake?

code.code:
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.tools import tool
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver

research = create_agent(model, tools=[search_vendor],
                        checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

@tool
def ask_research(question: str) -> str:
    """Ask the vendor research subagent."""
    out = research.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": question}]})
    return out["messages"][-1].content

main = create_agent(model, tools=[ask_research],
                    checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

options: Only the outermost graph should get a checkpointer, so remove it from the research subagent
Tools cannot call other agents
The main agent must not have a checkpointer; only workers do
Subagents must be built with langgraph-supervisor
objective.explanation: In the subagents pattern only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer. Here the inner one would also expect its own thread_id. langgraph-supervisor is no longer actively maintained, and wrapping a worker inside a tool is exactly the recommended pattern. On the Agent Server, persistence for the outer graph is handled automatically.

objective.question: Your automation has a 99% monthly success target on about 3,000 runs, which gives an error budget of 30 failed runs. By day 8 you have already had 24 failures. What is the best response?
options: Freeze risky changes, look at the failed traces to find the cause, and spend the next work on reliability fixes such as retries or fallbacks
Turn off tracing to reduce load
Raise the target to 98% so the budget is not breached
Nothing yet; the budget resets at month end
objective.explanation: Using 80% of the budget in a quarter of the month is a fast burn. Error-budget policy says you stop shipping risky changes and fix reliability. Changing the target hides the problem, and turning off tracing removes the evidence you need.

objective.question: Last month the pipeline processed 6,000 documents. The pipeline's own LLM calls cost ₹15,000 and the online LLM-as-judge evaluator cost ₹3,000. What cost per document should the case study report, including monitoring?
objective.explanation: Total cost is ₹15,000 + ₹3,000 = ₹18,000, and ₹18,000 ÷ 6,000 = ₹3.00. ₹2.50 leaves out evaluation cost, and ₹0.50 counts only the judge. Monitoring is part of the real cost of running the automation.

objective.question: A support agent has three tools. search_orders is read-only. issue_refund must be approved or rejected but never edited. send_email must allow approve, edit or reject. Which HumanInTheLoopMiddleware configuration is best?
options: interrupt_on={"issue_refund": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "reject"]}, "send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}}
interrupt_on={"issue_refund": {"allowed_decisions": ["reject"]}, "send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["edit"]}}
interrupt_on={"send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}}

interrupt_on={"search_orders": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve"]}, "issue_refund": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}, "send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}}
objective.explanation: Only the tools with side effects need review, each with exactly the decisions the policy allows. Option A pauses on harmless reads and lets reviewers edit refunds. Option C lets refunds run with no review. Option D removes approval paths that are required.

objective.question: You changed the extraction prompt and want to show in an interview that version 2 is better than version 1. Which method is most defensible?
options: Test v2 on five documents you choose by hand
Run v1 on the old dataset and v2 on a new, easier dataset
Run evaluate() for v1 and v2 against the same LangSmith dataset with the same evaluators, then compare the two experiments
Deploy v2 and compare this week's average feedback score with last week's
objective.explanation: Same dataset plus same evaluators gives a controlled comparison, and the two experiments sit side by side in LangSmith. Week-to-week production averages change with traffic. Five hand-picked documents are anecdote, and different datasets cannot be compared.

objective.question: Each time the nightly reconciliation cron finishes, an internal ERP job must start straight away. What is the simplest reliable trigger?
options: A LangSmith alert on latency
A second cron scheduled 30 minutes later
An automation rule on threads with sampling rate 1.0 and a webhook action
Give the cron a webhook URL; it is called when the run is done
objective.explanation: The cron webhook is called when the scheduled run completes, so it is tied directly to that run. Automation rules run on their own schedules, so they add delay. Alerts are for thresholds, not run completion. A fixed offset breaks whenever a run takes longer than expected.

objective.question: An ambient email assistant keeps one long-lived thread per client. After a few weeks, runs on busy threads start failing with context-length errors. What is the best fix?
options: Add SummarizationMiddleware(model=..., trigger=("tokens", 4000), keep=("messages", 20)) to create_agent
Raise the model call limit
Delete old checkpoints with get_state_history
Start a new thread for every email
objective.explanation: SummarizationMiddleware compresses older history once a token threshold is reached and keeps the recent messages. That keeps the context bounded without losing what the thread is about. A new thread per email throws away context. Call limits control loops, not context size, and get_state_history only reads checkpoints.

objective.question: Your main model provider has a 40-minute outage, and every run in that window fails, using up your error budget. Which built-in middleware most directly protects against this next time?
options: Model call limit middleware
LLM tool selection middleware
Model fallback middleware, which switches to a second model when the primary fails
Tool retry middleware
objective.explanation: Model fallback sends the call to an alternative model when the primary errors, so runs still succeed during a provider outage. Tool retry handles failing tools, not the model. Call limits cap usage, and tool selection trims the tool list.

objective.question: A support inbox gets about 50 emails a day at random times. Drafts must be ready within 2 minutes of an email arriving. Which design is better?
options: A daily cron at 09:00 Asia/Kolkata
langgraph dev polling the inbox in a loop
Event-driven: the email provider's webhook calls your service, which starts one background run on the Agent Server per email
A cron every minute that checks the inbox
objective.explanation: Event-driven runs start only when an email arrives and meet the 2-minute target. The Agent Server's task queue handles background runs. A one-minute cron creates a new thread on every firing, so about 1,440 mostly empty runs a day waste cost. A daily cron misses the target, and langgraph dev is not production.

subjective.question: Explain the difference between `langgraph dev` and LangSmith Deployment. When would you use each?
subjective.answer: `langgraph dev` is the LangGraph CLI command that starts an in-memory local server. It reads my langgraph.json, serves the graphs I listed, and lets me open LangSmith Studio. In Studio I can step through the graph, view state, and test interrupts. Because state is in memory, it is lost on restart, so I use it only for development and debugging. LangSmith Deployment runs the Agent Server. It is built on assistants, threads, runs and cron jobs. It has built-in persistence and a task queue for background runs. That makes it right for production: scheduled automations, long approvals that may wait for hours, and durable thread history. One practical rule: I do not pass my own checkpointer to graphs I deploy there, because the server handles persistence.
keyPoints: langgraph dev runs an in-memory local server for development and Studio
State is not durable locally
LangSmith Deployment (Agent Server) is built on assistants, threads, runs and crons, with persistence and a task queue
Do not pass your own checkpointer when deploying

subjective.question: Walk through the langgraph.json you would write for a document-processing automation, and name the common mistakes.
subjective.answer: langgraph.json tells the CLI and the Agent Server what to serve. The key section is `graphs`. It maps a graph ID to a path in 'file.py:variable' format, for example "invoice_agent": "./src/agent.py:graph". The variable must be a compiled graph. For example, the result of create_agent, or of StateGraph.compile(). I also declare dependencies and point to an env file for local secrets such as model keys and LANGSMITH_API_KEY. Common mistakes are: pointing at the uncompiled builder; adding a checkpointer to the compiled graph for deployment; leaving out the variable name; and assuming local env vars exist in production. For multi-agent setups, I expose only the outer supervisor-style agent whose tools wrap the subagents, because only the outermost graph is checkpointed.
keyPoints: graphs uses 'file.py:variable' format
The variable must be a compiled graph
Dependencies and env configuration
No custom checkpointer when deploying
Expose only the outer agent in multi-agent designs

subjective.question: Design a cron job that sends a daily overdue-invoice digest at 09:00 IST on weekdays, and that you can debug later.
subjective.answer: I would call POST /runs/crons, or client.crons in the Python SDK, with these settings: assistant_id set to my digest assistant; input set to a fixed instruction such as "summarise overdue invoices"; schedule "0 9 * * 1-5"; and timezone "Asia/Kolkata". Without a timezone, the schedule is read as UTC, so I would have to write "30 3 * * 1-5" instead. Each firing creates a new thread with the same input. Because I want to debug past runs, I set on_run_completed to "keep", since the default "delete" removes those threads. I add a webhook URL so my system is notified when each run finishes. I keep `enabled` available to pause the cron during a freeze. If the job is for a fixed project, I set end_time. Tracing env vars in the deployment let me see every run in LangSmith.
keyPoints: POST /runs/crons with schedule, assistant_id and input
Timezone Asia/Kolkata; otherwise the schedule is UTC (03:30 UTC = 09:00 IST)
Each firing creates a new thread; set on_run_completed to keep
Use the webhook on completion, enabled to pause, and end_time to stop

subjective.question: How do you implement human approval for an ambient email assistant in production, and what pitfalls do you guard against?
subjective.answer: I build the agent with create_agent and add HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with interrupt_on={"send_email": {"allowed_decisions": ["approve", "edit", "reject"]}}. When the agent tries to send an email, the run pauses with an interrupt payload. On the Agent Server, the thread is persisted, so the approval can wait hours. My review UI, or Agent Inbox-style tooling, reads the interrupt. The reviewer's decision is resumed with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id. The pitfalls are these. First, resume must use the same thread_id, or nothing resumes. Second, the interrupted node re-runs from its start, so any side effect before the interrupt must be idempotent or moved. Third, I track every decision as data: approve, edit or reject. Those decisions give me my approval-rate metric for the case study.
keyPoints: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware with interrupt_on and allowed_decisions
The Agent Server persists the paused thread
Resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id
The node re-runs on resume, so side effects must be idempotent
Log decisions to compute the approval rate

subjective.question: What are cost, latency and error budgets for an AI automation, and how would you set and enforce them?
subjective.answer: A budget is an agreed limit that I measure against. A cost budget is a target such as rupees per document or per month. I estimate it from token usage in LangSmith traces. A latency budget is a target such as p95 end-to-end time, for example under a set number of seconds for a background job. It is looser for background jobs than for chat. An error budget is the failure share I accept. With a 99% success target over 3,000 runs, I can afford 30 failures. To enforce them, I use middleware. Model call limits cap runaway loops. Summarization limits context size. Model fallback and tool retry reduce errors. I monitor with LangSmith alerts on error rate and latency, sent to Slack. If the error budget burns early, I freeze feature work and fix reliability first.
keyPoints: Clear definitions of cost, latency and error budgets
Measure from LangSmith traces (tokens, latency, errors)
Enforce with middleware: call limits, summarization, fallback, retry
Alerts on thresholds; budget burn drives priorities

subjective.question: Describe how you would use online evaluators and automation rules to catch bad extractions in a live document pipeline.
subjective.answer: First, I create an online evaluator on the production project. It can be an LLM-as-judge that checks extraction correctness, or a code evaluator that validates the schema. It writes a feedback key, say "extraction_ok". I decide on backfill at creation time, because backfill is not possible later. Next, I add automation rules. Each rule has an item type (runs), a filter, a sampling rate and an action. One rule sends low-scoring runs to an annotation queue for human review. Another adds them to a dataset for regression tests. A third triggers a webhook to open a ticket. Rules run on independent schedules. So the webhook rule must filter on eq(feedback_key, "extraction_ok") plus a low score, otherwise it may fire before scoring. Finally, alerts on the feedback score notify Slack.
keyPoints: Online evaluator (LLM-as-judge or code) writes a feedback key
Backfill only at rule creation
A rule = item type + filter + sampling rate + action
Actions: dataset, annotation queue, webhook, extended retention
Filter on eq(feedback_key, ...) because rules are independent

subjective.question: Your scheduled agent runs in production, but LangSmith shows no traces. How do you troubleshoot?
subjective.answer: First, I check the deployment environment, not my laptop. LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY must both be set there. A missing key is the most common cause. Second, I confirm that the project name points where I am looking. Third, I check that the cron actually fired. The cron webhook or the run list on the Agent Server shows whether runs happened. If on_run_completed is "delete", the threads may be gone, but traces should still exist if tracing was on. Fourth, I check the cron timing. A schedule without a timezone is in UTC, so a job I expected at 09:00 IST may run at 14:30 IST. Once traces appear, I add an error-rate alert, so silent failures do not recur.
keyPoints: Env vars must be set in the deployment environment
Check the project name
Verify cron firing through the webhook or run history
UTC vs timezone confusion
Add alerts afterwards

subjective.question: How do you calculate hours saved, accuracy and approval rate for your case study so the numbers hold up in an interview?
subjective.answer: Hours saved: I measure the manual baseline first, for example by timing 20 invoices done by hand to get minutes per document. Then: hours saved = (baseline minutes − remaining human review minutes) × volume ÷ 60. Volume comes from the run counts in LangSmith. Accuracy: I build a LangSmith dataset of labelled examples and run evaluate() with evaluators. These can be code checks for fields, or openevals create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT. I report the experiment result, and I watch online evaluator scores in production. Approval rate: from the human-in-the-loop decisions, approval rate = approvals ÷ total reviews. I report edit and reject rates separately. I also state the sample size, the time period and the cost per run. An interviewer trusts numbers with a clear method and honest limits more than big round claims.
keyPoints: Measure a manual baseline before automating
Hours saved formula using run volume
Accuracy from an evaluate() experiment on a labelled dataset plus online scores
Approval rate from HITL decisions, with edit and reject rates separate
State the sample size, period and cost

subjective.question: When would you use POST /threads/{thread_id}/runs/crons instead of POST /runs/crons?
subjective.answer: POST /runs/crons creates a new thread on every firing. Each run starts fresh with the same input. That suits stateless jobs like a daily report, where yesterday's conversation should not affect today's run. POST /threads/{thread_id}/runs/crons schedules runs on one existing thread. State then accumulates across firings. That is useful when the agent must remember context over time. Examples are a weekly vendor follow-up that tracks which reminders were already sent, or a monitoring agent that compares today's numbers with what it saw before. The trade-off is that a single thread grows, so I would add SummarizationMiddleware to keep context manageable. I would also watch the cost per run, which can rise as history grows.
keyPoints: /runs/crons creates a new thread per firing (stateless)
Thread cron reuses one thread (stateful)
Use cases for each
Context growth: use summarization and watch cost

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: 'You claim 94% accuracy. How was that measured, and how do you know it stays true in production?'
subjective.answer: I would explain both offline and online evidence. Offline: I created a LangSmith dataset of real, anonymised documents, with expected outputs labelled by the finance team. I ran evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]). The evaluators were code checks for exact fields like invoice number and amount, and an LLM-as-judge built with openevals create_llm_as_judge and CORRECTNESS_PROMPT for free-text fields. The 94% is from that experiment, and I can say how many examples it used. Online: an online evaluator scores sampled production runs. An alert notifies Slack if the feedback score drops. Low-scoring runs go to an annotation queue, and confirmed failures go back into the dataset. Any prompt or model change is re-run as a new experiment before release.
keyPoints: Labelled LangSmith dataset with known size
evaluate() with code evaluators and an LLM-as-judge
Online evaluator on sampled live runs
Alerts on feedback score; annotation queue feeds the dataset
Re-run experiments before changes

subjective.question: How would you set up LangSmith alerts for an automation, and what thresholds would you choose?
subjective.answer: I set alerts on the production project for three signals. The first is error rate, tied to my error budget. If I accept 1% failures, I alert well before that, so I have time to react. The second is latency, for example p95 above my latency budget, which often signals a slow tool or a model provider issue. The third is feedback score from my online evaluator, for example average correctness dropping below my offline baseline. Alerts go to Slack through the native integration for the team channel. Alerts can also go to a webhook, for example to page on-call or open a ticket. I avoid noisy thresholds, because alert fatigue makes people ignore real problems. I review the thresholds after the first few weeks of real traffic.
keyPoints: Alert on error rate, latency and feedback scores
Thresholds tied to the budgets and the offline baseline
Slack native integration or webhook
Avoid noise; tune after real traffic

subjective.question: Describe the end-to-end architecture of the automation you shipped for this step, as you would in a demo.
subjective.answer: Example: an invoice approval automation. A cron on the Agent Server runs at 09:00 with timezone Asia/Kolkata and on_run_completed set to "keep". Each run starts a new thread with the main create_agent. Its tools wrap an extraction subagent and an ERP lookup. Middleware adds PIIMiddleware to redact emails, tool retry, model fallback and call limits. Before posting a payment, HumanInTheLoopMiddleware interrupts. The finance manager approves, edits or rejects, and the run resumes with Command(resume=...) on the same thread. The deployment sets LANGSMITH_TRACING and LANGSMITH_API_KEY, so every run is traced. An online evaluator scores extraction, and a rule filtered on its feedback key sends failures to an annotation queue. Alerts notify Slack on error rate and latency. The demo ends with the case-study numbers: hours saved, accuracy, approval rate and cost per run.
keyPoints: Cron with timezone and keep
create_agent with subagents as tools and middleware
HITL approval with resume on the same thread
Tracing, online evaluator, rules and alerts
Closes with measured case-study numbers

subjective.question: A high-volume document pipeline is going over its monthly LLM cost budget. How would you bring cost under control without hurting accuracy, using LangChain v1 and LangSmith features?
subjective.answer: First, I measure. I group LangSmith traces by step and model to find where tokens go, for example long OCR text sent on every turn, or retry loops. Then I make targeted fixes. I add SummarizationMiddleware with a token trigger so long histories are compacted instead of re-sent. I add a model call limit so a confused run cannot loop forever. I use tool retry with limits instead of letting the model retry freely. I route easy documents to a cheaper model and keep model fallback for outages. I also check my evaluation costs: I lower the online evaluator's sampling rate and filter it to the run types that matter. Before shipping any change, I run evaluate() on a fixed dataset and compare accuracy against the baseline experiment. Finally, I set an alert on cost or token trends so a future regression is caught early, not at month end.
keyPoints: Measure per-step token use from traces before changing anything
SummarizationMiddleware and model call limits stop runaway context and loops
Tool retry limits, cheaper model routing and fallback
Tune evaluator sampling rate and filters, since judge calls also cost money
Verify with an evaluate() experiment against the baseline before deploying

subjective.question: How would you turn production failures into a regression test suite that protects every future deployment of your automation?
subjective.answer: I close the loop between production and offline evaluation. An online evaluator scores live runs, for example extraction correctness. An automation rule filters on that feedback key for low scores and sends those traces to an annotation queue. There, a domain expert corrects the output, and the corrected example goes into a LangSmith dataset. Over time, the dataset collects real, hard cases instead of invented ones. Before each deployment, I run evaluate(target, data=dataset, evaluators=[...]), using a code check for exact fields and create_llm_as_judge with CORRECTNESS_PROMPT for free text. I compare the new experiment with the last one and block the release if key scores drop. I keep the dataset versioned, and I watch for duplicates so one noisy customer does not dominate it. This makes my accuracy claim repeatable, not a single lucky number.
keyPoints: Online evaluator plus a rule filtered on the feedback key
Annotation queue for human correction before data enters the dataset
Dataset built from real production failures
evaluate() experiments compared against the previous version before each release
Release gate on score regression

subjective.question: A weekday cron triggers an approval agent, but managers do not notice that runs are waiting, so approvals pile up for days. How would you fix the notification design, and what must you be careful about?
subjective.answer: The run is paused at an interrupt and waiting on its thread, so the fix is to tell a human immediately. I have a few options. The cron job can use its webhook URL, which is called when the run is done. A small service receives it, checks whether the thread is interrupted, and posts the approval link with the thread_id to Slack or email. Another option is to notify from inside the graph, before the interrupt. But a node re-runs from its start on resume, so a notification inside the interrupting node would fire twice. I put it in a separate earlier node, or make it idempotent with a key. I also set on_run_completed to "keep" so the threads stay visible. I track how long threads wait for approval as a metric. Finally, I define what happens to stale approvals, for example an escalation after 24 hours.
keyPoints: Interrupted runs wait on their thread; reviewers need a link containing the thread_id
Cron webhook or a dedicated notify step
Node re-runs from its start on resume, so side effects must be idempotent or placed in a separate node
on_run_completed "keep" so threads stay inspectable
Track approval wait time and plan escalation for stale items

subjective.question: What does this code do, and how would you use it in an incident review after a wrong payment was approved?
subjective.answer: It lists every saved checkpoint for the thread inv-2026-0412, newest first. For each one it prints the checkpoint ID, the next node or nodes to run, and two state fields: the approval decision and the amount. In an incident review, I read it from the bottom up to rebuild the timeline. I look at what amount the extraction produced, what state the graph was in when it paused for approval, what the reviewer actually returned, and whether the amount changed after approval. This tells me whether the fault was a bad extraction, a reviewer error, or a bug after approval. I pair this with the LangSmith trace for the same thread to see the model inputs and outputs. On the Agent Server, persistence is automatic, so I can do this for any kept thread. That is one reason to keep threads for financial automations.
keyPoints: get_state_history returns checkpoints newest first for one thread_id
snap.next shows where the graph was paused or heading
Rebuild the timeline: extraction, then interrupt, then reviewer decision, then later steps
Combine with LangSmith traces to see model inputs and outputs
Threads must be kept, so set retention and on_run_completed deliberately

subjective.question: Your email automation processes customer messages containing email addresses and phone numbers. How do you reduce PII exposure in production while still keeping traces useful?
subjective.answer: I use layers. In the agent, I add PIIMiddleware, for example PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="redact", apply_to_input=True). This redacts the email before it reaches the model, so the model and its recorded inputs do not see the raw value. I add similar handling for other PII types the business cares about. Tools that genuinely need the real address, such as send_email, get it from a trusted lookup by customer ID, not from the model's text. In LangSmith, I keep tracing on, because I need traces for debugging. But I review what gets logged, keep retention to what the policy needs, and use extended retention only for traces flagged for review. I limit project access to the right team. Then I test with a dataset of messages that contain PII, and I check that the redaction actually appears in traces before going live.
keyPoints: PIIMiddleware with redact strategy on input before the model call
Tools fetch real contact data from trusted systems by ID
Tracing stays on, but retention and access are controlled
Extend retention only for flagged traces
Test redaction on a PII-heavy dataset before launch

subjective.question: An interviewer says: 'You claim 120 hours saved per month. Did you subtract reviewer time and running costs?' How do you answer with a net figure?
subjective.answer: I separate gross from net. Gross hours saved comes from a measured baseline: the manual time per document, timed on a sample, multiplied by the documents processed. Then I subtract the human time that remains. That includes reviewer minutes per approval, measured from the time between interrupt and resume or from reviewer logs, plus extra time for edited and rejected items, plus time spent fixing errors. For example: 1,200 documents at 7 minutes manual is 140 hours. Review takes 1 minute each, which is 20 hours. That leaves about 120 hours net. I also state the monthly LLM and infrastructure cost from LangSmith cost tracking and the deployment bill, and I compare it with the loaded hourly cost of the team. I mention the assumptions and the sample size. If the error budget was breached in a month, I include that rework too.
keyPoints: Gross savings from a timed manual baseline multiplied by volume
Subtract measured reviewer and rework time
Show a worked example with the formula
Include LLM and infrastructure cost against the cost of staff time
State assumptions, sample size and the measurement period

subjective.question: You prototyped an approval flow in Langflow. How do you decide what to move to LangGraph for production, and what do you show on your portfolio, given that Langflow has no official certification?
subjective.answer: Langflow is my visual sandbox. I use it to test prompts, component choices and the rough flow quickly in the Playground, and to show stakeholders something working early. For production, I rebuild the core in LangGraph or create_agent, because I need things the production requirements depend on. These are human approval with interrupts or HumanInTheLoopMiddleware, threads with persistence on the Agent Server, cron schedules, and LangSmith evaluation and alerts. The prompts and test cases from the prototype carry over. I turn them into a LangSmith dataset, so I can show that the production version matches or beats the prototype. Since there is no Langflow certificate, my evidence is a published flow exposed through its API, a short write-up of what changed when I moved to production and why, and the case study numbers. I am also clear that the Academy certificates cover LangGraph and LangSmith, not Langflow.
keyPoints: Langflow is for fast visual prototyping and stakeholder demos
Production needs interrupts, persistence, crons, evaluation and alerts in LangGraph and LangSmith
Reuse prompts and test cases as a LangSmith dataset to compare versions
Evidence: a published flow plus a migration write-up
Be honest that Langflow has no official certification

subjective.question: Case study: an HR team in Pune wants an onboarding automation. Requirements: process offer-letter PDFs every weekday at 10:00 IST; an HR manager must approve each letter before it is emailed, and may edit the salary line; candidate phone numbers and emails must not show up in traces; Slack must be alerted on failures; cost must stay under a monthly budget. Design it.
subjective.answer: I would build the agent with create_agent and register it in langgraph.json. I test it with langgraph dev and Studio, then deploy to LangSmith Deployment so threads and interrupts persist. The schedule is a cron on POST /runs/crons with schedule "0 10 * * 1-5", timezone "Asia/Kolkata", and on_run_completed "keep" so every run can be audited. For approval I add HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on send_email with approve, edit and reject, so the manager can correct the salary line. Approvals resume with Command(resume=...) on the same thread_id. PIIMiddleware for email and phone with strategy "redact" and apply_to_input=True keeps raw PII away from the model and out of traces. LangSmith alerts on error rate and latency go to Slack. For cost, I track cost per letter in traces, use a model call limit, and sample online evaluators. Finally, I report the approval rate and the edit rate.
keyPoints: Weekday cron with Asia/Kolkata timezone and on_run_completed keep
HITL middleware on send_email with edit allowed; resume on the same thread_id
PIIMiddleware with redact on input
Slack alerts on error rate and latency
Cost per item tracked, with call limits and sampling

subjective.question: A UK client's cron is set to "0 9 * * *" with no timezone. From November to March their team gets the report at 09:00 local time, but from April onwards it arrives at 10:00. What is happening, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: With no timezone, the cron schedule is read as UTC. London uses GMT (UTC+0) in winter and BST (UTC+1) in summer. So 09:00 UTC is 09:00 in winter but 10:00 in summer. The cron itself is working exactly as configured; the drift comes from daylight saving. The fix is to set timezone to the IANA name "Europe/London". The scheduler then follows the clock change and fires at 09:00 local time all year. This is why you use IANA names rather than fixed offsets: a fixed offset cannot follow DST. For Indian teams, "Asia/Kolkata" has no DST, but leaving it out still causes a fixed 5h30m error. I would also check the next few firing times after updating, and record in the runbook which timezone each cron uses.
keyPoints: No timezone means UTC
DST shifts the local time of a UTC schedule
Use IANA timezone Europe/London, not a fixed offset
Asia/Kolkata has no DST, but leaving it out still causes a 5h30m error

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this offline evaluation script for a deployed invoice agent. The graph is compiled with a checkpointer and has a HITL approval step. The dataset was built by copying last month's agent outputs as reference outputs.
subjective.answer: There are three problems. First, target calls graph.invoke without a config. The graph has a checkpointer, so it needs {"configurable": {"thread_id": ...}}, otherwise it fails. Each example should get a fresh thread_id. Second, the graph stops at the approval interrupt, so outputs are partial and you end up judging an unfinished run. Either evaluate the extraction step on its own (as a subgraph or a function) or run an evaluation build without the approval pause. Third, and most serious, the references are copies of the agent's own past outputs. A correctness score then only measures agreement with old behaviour, not truth, so the 'accuracy' number is meaningless. The reference outputs must be checked or corrected by people, for example through an annotation queue. The judge setup itself is fine.
keyPoints: Checkpointer requires thread_id in config
Interrupt makes outputs partial; evaluate the extraction step separately
Self-generated references make accuracy meaningless
Use human-verified reference outputs

subjective.question: Compare HumanInTheLoopMiddleware on create_agent with a hand-written interrupt() node in a StateGraph for approvals. Which would you pick for an invoice approval flow, and why?
subjective.answer: HumanInTheLoopMiddleware is the quick, standard option. You list tools in interrupt_on with allowed decisions such as approve, edit and reject. The agent pauses before that tool call runs, and the reviewer's decision is applied to the call. It suits agent-style flows where the risky action is a tool call, like send_email. A hand-written interrupt() node in a StateGraph gives full control. You choose exactly where to pause, what payload to show (amount, vendor, PO match), and how to branch on the answer with conditional edges. It suits fixed business processes. For invoice approval, which has set stages and rules like 'over ₹1 lakh needs a finance head', I would use an explicit StateGraph node. With hand-written nodes, the side effects must come after interrupt() and resume must use the same thread_id, because the node re-runs from its start. If the flow is mostly an agent deciding which tools to call, the middleware is simpler and less error-prone.
keyPoints: Middleware: per-tool approve/edit/reject, minimal code
Custom interrupt: custom payload, branching, fixed process stages
Invoice approval with rules suits an explicit StateGraph
Node re-runs on resume: side effects after interrupt, same thread_id

subjective.question: A legal team wants an agent that reviews 40-page vendor contracts, compares clauses with a playbook, and writes a risk memo. Some reviews take many steps. Would you use create_agent or create_deep_agent, and why?
subjective.answer: I would start from create_deep_agent. It comes with a filesystem, summarization, subagents and prompt caching already set up, which is what long, multi-step tasks need. The agent can write extracted clauses and notes to files instead of holding everything in context. It can hand clause-by-clause comparison to subagents. Summarization keeps long sessions inside the context limit, and prompt caching cuts cost when the same playbook prompt is sent again and again. With plain create_agent I would have to put together the same middleware and tools myself. create_agent is the better choice for short, bounded tasks such as extracting five fields from an invoice, where a deep agent only adds overhead and cost. Either way, I would keep human review on the final memo, trace everything in LangSmith, and measure accuracy on a set of contracts annotated by lawyers.
keyPoints: Deep agents pre-assemble filesystem, summarization, subagents and prompt caching
Suits long-running, multi-step work
create_agent for short, bounded tasks
Still evaluate on a labelled dataset and keep human review

subjective.question: Put in order, and justify, the steps to roll out a new prompt or model version of a live automation safely.
subjective.answer: 1. Make the change in code and test it locally with langgraph dev and Studio on a few real cases. 2.
