Run evaluate() on the regression dataset and compare the new experiment with the current production experiment using the same evaluators. Do not continue if accuracy drops. 3. Check cost per item and latency in the experiment traces against the budgets. 4. Deploy the new revision to LangSmith Deployment, ideally to a staging deployment first, with a test cron or a test thread. 5. Promote it to production and watch the online evaluators, error rate and p95 latency. The alerts are already in place. 6. Keep the previous revision ready for rollback. 7. Send new failures to an annotation queue and add the corrected cases to the dataset. Offline evaluation comes first because it is cheap and controlled. Online monitoring comes after because it is the only place real traffic shows up. Rollback is planned before release, not after an incident.
keyPoints: Local test, then offline evaluate() against baseline
Check cost and latency budgets before deploy
Staging, then production, with alerts already on
Rollback plan and a feedback loop into the dataset

subjective.question: After you add new middleware, p95 latency jumps from 20 s to 50 s, while the average rises only a little. How do you diagnose and fix this?
subjective.answer: A big p95 jump with a small change in the average means some runs are much slower, not all of them. In LangSmith I filter production traces by latency above the p95 and open a few. In the trace tree I check which spans are slow. The usual suspects are an extra model call from LLM tool selection, a SummarizationMiddleware call firing on long threads, tool retries backing off, or fallbacks to a slower model. Then I compare slow runs with fast ones: are the slow ones long threads, big documents or a specific tool? Fixes depend on the cause. Raise the summarization trigger or use a smaller summarizer model. Limit the number of retries. Use a faster model for tool selection. Remove middleware that does not pay for itself. I check the fix with an experiment, then watch p95 in monitoring with a latency alert set against the budget.
keyPoints: p95 vs average shows a tail problem
Filter slow traces and inspect spans
Suspect summarization, tool selection, retries, fallbacks
Verify the fix and alert on p95 against the budget

subjective.question: Spot the design mistake. A teammate creates an automation rule on all runs, sampling rate 1.0, with the action 'add to dataset' called invoice-regression, so that 'the regression set grows automatically'.
subjective.answer: This rule copies every production run, including good, bad and duplicate ones, straight into the regression dataset, with no human checking. A regression dataset needs correct reference outputs. Here the references are just whatever the agent produced, so failures get saved as 'expected' answers. Later evaluations then reward the bug. The dataset also grows to thousands of near-identical examples, which makes evaluation slow and costly. A better design has three parts. Filter to interesting runs: low online-evaluator scores (filter on that feedback key so scoring has finished), errors, or negative user feedback. Send those runs to an annotation queue so experts can correct the outputs. Add only the corrected examples to the dataset. Use a sampling rate below 1.0 for healthy traffic, and check the dataset for duplicates from time to time.
keyPoints: Unreviewed outputs become wrong references
Dataset bloat and evaluation cost
Filter on feedback key, errors or negative feedback
Annotation queue first, then the dataset

subjective.question: An interviewer asks: 'What happens in your team when an automation runs out of its error budget?' Give a strong answer.
subjective.answer: Our policy is written down before launch. The automation had a 99% monthly success target, so about 30 failures on 3,000 runs. We had LangSmith alerts on error rate going to Slack, so we saw fast burn early, not at month end. When the budget is close to used up, we stop shipping new features or prompt experiments to that automation. Then we triage failed traces, group them by cause, and fix the biggest group. Examples: adding model fallback for provider outages, tool retry for a flaky ERP API, or a fix for a parsing bug. Each fix is checked against the regression dataset before deploy. Every failure class we fix becomes a dataset example, so it cannot quietly come back. Once the burn rate is normal again, feature work restarts. The budget makes the trade-off between speed and reliability a shared rule, not an argument.
keyPoints: Policy agreed before launch, with a numeric budget
Alerts catch fast burn early
Freeze features, triage traces, fix the top cause
Fallback/retry middleware; regression examples prevent repeats

subjective.question: You set up an online LLM-as-judge evaluator for extraction correctness, but the feedback it writes is empty or nonsensical for every run. How do you troubleshoot?
subjective.answer: First, check the rule's filter and sampling, and confirm it targets the right item type and the right runs. A rule on child runs or the wrong project scores the wrong thing. Next, open a few scored runs and the evaluator's own traces. Look at the exact prompt the judge received. The common cause is a wrong mapping: the judge prompt expects variables such as the input document and the extracted output, but the run's input and output keys are named differently, so the judge sees empty or wrong text. Fix the mapping to the real keys of the run. Then check the rubric. A correctness prompt that expects a reference answer cannot work online, because live runs have no reference, so use a reference-free rubric. Test the evaluator on a handful of runs, and remember backfill only happens when a rule is created.
keyPoints: Check filter, item type and sampling
Inspect evaluator traces for the actual judge prompt
Fix variable mapping to real run input/output keys
Online runs lack references: use a reference-free rubric

subjective.question: Compare a LangSmith alert, an automation rule with a webhook action, and a cron webhook. Which do you use for what in a production automation?
subjective.answer: A LangSmith alert watches aggregate thresholds such as error rate, latency or feedback scores over a time window. It notifies Slack natively, or a webhook. I use it for operational health, for example 'error rate above 5% in 15 minutes'. An automation rule with a webhook acts on individual runs or threads that match a filter, with a sampling rate. I use it for per-item actions, like sending low-scoring extractions to finance. It runs on its own schedule, so I filter on the evaluator's feedback key so it fires only after scoring. A cron webhook is called when a scheduled run is done. I use it for chaining, for example starting the ERP sync after the nightly reconciliation. In short: alerts for system health, rules for per-item quality actions, and cron webhooks for workflow completion. Using one in place of another causes noise or delays.
keyPoints: Alerts: aggregate thresholds, Slack or webhook
Rules: per-run filter, sampling and action; filter on feedback key
Cron webhook: fires on scheduled run completion
Choose by purpose: health vs item quality vs chaining

subjective.question: An older project uses the langgraph-supervisor package, with a separate checkpointer on each worker agent. How would you migrate it, and what mistakes does the current design have?
subjective.answer: langgraph-supervisor is no longer actively maintained, so new work should not depend on it. The current pattern is subagents: one main create_agent whose tools wrap the worker agents. Each worker, such as an extractor or a validator, is built with create_agent and called inside a @tool function that takes a task and returns a short result. The other mistake is giving every worker its own checkpointer. Only the outermost graph should have one. Extra checkpointers add confusing thread state, and they can break interrupt and resume. On LangSmith Deployment the Agent Server provides persistence for the outer graph, so you do not pass your own checkpointer there at all. For the migration, I would first record baseline experiments on the existing dataset. Then I rebuild as subagents, check that accuracy and cost are equal or better, update the graph path in langgraph.json, and redeploy. Each subagent then shows up as a nested span in its traces.
keyPoints: langgraph-supervisor no longer actively maintained
Subagents: main agent with tools wrapping workers
Only the outermost graph gets a checkpointer; Agent Server handles persistence
Baseline evaluation before and after migration

subjective.question: The overdue-invoice digest is now sent twice every weekday morning, and after the last release it went out three times. The CI pipeline runs this setup script after every deploy. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

code.code:
from langgraph_sdk import get_client

async def setup_crons():
    client = get_client(url=DEPLOYMENT_URL)
    await client.crons.create(
        "digest",
        schedule="0 9 * * 1-5",
        input={"task": "send overdue invoice digest"},
        timezone="Asia/Kolkata",
    )

subjective.answer: The script is not idempotent. Every deploy creates another cron with the same schedule, and the old ones keep running, so each release adds one more digest. The cron settings themselves are fine: weekdays, 09:00, Asia/Kolkata. To fix it, first use client.crons.search to list the crons for that assistant, and delete the duplicates so only one is left. Then change the setup so it checks for an existing cron before creating one: if a matching cron exists, update or skip it; otherwise create it. Or keep cron creation out of CI completely and manage it as a one-time, documented operation. I would also set on_run_completed to "keep" for auditability. Then add a check that alerts if more than one digest run happens per day, so this class of bug is caught by monitoring, not by annoyed recipients.
keyPoints: Each deploy creates a new cron; old ones keep firing
Find and delete duplicates with client.crons.search
Make setup idempotent or move it out of CI
Monitor for unexpected run counts
